source_text:
Dolendum profecto illud est et valde deplorandum, hujus nostri seculi sive infortunio sive morbo semper fere accidere, ut ea religionis nostrae mysteria quae sunt ad pacem et solatium animarum promulgata, in solam pene litigandi et pugnandi materiam vertantur. Quis unquam putasset Christi mortem paci sanciendae et perimendis inimicitiis destinatam, ut loquitur Apostolus, Ephes. ii. 14, 17, et Coloss. i. 20, 21, litibus pariendis tam foecundam fieri potuisse? Sed illud evenire videtur innata hominum curiositate, qui magis soliciti esse solent ut arcana Dei consilia scrutentur quam ut beneficia publice oblata amplexentur. Hinc fit, nimium altercando pro quibus Christus mortuus, pro quibus non mortuus statuatur, ut de Christi morte per veram et vivam fidem ad animarum nostrarum salutem nobis applicanda, ab omnibus et singulis parum cogitetur.

Mihi in hoc negotio tractando animus est illam viam inire quae lites potius componat quam litem de lite serat. Cum igitur in confesso sit apud eos qui mortem Christi ad omnes et singulos diffundunt, illam tamen esse quoad fructuosam perceptionem ad certas quasdam personas applicatam; cumque e contra illi qui ad solos electos eandem restringunt, fateantur nihilominus illam omnibus vocatis, imo omnibus hominibus si crederent, profuturam; utraque pars duplicem mortis Christi considerationem videtur agnoscere. Ab utrisque enim consideratur ut universalis causa salutis omnibus et singulis applicabilis, si crederent, et ut specialis causa salutis certis quibusdam personis efficaciter applicata, qui crediderunt. Si de morte Christi sub duplici hac consideratione tractavero, apparebit fortassis in nonnullis de quibus acriter certatur diversos potius loquendi modos quam discrepantes sententias contineri. Revocabo igitur ad breves quasdam et perspicuas theses, primò ea quae de morte Christi ut universali causa salutis omnibus applicabili sunt edisserenda, dein adjungam et alias theses de morte Christi ut speciali causa salutis efficaciter quibusdam applicata, aut saltem suo tempore infallibiliter applicanda.
english: It is indeed to be lamented, and deeply deplored, that by the misfortune or disease of our age it almost always happens that those mysteries of our religion which were published for the peace and comfort of souls are turned nearly into matter for litigation and fighting alone. Who would ever have thought that the death of Christ, appointed for establishing peace and for destroying enmities, as the Apostle speaks ([[Ephesians 2:14-17 >> Bible:Ephesians 2:14-17]]; [[Colossians 1:20-21 >> Bible:Colossians 1:20-21]]), could become so fertile in breeding disputes? But this seems to come about by the innate curiosity of men, who are commonly more eager to pry into the secret counsels of God than to embrace the benefits publicly offered. Hence it happens that, by overmuch disputing for whom Christ died and for whom he did not die, little thought is given by each and all to applying the death of Christ to the salvation of our souls by true and living faith.

In treating this matter my purpose is to enter that path which composes quarrels rather than sows a quarrel upon a quarrel. Since, then, it is confessed among those who extend the death of Christ to each and every person that it is nevertheless applied, as to fruitful reception, to certain particular persons; and since, on the other side, those who restrict the same death to the elect alone still confess that it would profit all who are called — indeed all human beings, if they believed — each side seems to acknowledge a twofold consideration of the death of Christ. For by both it is considered as a universal cause of salvation applicable to each and every person if they believed, and as a special cause of salvation efficaciously applied to certain particular persons who have believed. If I treat the death of Christ under this twofold consideration, it will perhaps appear that in some of the points so fiercely contested there are different manners of speaking rather than discrepant judgments. I will therefore recall the matter to certain brief and clear theses: first those things which are to be set out concerning the death of Christ as a universal cause of salvation applicable to all; then I will add other theses concerning the death of Christ as a special cause of salvation efficaciously applied to some, or at least to be applied infallibly in its own time.

source_text:
Cedamus jam ad institutum nostrum: et primo in loco de morte Christi disseremus uti ea in Scripturis sanctis proponi solet et a nobis considerari debet, nempe uti est remedium quoddam universale a Deo institutum, et toti humano generi ad salutem applicabile. Dein veniemus ad illam alteram partem disputationis nostrae, de morte scilicet Christi quatenus ex speciali decreto Dei est remedium particulare ad certarum personarum salutem efficaciter et infallibiliter applicandum. In priore consideratione mortis Christi variae theses nobis discutiendae occurrent, quarum haec prima est et praecipua, utpote basis reliquarum, quam hisce verbis efformamus:

Mors Christi in sacra Scriptura proponitur ut universale remedium omnibus et singulis hominibus ex ordinatione Dei et natura rei ad salutem applicabile.

Thesis haec primum est explicanda, dein testimoniis et argumentis confirmanda, demum ab objectionibus contrariis vindicanda. Ad explicationem quod attinet, quando mortem Christi nominamus, comprehendimus totam Christi obedientiam, activam et passivam, cujus complementum et quasi actus extremus in ipsa morte fuit: quam ob causam Theologi solent per Synecdochen id morti tribuere quod integrae obedientiae convenit. Quicquid igitur Christus egit, quicquid passus est, a cunabulis usque ad crucem, totum inquam hoc opus Redemptoris satisfactorium et meritorium cum ipsa morte in hac thesi nostra consociandum et copulandum esse intelligimus. Sic Apostolus, Rom. v. 19, obedientiam Christi universaliter sumptam posuit causam salutis humanae: propter obedientiam unius multi justi fiunt. Et Phil. ii. 7, 8, quando dicitur Christus obedientem se praestitisse usque ad mortem crucis, Apostolus non excludit a ratione merendi antecedaneam omnem Christi obedientiam, sed includit potius, atque docet hanc meritoriam Christi obedientiam jam tum incepisse ex quo formam servi accepit, consummatam autem fuisse cum in cruce se obtulit. Sub mortis itaque vocabulo infinitum illum thesaurum meritorum comprehendimus, quem Mediator Dei et hominum, homo Jesus Christus, sive agendo sive patiendo in nostrum usum comparavit et congessit.

Secundò, cum dicimus hanc mortem, sive hoc meritum, in sacris Scripturis proponi ut universalem causam salutis, id volumus: juxta voluntatem Dei in verbo patefactam hoc remedium nullo discrimine cuivis individuo humanae naturae esse propositum ad salutem, prodesse tamen non posse cuilibet ad salutem nisi interveniente speciali applicatione. Nam universalis causa salutis sive universale remedium haec duo involvit: unum, quod ejusmodi sit ut possit omnes et singulos curare et servare; alterum, quod ejusmodi sit ut ad productionem hujus determinati effectus in quolibet singulari homine requirat applicationem determinatam.

Primum testimonium petimus ex Johan. iii. 16: Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum daret, ut omnis qui credit in eum non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Hoc testimonio efficaciter concludimus, Christi mortem esse cuivis homini applicabilem ex ordinatione Dei, et fore applicatam si crediderit in Christum. Detur mihi illud individuum humani generis cui non vere dicat Minister Evangelicus: Sic Deus te dilexit ut Filium suum unigenitum daret, ut si tu in eum credas, non pereas, sed habeas vitam aeternam. Hoc ex certitudine fidei cuivis singulari homini potest annunciari; ergo Christi mors est cuivis homini juxta hanc voluntatem et ordinationem Dei applicabilis.
english: Let us now come to our purpose. And first we will treat of the death of Christ as it is commonly proposed in the Holy Scriptures and ought to be considered by us — namely as a certain universal remedy instituted by God and applicable to the whole human race unto salvation. Then we will come to that other part of our dispute, concerning the death of Christ insofar as, by a special decree of God, it is a particular remedy to be applied efficaciously and infallibly to the salvation of certain persons. In the former consideration of the death of Christ various theses will meet us to be discussed, of which this is the first and principal, as being the basis of the rest, which we form in these words:
The death of Christ is proposed in Holy Scripture as a universal remedy applicable unto salvation to each and every human being by the ordination of God and by the nature of the thing.

This thesis is first to be explained, then confirmed by testimonies and arguments, and finally vindicated from contrary objections. As to the explanation: when we name the death of Christ, we comprehend the whole obedience of Christ, active and passive, whose completion and as it were final act was in the death itself — for which reason theologians commonly attribute by synecdoche to the death what belongs to the whole obedience. Whatever therefore Christ did, whatever he suffered, from the cradle to the cross, this whole satisfactory and meritorious work of the Redeemer we understand is to be joined and coupled with the death itself in this our thesis. So the Apostle ([[Romans 5:19 >> Bible:Romans 5:19]]) set the obedience of Christ taken universally as the cause of human salvation: by the obedience of one many are made righteous. And when it is said that Christ made himself obedient unto the death of the cross ([[Philippians 2:7-8 >> Bible:Philippians 2:7-8]]), the Apostle does not exclude from the ground of meriting all the preceding obedience of Christ, but rather includes it, and teaches that this meritorious obedience of Christ already began when he took the form of a servant, and was consummated when he offered himself on the cross. Under the word death, therefore, we comprehend that infinite treasury of merits which the Mediator of God and men, the man Jesus Christ, whether by doing or by suffering, procured and heaped up for our use.

Secondly, when we say that this death, or this merit, is proposed in the Holy Scriptures as a universal cause of salvation, we mean this: according to the will of God made known in the word, this remedy is proposed without distinction to any individual of human nature unto salvation, yet cannot profit anyone unto salvation unless a special application intervene. For a universal cause of salvation, or a universal remedy, involves these two things: one, that it be of such a kind that it can cure and save each and every person; the other, that it be of such a kind that for producing this determined effect in any singular human being it requires a determined application.

We take the first testimony from ([[John 3:16 >> Bible:John 3:16]]): God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. By this testimony we effectively conclude that the death of Christ is applicable to any human being by the ordination of God, and will be applied if that person believes in Christ. Give me that individual of the human race to whom an evangelical minister cannot truly say: God so loved you that he gave his only-begotten Son, that if you believe in him you should not perish but have eternal life. This can be announced from the certainty of faith to any singular human being; therefore the death of Christ is applicable to any human being according to this will and ordination of God.

source_text:
Scio nonnullos doctos et pios Theologos per mundum hic intelligere mundum sive universitatem electorum, atque nituntur hoc argumento, quod Filius Dei datus dicitur, ut omnis qui credit in eum non pereat: Soli autem electi sunt qui ita in Christum credunt ut non pereant sed vitam aeternam consequantur. Sed respondeo, nihil aliud hinc inferri posse quam mortem Christi solis electis in eventu esse salutiferam, et ipso facto per fidem intervenientem applicatam: non autem fuisse remedium aliis applicabile, et, si credidissent, ex Dei ordinatione applicandum, colligi non potest.

Fac similitudine rem illustrabimus. Fac in urbe aliqua omnes et singulos morbo aliquo epidemico et mortifero laborare: Regem autem ad illos mittere medicum peritissimum pharmaco efficacissimo instructum, atque publice edicere omnes curandos qui hoc pharmaco uti voluerint. Proculdubio de hoc Rege vere dicere possemus, Sic dilexit hanc urbem, ut medicum suum peritissimum ad eam mitteret, ut omnes qui ejus opera et pharmaco uti voluerint, non pereant, sed pristinam valetudinem recuperent. Quod si quis excipiat, hunc medicum missum fuisse solummodo ad eos qui ejus opera utuntur, et pharmacum ejus ex ordinatione Regis fuisse tantum applicabile illis qui illud bibere voluerunt, nae ille et Regis beneficentiam extenuat, et aperte falsum dicit. Nam missus est ad omnes, nulla conditione ex parte missi aut aegrotum prerequisita: instructus etiam fuit pharmaco salutifero omnibus promiscue applicabili: Velle autem medicum admittere et pharmacum ebibere, non ad destinationem medici aut pharmaci spectat, sed ad indubitam sanitatis perceptionem.

Antiqui Patres valde videntur hac similitudine delectati. Prosper ad illam respicit, quando Vincentio objicienti, Quod ex sententia Augustini Dominus noster Jesus Christus non pro omnium hominum salute et redemtione sit passus, respondet, Contra vulnus originalis peccati, quo omnium hominum mortificata est natura, remedium esse mortem Filii Dei. Et paulo post, Poculum hoc immortalitatis habet quidem in se ut omnibus prosit; sed si non bibitur, non medetur. Fides igitur nostra requiritur, non ut Deus dicatur dedisse aut destinasse nobis Filium suum in remedium, sed ut datus et destinatus percipiatur a nobis ad consecutionem vitae aeternae.

Secundum testimonium petitur ex duobus locis conjunctis et inter se collatis. Prior habetur Johan. iii. 17, 18: Non misit Deus Filium suum ut mundum judicet, sed ut mundus per eum servetur. Qui credit in eum, non condemnatur: qui vero non credit, jam condemnatus est, quia non credidit in nomen unigeniti Filii Dei. Hisce verbis addamus et illa Johann. xii. 47, 48: Si quis audierit verba mea, neque crediderit, ego non judico eum: non enim veni ut judicem mundum, sed ut servem mundum. Qui rejicit me, habet qui ipsum judicet; Sermo quem locutus sum ille judicabit eum in novissimo die. Ex hisce habemus Filium Dei a Patre missum, ut apportaret remedium universale toti mundo applicabile: Neque possunt haec verba ad mundum electorum restringi. Primo, quia hic mundus, ad quem servandum Christus missus est, dividitur in credentes et non-credentes: At mundus electorum ex solis credentibus, aut saltem suo tempore credituris, consistit. Secundo, quia condemnandi sunt quidam ex iis ad quos servandos Christus hisce in locis missus affirmatur: At nemo electorum damnabitur. Tertio, quia illi ipsi qui damnandi hoc in loco pronunciantur, damnationem subituri dicuntur ob hoc, quia non crediderunt in unigenitum Dei Filium, vel, quia rejecerunt eum. Quibus loquendi formulis fuisse iis a Deo oblatum et ad eos salvandos missum satis perspicue innuitur. Sed quomodo aut quo sensu recte intelligamus Christum missum ad eos servandos qui suo vitio, hoc est, sua incredulitate, pereunt? Non alio quam in thesi nostra expresso; nimirum, quod mors Christi universalis causa salutis a Deo constituta sit, et cuilibet homini applicabilis sub conditione fidei; quam conditionem isti voluntaria sua malitia sunt aspernati. Non aliter Calvinus haec verba intellexit; qui in Johann. iii. notavit, Mundi nomen iterum iterumque repeti, ne quis omnino arceri se putet, modo fidei viam teneat. Atque in Johann. xii. 47. observavit, Quo plus animi omnes haberent ad resipiscentiam, salutem hic promiscue omnibus offerri. Liquit igitur ex hisce locis Christi mortem proponi et considerari ut remedium ex Dei ordinatione omnibus applicabile ad salutem, etiamsi ab incredulis rejiciatur.

Tertium testimonium proferemus ex Actor. xiii. 38, etc. Notum sit vobis, viri fratres, annunciari vobis remissionem peccatorum per Jesum Christum; et ab omnibus a quibus per legem Mosis absolvi non potuistis, per hunc quemvis qui credat absolvi. Videte, contemtores, et admiramini, etc. Dein versu 46: Postquam repellitis sermonem Dei, et indignos vos ipsos decernitis vita aeterna, ecce convertimur ad gentes. Ex quibus verbis manifestum est, Dei ipsius ordinatione Christum Christique mortem promiscue hominibus proponi et offerri, ut remedium omnibus et singulis applicabile ad consecutionem remissionis et vitae aeternae. Secundo, et illud perspicuum est, ex voluntate et ordinatione Dei hoc remedium fuisse applicabile, non modo illis quibus actu sic applicatum per fidem, sed ipsis contemtoribus, qui repulerunt Christum et vitam aeternam per suam infidelitatem. Denique, et hoc patet vers. 48: ipsam fidem, cujus interventu fit actu applicatum quibusdam quod est Dei decreto applicabile omnibus, ipsorum vitio non reperiri in incredulis, Dei autem miserentis speciali beneficio exoriri in credentibus. Atque hic demum se exserit arcanum electionis, ex cujus intempestiva et nimis alta speculatione non debemus illam philanthropian Dei obruere, ex qua ordinavit et dedit remedium peccatoribus omnibus et singulis applicabile ad salutem, profuturum utique illis solis et omnibus qui crediderint.
english: I know that some learned and godly theologians take “the world” here for the world, or university, of the elect, and they lean on this argument: that the Son of God is said to be given so that everyone who believes in him should not perish; yet only the elect are those who so believe in Christ that they do not perish but obtain eternal life. I answer that nothing more can be inferred from this than that the death of Christ is in the event saving to the elect alone, and is in fact applied through intervening faith. It cannot be gathered that it was not a remedy applicable to others, and to be applied, if they had believed, by God’s ordination.

Let us illustrate the matter by a similitude. Suppose that in some city each and every person is laboring under an epidemic and deadly disease, and that the king sends to them a most skilled physician furnished with a most efficacious medicine, and publicly proclaims that all shall be cured who are willing to use this medicine. Without doubt we could truly say of this king: So he loved this city that he sent his most skilled physician to it, that all who were willing to use his labor and medicine should not perish but recover their former health. If anyone should reply that this physician was sent only to those who use his labor, and that by the king’s ordinance his medicine was applicable only to those who were willing to drink it, that man both diminishes the king’s beneficence and says what is openly false. For the physician was sent to all, with no condition presupposed on the side of the one sent or of the sick; he was also furnished with a saving medicine applicable promiscuously to all. Willingness to admit the physician and to drink the medicine does not belong to the destination of the physician or of the medicine, but to the undoubted perception of health.

The ancient Fathers seem to have delighted greatly in this similitude. Prosper looks to it when, answering Vincent’s objection that on Augustine’s view our Lord Jesus Christ did not suffer for the salvation and redemption of all human beings, he replies that against the wound of original sin, by which the nature of all human beings was mortified, the remedy is the death of the Son of God. And a little later: This cup of immortality has indeed in itself what would profit all; but if it is not drunk, it does not heal. Our faith is therefore required not so that God may be said to have given or destined his Son to us as a remedy, but so that the Son given and destined may be received by us unto the obtaining of eternal life.

The second testimony is drawn from two places joined and compared with each other. The former is ([[John 3:17-18 >> Bible:John 3:17-18]]): God did not send his Son to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him. Whoever believes in him is not condemned; but whoever does not believe is already condemned, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. To these words let us add also ([[John 12:47-48 >> Bible:John 12:47-48]]): If anyone hears my words and does not believe, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world, but to save the world. Whoever rejects me has one who judges him; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day. From these we have that the Son of God was sent by the Father to bring a universal remedy applicable to the whole world. Nor can these words be restricted to the world of the elect. First, because this world, to save which Christ was sent, is divided into believers and unbelievers; but the world of the elect consists of believers alone, or at least of those who will believe in their time. Second, because some of those to save whom Christ is here affirmed to have been sent are to be condemned; yet none of the elect will be damned. Third, because those who are here pronounced to be damned are said to undergo damnation because they did not believe in the only-begotten Son of God, or because they rejected him. By these forms of speech it is sufficiently clearly intimated that he was offered to them by God and sent to save them. But how, or in what sense, are we rightly to understand that Christ was sent to save those who perish by their own fault — that is, by their own unbelief? In no other sense than that expressed in our thesis: namely, that the death of Christ was constituted by God as a universal cause of salvation, and is applicable to any human being under the condition of faith — a condition which those persons by their voluntary malice have despised. Calvin understood these words no otherwise; on ([[John 3 >> Bible:John 3]]) he noted that the name “world” is repeated again and again, lest anyone think himself altogether shut out, provided he holds the way of faith. And on ([[John 12:47 >> Bible:John 12:47]]) he observed that, so that all might have more courage toward repentance, salvation is here offered promiscuously to all. It is therefore clear from these places that the death of Christ is proposed and considered as a remedy applicable to all unto salvation by God’s ordination, even if it is rejected by unbelievers.

We will bring forward a third testimony from ([[Acts 13:38 >> Bible:Acts 13:38]]) and following: Be it known to you, men and brethren, that through this man remission of sins is announced to you; and from all things from which you could not be absolved by the law of Moses, by him everyone who believes is absolved. See, you despisers, and wonder, etc. Then in verse 46: Since you thrust away the word of God and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. From these words it is plain that by God’s own ordination Christ and the death of Christ are proposed and offered promiscuously to human beings as a remedy applicable to each and every person unto the obtaining of remission and eternal life. Second, it is also clear that by the will and ordination of God this remedy was applicable not only to those to whom it is in fact so applied through faith, but even to the despisers themselves, who thrust away Christ and eternal life by their unbelief. Finally, verse 48 also makes plain that faith itself — by whose intervention what is by God’s decree applicable to all is in fact applied to some — is not found in unbelievers by their own fault, but arises in believers by the special benefit of a merciful God. And here at last the secret of election puts itself forth — from whose untimely and too lofty speculation we ought not to overwhelm that philanthropy of God by which he ordained and gave a remedy applicable to each and every sinner unto salvation, a remedy that will indeed profit those alone, and all, who have believed.

source_text:
Quartum testimonium habetur 2 Corinth. v. 19, 20: Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi, non imputando eis peccata ipsorum: et posuit in nobis verbum reconciliationis. Itaque nomine Christi legatione fungimur, velut Deo vos precante per nos: Oramus Christi nomine, reconciliamini Deo. Observandum est primo, Apostolum hoc in loco ponere commune beneficium toti mundo hanc quam vocat reconciliationem ab ipso Deo mediante Christo procuratam. At sane reconciliasse mundum promiscue, nil aliud denotat, quam universale illud remedium sive propitiatorium mortis Christi sacrificium, quod est omnibus applicabile, ordinasse et mundo concessisse. Secundo observare oportet quo sensu Deus mundum reconciliasse sibi dicitur ipso facto merito oblationis Christi, nempe quod posito hoc Christi sacrificio, non imputet illis peccata, hoc est, non exigat ab ullo homine ut pro peccatis suis ipse satisfaciat (quod est impossibile) neque ultra velit quenquam punire pro peccatis suis qui hoc sacrificio propitiatorio utetur. Denique et illud notandum est, hanc reconciliationem, hanc non-imputationem peccatorum, de qua loquitur Apostolus, peractam considerari ex parte Dei et Christi, simulac Christus pro peccatis mundi animam posuisse intelligitur: At ex parte hominum peccatorum, restat ministerium Evangelii per quod testetur hominibus, restat ut Evangelio credatur priusquam homines quasi in actualem possessionem hujus gratiae deducantur. Et ob hoc subjunxit Apostolus, postquam dixerat Deum in Christo mundum reconciliasse, nihilominus oportere ministros fungi legatione sua, et hortari quosvis ut ipsi reconcilientur Deo. Ex quibus omnibus liquet, quod in thesi nostra posuimus, Christi mortem a Deo ordinatam et ab Apostolis praedicatam ut remedium ex voluntate Dei omnibus applicabile ad reconciliationem et salutem, quamvis ut homines reconcilientur ipso actu, opus sit resipiscentia et fide praecedente.

Sic Aquinas hunc locum intellexit: Reconciliemini Deo — videtur, inquit, hoc esse contrarium ei quod dixit, Deus nos reconciliavit sibi: Si enim ipse reconciliavit, quid necesse est ut nos reconciliemus? jam enim reconciliati sumus. Ad hoc dicendum, quod Deus nos reconciliavit sibi, ut causa efficiens, scilicet, ex parte sua; sed ut sit nobis meritoria, oportet etiam quod fiat reconciliatio ex parte nostra. Sed clarissime totum hunc locum explicavit Musculus, cujus verba apponere non pigebit: Deus, inquit, omne humanum genus, quod inde ab initio ad finem usque mundi fuit, et est, et erit, sibi reconciliavit, dum Filium in mortem pro omnibus dedit. Dein paucis interjectis, Atqui sibi in Christo Deus reconciliavit, non imputans eis peccata ipsorum, quantum attinet ipsum reconciliationis opus toti generi humano reconciliando paratum, et sufficiens. Verum quoniam reconciliatio inter invitos locum habere non potest, institutum est ab ipso Deo ministerium reconciliationis, quo cuncti ad hanc gratiam cupide amplexandam vocentur et invitentur. Hanc si totus mundus amplexaretur, utique totus mundus omni peccatorum imputatione rejecta cum Deo reconciliaretur ac salvaretur, nec periret mortalium quisquam. Qui igitur praedestinationis arcano ita toti incumbunt et inhaerent ut interim obruant et plane evertant hanc mundi reconciliationem, evertunt simul Evangelicae nostrae praedicationis materiam, quae in hoc potissimum sita est, quod quemvis hominem certiorem facimus, Deum esse illi per mortem Christi sic reconciliatum, ut si in Christum credat, non sit illi imputaturus peccata, sed vitam aeternam adjudicaturus. Hoc opus ex Dei et Christi parte stabilitum vocatur reconciliatio et redemtio mundi, quamvis increduli et impoenitentes nolint reconciliari et redimi. Sic loquitur Prosper ad Capit. Gallor. object. 9: Redemtor mundi dedit pro mundo sanguinem suum, et mundus redimi noluit. Sic loquitur Ecclesia nostra Anglicana, Artic. 31: Oblatio Christi semel facta perfecta est redemtio, propitiatio et satisfactio pro omnibus peccatis totius mundi tam originalibus quam actualibus; Neque est alia satisfactio praeter illam. Sic denique loquitur Paulus, quando dicit, Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi: Hoc est, Deus, dando Filium suum in mortem, ipse suppeditavit inimicis suis asylum reconciliationis, ad quod, quisquis tandem ille sit, qui confugerit, habet ejus beneficio Deum adeo pacatum et reconciliatum ut protinus illum in gratiam sit recepturus.

Quintum testimonium petitur ex epistola ad Hebraeos, cap. 2. vers. 3. et cap. 4. vers. 1, 2, etc.: Quomodo nos effugiemus, si tantam neglexerimus salutem? quae quamprimum enarrari coepit per ipsum Dominum, ab iis qui ipsum audierunt fuit nobis confirmata, etc. Metuamus igitur ne quando derelicta promissione introeundi in requiem ejus, videatur aliquis ex vobis fuisse frustratus. Etenim vobis evangelizatum est, sicut et illis: at non profuit illis auditus sermo, ut qui fide contemperatus non fuerit ipsis qui audierant. Ex toto hoc discursu Apostoli patet primo, in Evangelio offerri promiscue salutem omnibus illis quibus praedicatur; nam ob hanc ipsam causam euangelion nominatur. Dein liquet, hanc salutem in Christo repositam, et in Evangelio hominibus oblatam, a multis negligi et repelli; nimirum ab omnibus incredulis qui promissionibus Evangelicis fidem non adhibent. Denique constat et illud, hanc neglectionem et incredulitatem esse veram causam quae impios arceat a requie Domini, hoc est, quae privet eos vita aeterna in Christo illis oblata. At nihil horum vere et serio dici posset, nisi praesupponatur quod salus per mortem Christi sit ex ordinatione Dei omnibus hominibus applicabilis. Quis enim recte dicatur neglexisse salutem, id est, causam salutis a Deo constitutam et paratam, quae nunquam fuit illi parata, constituta aut applicabilis? Aut quomodo haec neglectio et incredulitas excludit eos a participatione salutis oblatae in Christo, qui erant ob defectum ordinationis Divinae omnibus modis ab ea exclusissimi? Concedamus ergo oportet aliquam Dei ordinationem, juxta quam Christus, ut causa salutis, fuit illis ipsis applicabilis qui suo vitio salute exciderunt.

Ultimum testimonium ex illis locis conglobatis depromitur in quibus voluntas Christi morientis ad omnium salutem procurandam extensa declaratur. Hujusmodi sunt, 2 Cor. v. 15: Unus pro omnibus mortuus est. 1 Tim. ii. 6: Semetipsum dedit redemtionis pretium pro omnibus. Heb. ii. 9: Beneficio Dei pro omnibus mortem gustavit. et 1 Johann. ii. 2: Et propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, nec pro nostris solum, sed etiam pro totius mundi peccatis. Mitto reliqua. Haec et consimilia loca quamvis non valeant ad inferendam illam conclusionem quorundam Remonstrantium, Hac nempe morte Christi acquisitam sive impetratam esse reconciliationem et remissionem peccatorum omnibus et singulis hominibus, vel, Omnes et singulos homines ipsa morte Christi in statum gratiae et salutis esse restitutos, tamen satis efficaciter probant quod nos intendimus, mortem hanc Christi ab ipso Deo et Christo constitutam et ordinatam fuisse in universalem causam salutis, vel universale remedium omnibus hominibus ad reconciliationem et remissionem obtinendam applicabile. Non igitur video quo jure aut qua necessitate Theologi nonnulli hujusmodi loca, in quibus Christus diserte affirmatur pro omnibus passus, ad solos electos sive ad solam universitatem electorum restringunt, cum sensu praedicto ad alios quoslibet verissime extendantur. Nihil enim impedit quin ex aliqua ordinatione Divina sit applicabile omnibus, quod ex praedestinatione Divina sit infallibiliter applicandum solis electis. Collocutores Hagenses mihi videntur hoc ipsum sub aliis loquendi formulis concessisse. Nam illud Remonstrantium Dogma, Christum non pro solis electis, sed pro aliis etiam hominibus mortuum fuisse, si de sola sufficientia meritorum Christi intelligatur, concedunt; sed, si intelligatur de efficaci, sive actuali parta reconciliatione, negant. Hoc mihi satis est: Nam solam illam sufficientiam mortis Christi quoad omnes nunquam recte tuebuntur, nisi illam omnibus, secundum aliquam viam a Deo constitutam, ex ordinatione Dei ad salutem applicabilem simul fateantur. Sufficienter siquidem pro omnibus mortuus inepte et falso asseritur, qui pro solis electis mortuus affirmatur; cum vocabulum illud sufficienter non sit terminus diminuens, nec rei affirmatae veritatem perimat. Sed hac de re plura dicentur, cum ad secundam nostram thesin perventum fuerit. Hactenus pugnavimus Scripturae testimoniis. Deinceps texemus rationes quasdam in Scripturis satis (ut nobis videtur) solide fundatas.
english: The fourth testimony is found in ([[2 Corinthians 5:19-20 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 5:19-20]]): God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their sins to them; and he placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore we discharge an embassy in Christ’s name, as though God were beseeching you through us: We pray in Christ’s name, be reconciled to God. First it is to be observed that the Apostle here sets down as a common benefit to the whole world this reconciliation which he says was procured by God himself through the mediation of Christ. But to have reconciled the world promiscuously denotes nothing other than to have ordained and granted to the world that universal remedy, or propitiatory sacrifice of Christ’s death, which is applicable to all. Second, we must observe in what sense God is said to have reconciled the world to himself by the very fact of the merit of Christ’s offering — namely, that this sacrifice of Christ being posited, he does not impute sins to them: that is, he does not require of any human being that he himself make satisfaction for his sins (which is impossible), nor does he any longer will to punish anyone for his sins who will use this propitiatory sacrifice. Finally it is also to be noted that this reconciliation, this non-imputation of sins of which the Apostle speaks, is considered as already accomplished on the part of God and of Christ as soon as Christ is understood to have laid down his life for the sins of the world; but on the part of sinful human beings there remains the ministry of the Gospel, by which it is testified to human beings, and there remains that the Gospel must be believed before human beings are brought, as it were, into actual possession of this grace. And for this reason the Apostle added, after saying that God had reconciled the world to himself in Christ, that ministers must nonetheless discharge their embassy and exhort any and all to be themselves reconciled to God. From all of which it is clear what we posited in our thesis: that the death of Christ was ordained by God and preached by the Apostles as a remedy applicable to all unto reconciliation and salvation by the will of God, even though, for human beings to be reconciled in actual fact, preceding repentance and faith are needed.

So Aquinas understood this place: “Be reconciled to God” — this seems, he says, contrary to what he said, “God reconciled us to himself”: for if he himself reconciled, what need is there that we be reconciled? We are already reconciled. To this it must be said that God reconciled us to himself as efficient cause, namely on his own part; but that it may be meritorious for us, reconciliation must also be made on our part. But Musculus explained this whole place most clearly, and his words it will not be tedious to set down: God, he says, reconciled to himself the whole human race, which from the beginning to the end of the world was, and is, and will be, when he gave the Son unto death for all. Then after a few words interposed: Yet God reconciled them to himself in Christ, not imputing their sins to them, so far as concerns the very work of reconciliation prepared and sufficient for reconciling the whole human race. But because reconciliation cannot take place between unwilling parties, God himself instituted the ministry of reconciliation, by which all are called and invited eagerly to embrace this grace. If the whole world embraced it, the whole world would certainly be reconciled to God and saved, with every imputation of sins rejected, and not one of mortals would perish. Those therefore who so wholly lean upon and cling to the secret of predestination that meanwhile they overwhelm and plainly overturn this reconciliation of the world, at the same time overturn the matter of our evangelical preaching, which consists chiefly in this: that we make any human being certain that God is so reconciled to him through the death of Christ that, if he believes in Christ, God will not impute sins to him but will adjudge eternal life to him. This work, established on the part of God and of Christ, is called the reconciliation and redemption of the world, even though unbelievers and the impenitent refuse to be reconciled and redeemed. So Prosper speaks, answering the Chapters of the Gauls, objection 9: The Redeemer of the world gave his blood for the world, and the world refused to be redeemed. So our Church of England speaks, Article 31: The offering of Christ once made is a perfect redemption, propitiation, and satisfaction for all the sins of the whole world, both original and actual; and there is no other satisfaction besides that. So finally Paul speaks when he says that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself: that is, God, by giving his Son unto death, himself supplied to his enemies a refuge of reconciliation, to which whoever at length takes refuge has God, by its benefit, so pacified and reconciled that he will at once receive him into grace.

The fifth testimony is drawn from the Epistle to the Hebrews, ([[Hebrews 2:3 >> Bible:Hebrews 2:3]]) and ([[Hebrews 4:1-2 >> Bible:Hebrews 4:1-2]]) and following: How shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? which began first to be declared by the Lord himself, and was confirmed to us by those who heard him, etc. Let us therefore fear lest, the promise of entering into his rest being left, any of you should seem to have come short. For the gospel was preached to you as well as to them; but the word heard did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in those who heard. From this whole discourse of the Apostle it is plain, first, that in the Gospel salvation is offered promiscuously to all those to whom it is preached; for on this very account it is called euangelion. Next it is clear that this salvation laid up in Christ and offered to human beings in the Gospel is neglected and thrust away by many — namely by all unbelievers who do not give faith to the evangelical promises. Finally this also is established: that this neglect and unbelief is the true cause that keeps the ungodly from the Lord’s rest — that is, that deprives them of the eternal life offered to them in Christ. But none of these things could truly and seriously be said unless it be presupposed that salvation through the death of Christ is, by God’s ordination, applicable to all human beings. For who can rightly be said to have neglected salvation — that is, a cause of salvation constituted and prepared by God — which was never prepared, constituted, or applicable to him? Or how does this neglect and unbelief exclude from participation in the salvation offered in Christ those who, for want of a divine ordination, were in every way most shut out from it? We must therefore concede some ordination of God according to which Christ, as a cause of salvation, was applicable even to those who by their own fault fell short of salvation.

The last testimony is drawn from those places gathered together in which the will of Christ in dying is declared to have been extended to procuring the salvation of all. Of this sort are ([[2 Corinthians 5:15 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 5:15]]): One died for all; ([[1 Timothy 2:6 >> Bible:1 Timothy 2:6]]): He gave himself a ransom for all; ([[Hebrews 2:9 >> Bible:Hebrews 2:9]]): By the grace of God he tasted death for all; and ([[1 John 2:2 >> Bible:1 John 2:2]]): And he is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world. I pass over the rest. These and similar places, although they do not avail to infer that conclusion of certain Remonstrants — namely, that by this death of Christ reconciliation and remission of sins have been acquired or obtained for each and every human being, or that each and every human being has by the very death of Christ been restored into a state of grace and salvation — yet they prove sufficiently effectively what we intend: that this death of Christ was constituted and ordained by God himself and by Christ as a universal cause of salvation, or a universal remedy applicable to all human beings unto obtaining reconciliation and remission. I do not therefore see by what right or necessity some theologians restrict places of this kind, in which Christ is expressly affirmed to have suffered for all, to the elect alone or to the mere university of the elect, when in the sense aforesaid they most truly extend to any others whatever. For nothing hinders that what by divine predestination is to be applied infallibly to the elect alone should, by some divine ordination, be applicable to all. The Collocutors of the Hague seem to me to have conceded this very thing under other forms of speech. For that Remonstrant dogma, that Christ died not for the elect alone but also for other human beings, they concede if it is understood of the mere sufficiency of Christ’s merits; but if it is understood of an efficacious, or actually wrought, reconciliation, they deny it. This is enough for me: for they will never rightly maintain that mere sufficiency of Christ’s death with respect to all, unless they also confess that by God’s ordination it is applicable to all unto salvation according to some way constituted by God. For he is absurdly and falsely asserted to have died sufficiently for all who is affirmed to have died for the elect alone; since that word “sufficiently” is not a diminishing term, nor does it destroy the truth of the thing affirmed. But more will be said of this matter when we reach our second thesis. Thus far we have contended by the testimonies of Scripture. Next we will weave certain reasons grounded, as it seems to us, solidly enough in the Scriptures.

source_text:
Cujus mors fructus aliquos spirituales affert etiam illis qui non servantur, illa non est applicabilis solis electis: Christi autem mors affert fructus nonnullos etiam non-salvandis. Ad Majoris intelligentiam clariorem illud jam suggero, quod monui ab initio, Sub nomine mortis Christi nos totum illum cumulum meritoriae Christi obedientiae complecti, cui ipsa mors ejus extremam quasi clausulam imposuit. Hoc enim infinitum Mediatoris Christi meritum, illud est quod Deus Pater adspicit, quando perditis et miseris mortalibus beneficium quodcunque spirituale gratificatur in ordine ad salutem aeternam. Si igitur illud constiterit, etiam non-electos ex merito Christi percipere ejusmodi quaedam beneficia, tum clarum erit, mortem Christi, quoad aliquos saltem effectus, non modo applicabilem esse omnibus hominibus promiscue, sed ipso facto quibusdam non-salvandis applicatam.

Ad Minoris igitur probationem, quae sola in dubium venire potest, accedamus. Primo, hoc ipsum quod Deus dignatur multos etiam ex non-electis ad poenitentiam ac fidem, et sub fidei conditione ad vitam aeternam vocare, quaero, annon magni beneficii loco sit habendum? Habetur profecto ab ipso Deo, qui Evangelii praedicationem sermonem vitae appellat, Johann. vi. 68, Act. v. 20; gratiam Dei salutiferam, Tit. ii. 11; Qui Christum pati et resurgere oportuisse dicit, ut praedicaretur in nomine ejus resipiscentia ac remissio peccatorum apud omnes gentes, Luc. xxiv. 46, 47; Qui denique hanc ipsam annunciationem Evangelii thesaurum vocat, 2 Cor. iv. 7, et ipsos pedes evangelizantium speciosos pronunciat, Rom. x. 15, et summi supplicii loco ejus ablationem minitatur, Matth. xxi. 43, Eosque gravissime puniendos statuit qui tantum hoc bonum spreverunt et repulerunt, Luc. x. 12, 13, etc. et 2 Thess. i. 8. Haec omnia ostendunt Evangelium esse beneficium supernaturale concessum etiam iis qui eodem abutuntur.

Secundo, si quis praefracte negaret ipsius Evangelii annunciationem esse beneficium a Deo concessum quoad non-electos, tamen illam mentis illustrationem, doni caelestis gustationem, supernaturalium donorum aliquam communicationem, quorum mentio facta est, Hebr. vi., esse magna et praeclara beneficia, idque in ordine non ad hanc corporalem sed illam spiritualem vitam collata, nemo negaverit: At haec omnia saepenumero dantur iis qui non sunt e numero electorum: dantur autem per et propter Christum: Nam de ejus plenitudine omnes accepimus, Johann. i. 16, et Unicuique data est gratia secundum mensuram donationis Christi, Ephes. iv. 7. Imo de donis supernaturalibus quibuscunque recte dicamus cum Apostolo, omnia haec effecit unus et idem Spiritus, distribuens singulis sicut vult, 1 Cor. xii. 11. Jam adjungam et illud, Quicquid supernaturalis gratiae datur per Christum cuilibet homini, id datur ex merito Christi: Nam Christus nihil tale hominibus confert, quod obedientia sua non iisdem prius promeruit. Sic Bernardus, Serm. 13. in Cantic.: Quicquid sapientiae, quicquid virtutis te habere confidis, Dei Virtuti, Dei Sapientiae deputa Christo. Origo fontium et fluminum mare est; virtutum et scientiarum, Dominus Jesus Christus. Ambrosius magis generatim, Omne donum gratiae Dei in Christo est, In Ephes. i.

Denique, vel illud evincit, ex sententia saltem omnium antiquorum, Christi mortem esse ex ordinatione Dei applicabilem etiam non-electis, quod expresse docuerunt in Baptismo illam applicari ad remissionem originalis peccati cuivis infanti baptizato. Est hic eximius et supernaturalis effectus mortis Christi, de cujus applicatione ad non-praedestinatos in Ecclesia antiqua minime fuit dubitatum, ne ab illis quidem qui absolutam praedestinationem arctissime tenebant. Testis ad hanc rem valde locuples est ipse Prosper, Resp. 2. ad Capit. Gallor. et Sentent. 2. super eodem Capitulo. Cui addere licet Patres Africanos, in Epistola sua Synodica, et Concilium Valentinum, Canone 5. Primo igitur hoc argumento obtinemus, vim meritoriam mortis Christi non esse ad solos electos restringendam: sed applicabilem esse aliis ex ordinatione Dei, et quoad certos effectus aliquando actu applicatam.
english: That death whose fruit brings some spiritual benefits even to those who are not saved is not applicable to the elect alone; but the death of Christ does bring some fruits even to those who will not be saved. For a clearer understanding of the Major I now suggest what I warned from the beginning: under the name of the death of Christ we embrace that whole heap of Christ’s meritorious obedience, to which his very death set the last closing clause, as it were. For this infinite merit of the Mediator Christ is what God the Father looks upon when he grants to lost and miserable mortals any spiritual benefit whatever in order to eternal salvation. If therefore it shall be established that even the non-elect receive certain benefits of this kind from the merit of Christ, then it will be clear that the death of Christ, at least as to some effects, is not only applicable promiscuously to all human beings, but is in fact applied to certain persons who will not be saved.

Let us therefore come to the proof of the Minor, which alone can come into doubt. First, this very thing — that God deigns to call many even of the non-elect to repentance and faith, and under the condition of faith to eternal life — I ask, is it not to be counted a great benefit? It is certainly so counted by God himself, who calls the preaching of the Gospel the word of life ([[John 6:68 >> Bible:John 6:68]]; [[Acts 5:20 >> Bible:Acts 5:20]]); the saving grace of God ([[Titus 2:11 >> Bible:Titus 2:11]]); who says that Christ had to suffer and rise again, that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations ([[Luke 24:46-47 >> Bible:Luke 24:46-47]]); who finally calls this very announcement of the Gospel a treasure ([[2 Corinthians 4:7 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 4:7]]), pronounces the very feet of those who preach the gospel beautiful ([[Romans 10:15 >> Bible:Romans 10:15]]), and threatens its removal with the place of the highest punishment ([[Matthew 21:43 >> Bible:Matthew 21:43]]), and decrees that those who have despised and thrust away so great a good are to be punished most severely ([[Luke 10:12-13 >> Bible:Luke 10:12-13]]; [[2 Thessalonians 1:8 >> Bible:2 Thessalonians 1:8]]). All these things show that the Gospel is a supernatural benefit granted even to those who abuse it.

Second, if anyone should stubbornly deny that the announcement of the Gospel itself is a benefit granted by God with respect to the non-elect, yet no one will deny that that illumination of the mind, tasting of the heavenly gift, and some communication of supernatural gifts, of which mention is made in ([[Hebrews 6 >> Bible:Hebrews 6]]), are great and excellent benefits, and that they are conferred in order not to this bodily but to that spiritual life. Yet all these are often given to those who are not of the number of the elect; and they are given through and on account of Christ. For of his fullness we have all received ([[John 1:16 >> Bible:John 1:16]]), and to each one grace was given according to the measure of the gift of Christ ([[Ephesians 4:7 >> Bible:Ephesians 4:7]]). Indeed of supernatural gifts of whatever kind we may rightly say with the Apostle that one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills ([[1 Corinthians 12:11 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 12:11]]). I will also add this: whatever supernatural grace is given through Christ to any human being is given from the merit of Christ; for Christ confers nothing of this kind on human beings which he did not first merit for them by his obedience. So Bernard, Sermon 13 on the Song: Whatever wisdom, whatever virtue you trust yourself to have, ascribe to the Virtue of God, the Wisdom of God — to Christ. The origin of fountains and rivers is the sea; of virtues and sciences, the Lord Jesus Christ. Ambrose more generally: Every gift of the grace of God is in Christ (commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians).

Finally, this at least, on the judgment of all the ancients, proves that the death of Christ is by God’s ordination applicable even to the non-elect: that they expressly taught that in Baptism it is applied to the remission of original sin for any baptized infant. This is an excellent and supernatural effect of the death of Christ, concerning whose application to the non-predestinate there was scarcely any doubt in the ancient Church — not even among those who held absolute predestination most tightly. A very ample witness to this matter is Prosper himself (Response 2 to the Chapters of the Gauls, and Sentence 2 on the same Chapter). To him one may add the African Fathers in their Synodical Letter, and the Council of Valence, Canon 5. By this first argument, therefore, we obtain that the meritorious power of Christ’s death is not to be restricted to the elect alone, but is applicable to others by God’s ordination, and as to certain effects is sometimes in fact applied.
