Nam si amare sit bona velle alteri, tum majora bona velle est magis amare. Ad hunc autem modum se habuit Christi morientis amor erga electos et non-electos: nam ex unica et eadem morte plura et majora bona voluit ad illos, quam ad istos pervenire.
english: Obj. 14. If we posit that Christ died for all, it will follow: 1. That Christ pursued all human beings with supreme and greatest love ([[John 15:13 >> Bible:John 15:13]]): Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends. And ([[1 John 3:16 >> Bible:1 John 3:16]]): By this we have known the love of God, that he laid down his life for us. Which does not seem so, because he does not lead all to life by this death of his. 2. What is a corollary of this, that Christ equally loved Peter and Judas, the elect and the non-elect: For he would have exhibited to all the token of supreme love; but in the supreme there are no degrees. 3. Finally, if Christ so died for all that by this death of his he procured for the non-elect only the possibility of salvation under the condition of faith, or a remedy merely applicable, which he knows will not be applied, but for the elect the very application and salvation — he would seem to have loved the non-elect more than the elect, because it is of greater love to suffer death for someone in order that he may obtain some minute good than a great one; just as that man would show a more ardent love toward someone who exposed himself to death lest the other be ever so slightly hurt, than if he did it lest he be punished with death.

Sol. The aim of both places is the same, namely to kindle Christians to mutual and most tender love by the example of our Savior Jesus Christ, who so loved us that he endured to die for us. But the sense of the words here is that to undergo death, or to pour out one’s life for another, is the greatest external effect and the most evident proof of love — which, when Christ has exhibited toward us by laying down his life for us, we too ought, where need is, to lay down our lives for the brethren, as is had in the aforesaid place ([[1 John 3:16 >> Bible:1 John 3:16]]). It is therefore not enough that we be ready to spend gold and silver for the brethren, to undergo hard labors or dangers, because there is still a greater love — that is, a greater, surer, and clearer proof of our love — namely that we lay down our soul, that is, our life, for them. And because nothing is dearer to each than himself, therefore by this attestation of love, by which someone spends himself for a friend, there is no greater. I now come closer to the solution, and I say: Although we confess that no one has greater love — that is, can from his own side put forth a greater external effect of his love — than by laying down life, because each has nothing more precious than his life; yet we deny that it is rightly deduced from this that the love of one dying for some is absolutely, simply, and in every way, as regards all those, the supreme and greatest that anyone can conceive in his heart. For first, where one lays down life for many, nothing hinders that as to the internal act of loving he may love one more vehemently than another: as if we should think that Jacob underwent death for freeing all his sons from captivity, we would nevertheless rightly assert that he did not love all supremely, but Joseph and Benjamin above the others, and more than the others. Supreme love as to intention, therefore, cannot be inferred with respect to all to whom this greatest judgment of love is exhibited. Second, someone can pour out life promiscuously for many, and yet as to the magnitude of the good willed love some more intensely than others, and accordingly not embrace all with supreme or equal love. For the magnitude of love is not to be estimated only from the side of the precious thing which is spent on the beloved by the lover, but from the side of the benefits which are intended to be conferred on the beloved from that spent thing. For example: If a King’s son should undergo death for all guilty of treason, this law being set, that all and each be absolved who are willing to cast themselves as suppliants before the King’s throne and to pledge faithful obedience for the future; and if for certain ones he should further intend to obtain from the Father that, for the merit of his death, he deign to persuade them of this submission and obedience, and so persuaded not only to absolve them but even to raise them to the highest honors — who does not see that death was endured for all, and yet that all were not loved supremely and maximally? For since to love is to wish and confer goods on someone, once a common benefit granted to many is posited, those are more loved to whom greater goods from the aforesaid benefit are intended and conferred. Finally, although human beings cannot exhibit to human beings a greater external testimony of love than if someone die for another, yet God the Father, Christ the Mediator God-man, and the Holy Spirit can exhibit a greater secret act and effect of their love toward some of those for whom Christ died than toward others; namely if they establish not only to give to certain ones remission of sins and eternal life from the merit of Christ’s death, provided they believe in this their Redeemer, but also from eternity elect certain ones to life to be participated efficaciously in Christ the Redeemer, and prepare for them and infallibly give all those things which effect this infallible participation and application. From these you see that that inference does not hold: Christ died for all; Therefore he loved all with supreme and equal love: because, this common benefit of his death being granted to all, he can nevertheless love some more intently than others, and decree, prepare, and give to some more and greater goods from the merit of his death than to others. Which is clear even in the elect themselves, for all of whom all confess that Christ suffered, and yet no one will have affirmed that Christ embraces with equal love anyone (so to speak) from the common run of the elect and the Patriarchs, Apostles, or his most blessed mother, or enriches them with equal gifts of grace and glory overflowing from the merit of his death. But that other subtlety by which it is inferred, If Christ had undergone death for all, he would have shown greater love toward the non-elect than toward the elect, because it argues greater love to sustain death for someone to obtain for him some minute good than a great one, seems to me little agreeable to right reason. If diverse deaths were to be undergone for diverse persons, this objection would have some appearance of truth: but where a single death is sustained for diverse persons, there it is plain that he is more loved for whom the one who dies intends more and greater goods from this single death. For if to love is to will goods to another, then to will greater goods is to love more. But in this way the love of Christ dying stood toward the elect and the non-elect: for from one and the same death he willed more and greater goods to come to the former than to the latter.

source_text:
Obj. 15. Media sapienter destinata finem adaequatum non excedunt: At finis adaequatus mortis Christi est salus electorum: Ergo mors Christi nullam habet ordinationem ad alios quosvis non-electos: Ergo falso statuitur ex ordinatione Dei omnibus hominibus applicabilis.

Sol. Agnosco infallibilem salutem electorum esse, sub gloria Dei, finem quendam specialem et eximium cui consequendo mors Christi destinabatur: Nego tamen fuisse unicum aut solum finem. Deus enim misit in mundum Filium suum, eumque mori voluit, non modo ut efficaciter salvaret electos, sed etiam ut remissio peccatorum et vita aeterna hominibus quibuscunque in Evangelio generaliter afferri posset et etiam conferri, si crederent. Hoc autem pactum generale sive conditionale stabilitum haud intelligitur, nisi mors Christi ex ordinatione Dei omnibus hominibus applicabilis praesupponatur, et cuivis quamprimum crediderit actu applicanda. Hunc finem Scriptura clare indicavit multis in locis: Johan. iii. 14, 15. Sicut Moses exaltavit serpentem in deserto, ita exaltari oportet Filium hominis, ut omnis qui credit in ipsum non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Et Johan. vi. 40. Haec est voluntas Patris mei qui misit me, ut omnis qui videt Filium et credit in eum, habeat vitam aeternam. Act. x. 43. Huic omnes Prophetae testimonium perhibent, remissionem peccatorum accipere per nomen ejus, omnes qui credunt in eum. Mitto reliqua. Ex hisce satis liquet, utcunque non omnes sed soli electi credant, Deo ipsorum corda specialiter emolliente, tamen mortem Christi ita Deo Patri per Filium oblatam, ita etiam a Deo Patre hominibus indiscriminatim oblatam, ita a Ministris Evangelicis promiscue omnibus annunciatam, ut quivis inde colligat esse firmam et stabilem quandam Dei ordinationem, juxta quam mors Christi ad omnes homines pertineat. Hanc ordinationem sua infidelitate non-electi faciunt sibi inutilem: at non faciunt ut talis ordinatio pro nulla habeatur, aut quoad hosce incredulos morte Christi minime stabilita agnoscatur. Nam si hoc admittamus, quivis incredulus posset obtendere, Etiamsi ego credidissem Evangelio, non fuissem morte Christi a peccatis liberandus, quia mors Christi nullam habuit ordinationem juxta quam ego ejusdem particeps esse potuissem. Quod e diametro adversatur verbis ipsius Christi, Johan. iii. 17, 18. Non misit Deus Filium suum in mundum, ut condemnet mundum, sed ut servetur mundus per eum. Qui credit in eum, non condemnatur: qui vero non credit, jam condemnatus est, quia non credidit in nomen unigeniti Filii Dei. Atque hoc est quod sanctus Prosper, Mors Christi habet quidem in se ut omnibus prosit; sed si non bibitur, non medetur. Quod in se habeat ut omnibus prodesse possit, id habet ex generali ordinatione Divina: quod autem a multis per fidem non bibatur, id accidit ex communi infidelitate humana: quod ab aliquibus bibatur, id provenit ex speciali miseratione Divina.
english: Obj. 15. Means wisely destined do not exceed their adequate end: But the adequate end of Christ’s death is the salvation of the elect: Therefore Christ’s death has no ordination to any other non-elect whatever: Therefore it is falsely established as applicable to all human beings by God’s ordination.

Sol. I acknowledge that the infallible salvation of the elect is, under the glory of God, a certain special and outstanding end for attaining which Christ’s death was destined: Yet I deny that it was the unique or sole end. For God sent his Son into the world, and willed him to die, not only that he might efficaciously save the elect, but also that remission of sins and eternal life might be generally offered to any human beings whatever in the Gospel, and even conferred, if they believed. But this general or conditional covenant is not understood as established unless Christ’s death by God’s ordination is presupposed applicable to all human beings, and to be applied in fact to anyone as soon as he has believed. Scripture has clearly indicated this end in many places: ([[John 3:14–15 >> Bible:John 3:14]]): As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. And ([[John 6:40 >> Bible:John 6:40]]): This is the will of my Father who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life. ([[Acts 10:43 >> Bible:Acts 10:43]]): To him all the Prophets bear witness, that through his name everyone who believes in him receives remission of sins. I pass over the rest. From these it is plain enough that, although not all but the elect alone believe, God specially softening their hearts, yet Christ’s death was so offered by the Son to God the Father, so also offered indiscriminately by God the Father to human beings, so announced promiscuously to all by Evangelical ministers, that anyone may gather from this that there is a certain firm and stable ordination of God according to which Christ’s death pertains to all human beings. The non-elect by their unbelief make this ordination useless to themselves: but they do not make such an ordination to be counted as nothing, or to be acknowledged as by no means established by Christ’s death as regards these unbelievers. For if we admit this, any unbeliever could plead, Even if I had believed the Gospel, I would not have been freed from sins by Christ’s death, because Christ’s death had no ordination according to which I could have been partaker of it. Which is diametrically contrary to the words of Christ himself ([[John 3:17–18 >> Bible:John 3:17]]): God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but that the world might be saved through him. Whoever believes in him is not condemned; but whoever does not believe is already condemned, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. And this is what holy Prosper says: The death of Christ has indeed in itself what would profit all; but if it is not drunk, it does not heal. That it has in itself what can profit all, it has from the general Divine ordination: but that it is not drunk by many through faith, happens from common human unbelief: that it is drunk by some, comes from special Divine pity.

source_text:
Obj. 16. Absurdum est ponere Christi mortem ex ordinatione Divina esse λύτρον applicabile illis quibus non sit applicata; quia in ipsa morte Christi fuit firmissima applicatio mortis pro iis omnibus pro quibus mortuus et passus vere affirmatur: Ergo Christi mors non est ordinatum a Deo remedium, nisi singularibus quibusdam personis electis et Deo soli notis, quibus tandem quoad eventum sit salutifera.

Sol. Negamus quicquam absurdi inesse praedictae sententiae, quam veram et Divinae sapientiae consentaneam demonstravimus. Quod autem objicitur, Quoad omnes pro quibus Christus mortuus est, in ejusdem Christi morte includi quoque infallibilem mortis applicationem, id nobis non videtur concedendum. Nam oblatio Christi in se nude considerata id universim a Deo impetrat et obtinet, ut omnes et singuli qui in Christum credere voluerint salventur. Hanc mortis Christi efficaciam toti mundo Evangelium praedicat et pollicetur: at infallibile illud propositum applicandi hanc mortem his aut illis personis Evangelici praecones non possunt cuiquam mortalium nominatim polliceri. Dicimus mortem Christi esse iis omnibus ordinatam quibus potest annunciari remissio peccatorum per fidem in sanguine ejus: quae gratia ad quemlibet humanae naturae participem spectat. At mortem Christi infallibiliter applicandam solis electis fatemur; quia certitudo applicationis pendet, tanquam ex primaria causa, ab arcano et aeterno actu Dei praedestinantis, non a solo facto Christi seipsum pro hominibus offerentis. Habuit igitur Christus in seipso offerendo generalem intentionem ordinationi Paternae conformem, nempe ut quosvis homines indiscriminatim, modo in eum crederent, a peccatorum reatu liberaret, et hoc sensu pro omnibus seipsum dicitur obtulisse. Habuit etiam, ut conscius praedestinationis Divinae, specialem intentionem arcano et aeterno Patris beneplacito conformem, nempe ut ovibus juxta electionis decretum sibi dandis ex merito mortis suae impetraret atque donaret fidem, salutem, omnia: et cum hac speciali intentione pro populo suo peculiari, id est, pro singularibus quibusdam personis, dicitur vitam suam posuisse. Quod quibusdam ex morte Christi obvenit per specialem actum Divinae praedestinationis, non debet illud evertere quod omnibus est acquisitum per ipsum actum oblationis. Anne infallibilis applicatio potius praedestinationi adscribatur; at quod mors Christi sit omnibus et singulis per fidem applicabilis, ipsi oblationi ex tenore pacti Divini assignetur.
english: Obj. 16. It is absurd to posit that Christ’s death by Divine ordination is a lytron applicable to those to whom it is not applied; because in Christ’s death itself there was the firmest application of the death for all those for whom he is truly affirmed to have died and suffered: Therefore Christ’s death is not a remedy ordained by God except for certain singular elect persons known to God alone, to whom at length as to the event it is saving.

Sol. We deny that anything absurd inheres in the aforesaid opinion, which we have demonstrated to be true and agreeable to Divine wisdom. But what is objected — That as regards all for whom Christ died, an infallible application of the death is also included in that same death of Christ — does not seem to us to be conceded. For Christ’s offering considered in itself nakedly obtains and gets from God this universally, that all and each who have been willing to believe in Christ are saved. The Gospel preaches and promises this efficacy of Christ’s death to the whole world: but that infallible purpose of applying this death to these or those persons evangelical heralds cannot promise by name to any mortal. We say that Christ’s death is ordained for all those to whom remission of sins through faith in his blood can be announced: which grace looks to any participant of human nature. But we confess that Christ’s death is to be applied infallibly to the elect alone; because the certainty of application depends, as from a primary cause, on the secret and eternal act of God predestinating, not on the sole fact of Christ offering himself for human beings. Christ therefore in offering himself had a general intention conforming to the Father’s ordination, namely that he might indiscriminately free any human beings whatever, provided they believed in him, from the guilt of sins, and in this sense he is said to have offered himself for all. He also had, as conscious of Divine predestination, a special intention conforming to the Father’s secret and eternal good-pleasure, namely that for the sheep to be given to him according to the decree of election he might from the merit of his death obtain and give faith, salvation, all things: and with this special intention he is said to have laid down his life for his peculiar people, that is, for certain singular persons. What comes to certain ones from Christ’s death through a special act of Divine predestination ought not to overturn what was acquired for all through the very act of offering. Let infallible application rather be ascribed to predestination; but that Christ’s death is applicable to all and each through faith, let it be assigned to the offering itself from the tenor of the Divine covenant.

source_text:
Obj. 17. Ultima objectio petitur ex eis locis in quibus mors Christi expresse refertur ad certas quasdam personas: ex quibus inferunt, Ad alias non spectare. Loca quibus nituntur haec sunt, Matth. i. 21. Vocabis nomen ejus Jesum: Ipse enim servabit populum suum a peccatis suis. Johan. x. 15. Ego pono animam meam pro ovibus meis. Johan. xi. 51, 52. Jesus moritur, ut filios Dei dispersos cogeret in unum, et consimilia.

Sol. Ex praedictis testimoniis aliisque consimilibus bene concluditur mortem Christi, ex voluntate Dei Filium mittentis, et Filii seipsum offerentis, speciali quodam modo ad populum illum peculiarem Deo soli notum, id est, ad electos, pertinere. Specialis autem ille modus est hujusmodi, ut non pro hisce solis mortuus dicatur, sed pro hisce solis mortuus cum proposito certo, aeterno, gratuito eosdem infallibiliter salvandi, per specialis misericordiae gratiam a speciali quadam providentia, quam Praedestinationem appellamus, dimanantem. Ex testimoniis autem ejusmodi quae mortem Christi referunt ad certas personas, non simpliciter consideratam, sed cum arcanae praedestinationis decreto complicatam, male infertur hanc mortem generali quodam modo ad omnes homines minime pertinere. Generalis autem hic modus est ejusmodi, ut pro toto humano genere agnoscamus Christum fuisse mortuum cum pacto Evangelico, eodemque firmissimo de expiandis peccatis et vita aeterna conferenda omnibus et singulis hominibus modo hunc mundi Redemptorem vera fide amplectantur. Atque hinc est quod licet in sacris Scripturis occurrant loca nonnulla in quibus Christus pro electis sive pro populo suo peculiari mortuus dicatur, nulla tamen occurrunt in quibus pro ullis hominibus mortuus negetur, plurima in quibus pro omnibus mortuus afferatur. Voluit nempe Spiritus Dei speciale privilegium electorum in morte Christi ipsis fidelibus insinuare, noluit tamen commune jus humani generis in eadem Christi morte silentio obruere. Nostrum est igitur relinquere Deo occultae suae praedestinationis decretum, juxta quod statuit quousque et quibus vult hanc mortem Christi per specialis gratiae donationem efficaciter applicare; atque interim gratis animis agnoscere revelati Evangelii summam, quod promulgat Unum pro omnibus mortuum, ut quisquis credat in eum, habeat vitam aeternam. In hanc sententiam Ambrosius, Etsi Christus pro omnibus passus est, specialiter tamen pro nobis passus est, quia pro Ecclesia passus est, In Luc. lib. 6. cap. 7. Atque hactenus primam nostram thesin explicatam vobis dedimus, confirmatam, et a contrariis objectionibus vindicatam. Haesimus diutius in ejus tractatione, quia (ut dictum est) Caput rei continet, et viam aperit ad reliquas enodandas, in quibus disceptandis erimus multo breviores. Ad secundam igitur thesin deveniamus.
english: Obj. 17. The last objection is drawn from those places in which Christ’s death is expressly referred to certain particular persons: from which they infer that it does not look to others. The places on which they rely are these: ([[Matthew 1:21 >> Bible:Matthew 1:21]]): You shall call his name Jesus: for he himself will save his people from their sins. ([[John 10:15 >> Bible:John 10:15]]): I lay down my life for my sheep. ([[John 11:51–52 >> Bible:John 11:51]]): Jesus dies, that he might gather into one the children of God who were scattered, and the like.

Sol. From the aforesaid testimonies and others like them it is well concluded that Christ’s death, by the will of God sending the Son and of the Son offering himself, pertains in a certain special manner to that peculiar people known to God alone, that is, to the elect. But that special manner is of this kind: not that he is said to have died for these alone, but that he died for these alone with a certain, eternal, gratuitous purpose of saving them infallibly, through the grace of special mercy flowing from a certain special providence which we call Predestination. But from testimonies of that kind which refer Christ’s death to certain persons, not considered simply, but complicated with the decree of secret predestination, it is wrongly inferred that this death in a certain general manner by no means pertains to all human beings. But this general manner is of such a kind that we acknowledge Christ to have died for the whole human race with the Evangelical covenant, and that most firm one, concerning the expiating of sins and the conferring of eternal life on all and each human beings provided they embrace this Redeemer of the world with true faith. And hence it is that although in the sacred Scriptures some places occur in which Christ is said to have died for the elect or for his peculiar people, yet none occur in which he is denied to have died for any human beings, and very many in which he is affirmed to have died for all. For the Spirit of God willed to intimate to the faithful themselves the special privilege of the elect in Christ’s death, yet he did not will to overwhelm in silence the common right of the human race in that same death of Christ. It is ours therefore to leave to God the decree of his hidden predestination, according to which he has established how far and to whom he wills to apply this death of Christ efficaciously through the gift of special grace; and meanwhile with grateful minds to acknowledge the sum of the revealed Gospel, which proclaims One dead for all, that whoever believes in him should have eternal life. In this sense Ambrose: Although Christ suffered for all, yet he suffered specially for us, because he suffered for the Church (On Luke, book 6, chapter 7). And thus far we have given you our first thesis explained, confirmed, and vindicated from contrary objections. We have lingered longer in treating it, because (as was said) it contains the Caput of the matter, and opens the way to unraveling the rest, in discussing which we shall be much briefer. Let us therefore come to the second thesis.

source_text:
CAPUT IV. Thesis secunda proponitur, explicatur, stabilitur.

In prima nostra thesi conati sumus ostendere mortem sive meritum Christi a Deo constitutum, in sacris scripturis propositum, et a nobis considerandum tanquam remedium universale omnibus hominibus ad salutem ex ordinatione Dei applicabile. Atque hanc ob causam non dubitamus asserere Christum pro omnibus hominibus fuisse mortuum, quatenus mortem sustinuit cujus merito et virtute omnes et singuli mortales Evangelio obedientes possint a morte liberari, et salutem aeternam adipisci. Verum quia nonnulli ita concedunt Christum pro omnibus mortuum, ut eodem spiritu asserant, pro solis electis mortuum, et receptam Theologorum distinctionem, Pro omnibus mortuus est sufficienter, pro praedestinatis efficaciter, ita exponant, ut prius illud membrum plane exstinguant; nos secundam thesin apponemus quae occasionem praebebit ex instituto ea de re disputandi, quam hactenus obiter et leviter tantum perstrinximus. Secunda igitur haec thesis in hanc formam redigetur. Si paulo prolixior sit, ignoscite. Mors Christi universalis causa salutis humanae, et ipse Christus pro omnibus hominibus sufficienter mortuus agnoscitur, non ratione nudae sufficientiae sive intrinseci valoris, juxta quem mors Dei est pretium mille mundis redimendis plusquam sufficiens, sed ratione foederis Evangelici merito mortis hujus cum toto humano genere stabiliti, et ordinationis Divinae inde dependentis, juxta quam, sub possibili fidei conditione, remissio peccatorum et vita aeterna propter merita Christi mortui cuivis homini credituro exhibenda decernitur.

In hac thesi tractanda duo faciemus: Primo, quosdam terminos qui opus habent explicatione enodabimus. Secundo in membra quaedam partiemur hanc thesin nostram, eademque sigillatim confirmabimus aliquot argumentis.

Primo igitur in loco explicandum occurrit quid velimus per nudam sufficientiam, quid per illud, quod communiter a Theologis admittitur, Christum pro omnibus mortuum sufficienter. Si de redemtionis pretio loquamur, illud lytron esse sufficiens agnoscendum est quod ex aequo respondet captivi debito, vel quod facit satis ejus postulato penes quem potestas est hujus captivi liberandi. Aequalitas sive rei ad rem, sive ad postulata ejus qui Dominium habet in captivum, constituit hanc quam vocamus sufficientiam nudam. Exemplis hoc illustrabitur. Fac fratrem meum in carcere detentum ob debitum mille librarum. Si mihi in arca sint repositae totidem librae, vere affirmare possum, Hoc argentum est sufficiens ad dissolvendum debitum fratris mei illumque aere alieno liberandum. Veruntamen dum pro illo nondum offertur nuda rei sufficientia intelligitur, et ex solo valore aestimatur, deficiente adhuc actu offerendi illud ipsum lytron, absque quo nihil efficit praedicta sufficientia. Pari ratione, si multi ob crimen laesae majestatis capite damnentur, atque ipse Rex in quem hoc crimen admissum fuit paciscatur se velle omnibus reconciliari pro quibus Filius suus dignetur mortem subire: jam mors Filii ex pacto constitutum est lytron sufficiens pro omnibus redimendis pro quibus offeretur: at si qui sint pro quibus illud lytron nondum offeratur, quoad eos habet solummodo nudam et meram sufficientiam, quae ex rei valore in se considerato cogitatur, non autem illam quae ex actu offerentis intelligitur. Hisce addo: Si admittamus praedictum lytron, non modo sufficiens esse ex aequalitate rei ad rem, et ex ejus postulato qui nihil ultra requirit in redemtionem captivorum, sed etiam infinitis gradibus esse majus et melius, atque exsuperare omnia debita eorum, tamen si non accedat animus et actus offerendi pro quibusdam captivis, licet sit tale lytron quantumvis copiosum et superabundans, si spectetur in se et ex interno suo valore, tamen quod de sufficientia dictum fuit, idem de superabundantia dicatur, esse meram superabundantiam rei, nihil autem adhuc pro praedictis personis liberandis effecisse.

Jam huic sufficientiae merae, quae nihil aliud respicit quam aequalem vel superabundantem pretii signati dignitatem ad rem redimendam, oppono aliam, quam perspicuitatis causa appellabo sufficientiam ordinatam. Ea autem intelligitur, quando illa res quae habet rationem lutri sive pretii redemtorii, non modo aequivalet aut dignitate superat rem redimendam, sed insuper ex voluntate et actu aliquo offerentis ad eam redimendam ordinatur. Sic mille talenta in aerario Principis recondita dicantur sufficiens lytron ad redimendos decem cives ab hoste captos; verum si non accedat animus et actus offerendi et dandi haec talenta pro hisce captivis, aut pro aliquibus eorum, quoad illos pro quibus non datur sufficientia rei mera, non ordinata, supponitur. Adde vero actum et animum ea offerendi pro liberatione certarum personarum, et tum demum quoad illas solas ordinata sufficientia asseritur. Porro, haec ordinata sufficientia lytri ad redemtionem captivi duplex esse potest: Absoluta; quando inter illum qui dat et illum qui accipit hoc redemtionis pretium pro liberatione captivorum, ita convenit, ut simulac pretium solvatur, ipso facto solutionis captivi illico liberentur. Conditionata; quando pretium acceptatur, non ut statim solvatur, et libertati restituatur captivus, sed ut liberetur sub conditione, si hoc aut illud prius fecerit. Quando dicimus Christum pro omnibus mortuum sufficienter, non meram rei sufficientiam cum defectu oblationis quoad majorem hominum partem, sed sufficientiam illam ordinatam intelligimus, quae conjunctum habuit animum et actum offerentis, idque pro omnibus, sed conditionata illa, quam expressimus, non absoluta ordinatione. Uno verbo, quando affirmamus Christum pro omnibus mortuum sufficienter id volumus: Tum fuisse in ipsa hostia sufficientiam sive aequivalentiam, imo superabundantiam, pretii sive dignitatis, si comparetur ad totum humanum genus; tum in offerente atque acceptante fuisse ordinationem quandam, juxta quam praedicta hostia ad redemtionem omnium hominum fuit oblata et acceptata. Haec ad primi termini explicationem sufficiant.
english: Cap. 4. Thesis 2 is proposed, explained, and established. In our first thesis we tried to show that Christ’s death or merit, constituted by God, set forth in the sacred Scriptures, and to be considered by us, is a universal remedy applicable to all human beings unto salvation by God’s ordination. And for this reason we do not hesitate to assert that Christ died for all human beings, inasmuch as he underwent a death by whose merit and power all and each mortal who obeys the Gospel can be freed from death and obtain eternal salvation. But because some so concede that Christ died for all that with the same breath they assert he died for the elect alone, and so explain the received distinction of the Theologians — He died for all sufficiently, for the predestinate efficaciously — that they plainly extinguish the former limb, we will add a second thesis that will furnish occasion for disputing the matter on purpose, which until now we have only lightly touched in passing. This second thesis, then, will be cast in this form (pardon it if somewhat long): The death of Christ is acknowledged as the universal cause of human salvation, and Christ himself as having died sufficiently for all human beings, not by reason of a bare sufficiency or intrinsic value, according to which the death of God is a price more than sufficient for redeeming a thousand worlds, but by reason of the Evangelical covenant stabilized by the merit of this death with the whole human race, and of the Divine ordination depending thereon, according to which, under the possible condition of faith, remission of sins and eternal life are decreed to be exhibited, for the merits of the dead Christ, to any human being who will believe.

In treating this thesis we will do two things: First, we will untie certain terms that need explanation. Second, we will partition this thesis of ours into certain members and confirm them one by one with several arguments. First, then, it falls to be explained what we mean by bare sufficiency, and what by that which is commonly admitted by Theologians, that Christ died sufficiently for all. If we speak of the price of redemption, that lytron is to be acknowledged sufficient which answers equally to the captive’s debt, or which satisfies the demand of him in whose power it is to free this captive. Equality, whether of thing to thing, or to the demands of him who has dominion over the captive, constitutes what we call bare sufficiency. This will be illustrated by examples. Suppose my brother is held in prison for a debt of a thousand pounds. If I have as many pounds laid up in my chest, I can truly affirm, This silver is sufficient to dissolve my brother’s debt and free him from the debt. Yet so long as it is not yet offered for him, a bare sufficiency of the thing is understood, and it is estimated from value alone, while the act of offering that very lytron is still lacking, without which the aforesaid sufficiency effects nothing. By like reason, if many are condemned to death for the crime of treason, and the King himself against whom the crime was committed covenants that he is willing to be reconciled to all for whom his Son deigns to undergo death: already the Son’s death is by pact constituted a sufficient lytron for redeeming all for whom it shall be offered; but if there are any for whom that lytron is not yet offered, as to them it has only a bare and mere sufficiency, which is thought from the thing’s value considered in itself, not that which is understood from the offerer’s act. I add: even if we admit that the aforesaid lytron is not only sufficient by equality of thing to thing and by the demand of him who requires nothing further for redeeming captives, but is also greater and better by infinite degrees and exceeds all their debts, yet if the mind and act of offering for certain captives do not accompany it, although such a lytron be ever so copious and superabundant when viewed in itself and from its internal value, still what was said of sufficiency must be said of superabundance: it is a mere superabundance of the thing, and has as yet effected nothing for freeing the aforesaid persons.

To this mere sufficiency, which looks to nothing else than an equal or superabundant dignity of the appointed price for the thing to be redeemed, I oppose another, which for clarity’s sake I will call ordained sufficiency. That is understood when the thing that has the character of a lutron or redeeming price not only equals or by dignity surpasses the thing to be redeemed, but is moreover ordained to redeem it by some will and act of the offerer. Thus a thousand talents stored in a Prince’s treasury may be called a sufficient lytron for redeeming ten citizens captured by an enemy; but if the mind and act of offering and giving these talents for these captives, or for some of them, do not accompany it, as to those for whom it is not given a mere, not ordained, sufficiency of the thing is supposed. But add the act and mind of offering them for freeing certain persons, and then at last ordained sufficiency is asserted as to those alone. Further, this ordained sufficiency of the lytron for redeeming a captive can be twofold: Absolute, when between the one who gives and the one who receives this redeeming price for freeing captives it is so agreed that as soon as the price is paid, by the very fact of payment the captives are at once freed. Conditioned, when the price is accepted not that the captive be at once paid for and restored to liberty, but that he be freed under a condition, if he first does this or that. When we say that Christ died sufficiently for all, we understand not a mere sufficiency of the thing with a defect of oblation as to the greater part of human beings, but that ordained sufficiency which had joined to it the mind and act of the offerer, and that for all, yet by that conditioned, not absolute, ordination which we have expressed. In a word, when we affirm that Christ died sufficiently for all, we mean this: that there was in the victim itself a sufficiency or equivalence, indeed a superabundance, of price or dignity if compared to the whole human race; and that in the offerer and the accepter there was a certain ordination according to which the aforesaid victim was offered and accepted for the redemption of all human beings. Let this suffice for explaining the first term.

Secundo et illud explicandum est, quod in thesi positum fuit, scilicet merito praedictae mortis Christi esse novum quoddam foedus sancitum inter Deum et genus humanum. Per hoc foedus intelligimus illud quod urgetur ab Apostolo Galat. iii. Crede, et vives, et apponitur legali, Hoc fac et vives. Haec ipsa pactio, quae salutem cuilibet peccatori promittit sub conditione fidei, non habet alibi fundamentum et firmamentum suum, quam in sanguine Mediatoris: absque quo effuso ne credendo quidem ullus mortalium possit ad vitam aeternam aspirare. Morte autem Christi a Deo in lytron acceptata, jam fas est nullo discrimine cuivis homini adscendere in caelum credendo, ut ostendit Apostolus Rom. iii. 21-26, et ipse Christus Marc. xvi. 15, Abite, etc. In hoc igitur foedere Evangelico morte Christi stabilito, quod Apostoli toti mundo divulgarunt, et Ministri Evangelici etiamnum praedicant, nulla personarum ratio habetur. Tam Esavus servabitur, si crediderit in Messiam, quam Jacobus: tam Jacobus damnabitur, si non crediderit, quam Esavus. Veruntamen fatendum est, aliam quoque esse Dei ordinationem arcanam et absolutam, certas quasdam et definitas personas spectantem, et in morte Christi etiam fundatam, quae Novi foederis nomen sortitur. Sed hoc potius inter Deum Patrem et Christum quam inter Deum et nos pactum intelligitur. Est autem illud quod commemoratur a Propheta Isaia, Isa. liii. 10, Si posuerit pro peccato animam suam, semen longevum videbit: et explanatur ab Apostolo Hebr. viii. 10. Hoc est foedus quod paciscar, etc. Indam leges meas menti eorum, et cordi eorum inscribam eas, etc. quasi dixisset, Christum morte sua non modo stabilivisse illud foedus conditionatum quod omnibus et singulis hominibus promulgari potest sub hac formula, Si credideris, quisquis es, per mortem Christi servabere; sed etiam illud arcanum et absolutum de fide donanda quibusdam hominibus, eisdemque per et propter Christum infallibiliter servandis. Notandum autem est, hoc posterius foedus soli Christo notum esse, nec posse per Ministros Christi, quoad singulares personas quas complectitur, cuiquam patefieri. Ipsi enim Apostoli potuerunt, et nos possumus, cuivis homini praedicare foedus illud conditionatum et revelatum, Si credideris, salvus eris; at nec ipsi potuerunt, neque nos possumus, cuivis infallibiliter promittere, Tuus es ex illis quos Deus dedit Christo Mediatoris, quosque per et propter Christum fide perseverante donabit, et ad vitam aeternam infallibiliter perducet. Hoc enim perinde esset ac si profiteremur nos fuisse Deo a consiliis ante jacta mundi fundamenta, et posse electos ac non-electos digito demonstrare. Absque hoc posteriore foedere quod magis proprie inter Deum et Mediatorem, quam inter Deum et Homines stabilitum intelligitur, illud prius conditionatum humana improbitate et infidelitate in omnibus hominibus irritum foret, et ille pretiosus atque infiniti meriti sanguis in inane difflueret. Veruntamen quia, ut dictum est, Solus Deus novit eos ad quos hoc foedus spectat, nostrum est illud prius conditionatum foedus, nobisque revelatum, urgere et premere: atque hoc illud est quod morte Christi cum toto humano genere stabilitum defendimus. Denique et illud observandum est. Licet foedus illud conditionatum non actu divulgetur singulis hominibus, tamen esse ejusmodi quod divulgari et annunciari possit cuivis mortali: licet singuli non sibi vendicent jus suum in hoc foedus, neminem tamen esse cui non liceat merito mortis Christi hoc sibi promittere et ex pacto vendicare, Si credidero, salvus ero. Est quoad omnes et singulos stabilitum, sed speciali quadam providentia Dei rem gubernante hisce revelatum et annunciatum, illis minime.

Restat tertio in loco ut explicetur quod in thesi positum fuit de ordinatione Divina ex praedicto foedere dependente, juxta quam remissio peccatorum et vita aeterna sub possibili fidei conditione cuivis homini exhibenda decernitur. Atque hic illud unicum eget explicatione, quod affirmamus fidei conditionem esse unicuique possibilem. Hoc igitur nolumus ita intelligi, quasi unusquisque haberet in se naturale principium intrinsecum et proportionatum ad eliciendum actum verae et vivae fidei. Fuit enim hoc Fausti Rhegiensis et Semipelagianorum error, qui fidem libero arbitrio adscribunt, et donum credulitatis illi quasi naturaliter congenitum et infixum somniant. Huc spectant illa Fausto dicta, lib. 2. De lib. arbitr. cap. 6. Vides bonum credulitatis non novellum esse privilegium sed vetus, et inter ipsa mundi coalescentis exordia mentem hominis sicut intellectu et ratione, ita etiam fide a summo auctore donatam. Et ne quis putet hoc donum fidei in homine lapso amissum, paulo post addit cap. 7. Generale hoc fidei donum virtutis sectatorem quemlibet speciali in se studio excolere. Plura vide in hanc sententiam. Illud. Quamvis ergo fidem appellet donum, innuit tamen esse donum naturale et generale, atque quemvis posse viribus liberi arbitrii hunc actum credendi elicere. Sed hoc nos toto pectore aversamur, neque huc respicimus, dicendo fidei conditionem esse possibilem. Porro, neque hanc possibilitatem credendi fundamus in dono aliquo supernaturali ab omnibus recepto. Non enim audemus sustinere dari omnibus et singulis gratuita auxilia et sufficientia ad actum credendi expromendum; quandoquidem ipsa Scriptura sacra clare docet fidem esse speciale donum Dei. Illud igitur relinquitur, ut cum doctissimo Bannezio possibilitatem hujus conditionis praestandae fundemus neque in dono aliquo naturali et innato, neque in dono supernaturali et ab omnibus recepto, sed in dono supernaturali a viatore quocunque possibiliter recipiendo, secundum legem ordinariam, ut Schola loquitur. Hisce ita expositis et constitutis, divellam nunc thesin praedictam in tria membra, quae seorsim rationibus allatis confirmabo.
english: Second, that also must be explained which was set down in the thesis, namely that by the merit of the aforesaid death of Christ a certain new covenant has been sanctioned between God and the human race. By this covenant we understand that which is urged by the Apostle in ([[Galatians 3:11 >> Bible:Galatians 3:11]]): Believe, and you shall live, and is set over against the legal, Do this and you shall live. This very pact, which promises salvation to any sinner under the condition of faith, has its foundation and firmament nowhere else than in the Mediator’s blood: without which poured out, not even by believing could any mortal aspire to eternal life. But when Christ’s death has been accepted by God as a lytron, it is now lawful without distinction for any human being to ascend into heaven by believing, as the Apostle shows in ([[Romans 3:21–26 >> Bible:Romans 3:21]]) and Christ himself in ([[Mark 16:15 >> Bible:Mark 16:15]]), Go, etc. In this Evangelical covenant, then, stabilized by Christ’s death, which the Apostles published to the whole world and Evangelical ministers still preach, no respect of persons is had. Esau will be saved, if he believes in the Messiah, as much as Jacob; Jacob will be damned, if he does not believe, as much as Esau. Yet it must be confessed that there is also another ordination of God, secret and absolute, looking to certain definite persons, and founded also in Christ’s death, which receives the name of the New Covenant. But this is understood rather as a pact between God the Father and Christ than between God and us. It is that which is recalled by the prophet Isaiah ([[Isaiah 53:10 >> Bible:Isaiah 53:10]]): If he shall have set his soul for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed; and is explained by the Apostle ([[Hebrews 8:10 >> Bible:Hebrews 8:10]]): This is the covenant that I will make, etc. I will put my laws in their mind and write them on their heart, etc. — as if to say that by his death Christ not only stabilized that conditioned covenant which can be promulgated to all and each under this formula, If you believe, whoever you are, you will be saved through Christ’s death, but also that secret and absolute one concerning faith to be given to certain human beings, and those same to be saved infallibly through and on account of Christ. It is to be noted, however, that this latter covenant is known to Christ alone, and cannot through Christ’s ministers be made plain to anyone as to the singular persons it embraces. For the Apostles themselves could, and we can, preach to any human being that conditioned and revealed covenant, If you believe, you will be saved; but neither they could, nor can we, promise anyone infallibly, You are of those whom God gave to Christ the Mediator, and whom through and on account of Christ he will gift with persevering faith and lead infallibly to eternal life. For that would be as if we professed we had been of God’s counsel before the foundations of the world were laid, and could point out elect and non-elect with the finger. Without this latter covenant, which is more properly understood as stabilized between God and the Mediator than between God and human beings, that former conditioned one would by human wickedness and unbelief be void in all human beings, and that precious blood of infinite merit would flow away into emptiness. Yet because, as has been said, God alone knows those to whom this covenant looks, it is ours to urge and press that former conditioned covenant revealed to us: and that is what we defend as stabilized by Christ’s death with the whole human race. Finally this too is to be observed. Although that conditioned covenant is not actually published to each human being, yet it is of such a kind that it can be published and announced to any mortal: although individuals do not claim their right in this covenant for themselves, yet there is no one to whom it is not lawful, by the merit of Christ’s death, to promise this to himself and claim it from the pact, If I believe, I will be saved. It is stabilized as to all and each, but by a certain special providence of God governing the matter it is revealed and announced to these, not to those.

It remains third to explain what was set down in the thesis concerning the Divine ordination depending on the aforesaid covenant, according to which remission of sins and eternal life are decreed to be exhibited to any human being under the possible condition of faith. And here that one point needs explanation, that we affirm the condition of faith to be possible for each one. We do not want this so understood as if each one had in himself a natural intrinsic principle proportioned to eliciting an act of true and living faith. For that was the error of Faustus of Riez and the Semi-Pelagians, who ascribe faith to free choice and dream that the gift of believing is as it were naturally inborn and fixed in it. To this look those words of Faustus, On Free Choice, book 2, chapter 6: You see that the good of believing is not a novel privilege but an old one, and that from the very beginnings of the coalescing world the human mind was gifted by the highest Author with faith as with intellect and reason. And lest anyone think this gift of faith lost in fallen man, a little later he adds chapter 7: Let any pursuer of virtue cultivate in himself by special study this general gift of faith. See more in that sense. Although therefore he calls faith a gift, he still hints that it is a natural and general gift, and that anyone can elicit this act of believing by the powers of free choice. But this we wholly abhor, and we do not look to it when we say the condition of faith is possible. Further, neither do we found this possibility of believing in some supernatural gift already received by all. For we do not dare to maintain that gratuitous and sufficient helps for bringing forth the act of believing are given to all and each; since sacred Scripture itself clearly teaches that faith is a special gift of God. It remains, then, that with the most learned Báñez we found the possibility of performing this condition neither in some natural and innate gift, nor in a supernatural gift received by all, but in a supernatural gift possibly to be received by any wayfarer, according to the ordinary law, as the School speaks. These things thus set out and established, I will now divide the aforesaid thesis into three members, which I will confirm separately with reasons brought forward.

1. Mera sufficientia mortis Christi, quae ex solo valore intrinseco hujus lutri aestimatur, absque illa ordinata sufficientia quae ex animo et actu offerendi oritur, non eo valet ut Christus vere dicatur pro omnibus mortuus sufficienter. Hanc thesin apponendam putavi propter eos qui arcte tenent Christum pro solis electis mortuum fuisse, et tamen (quod ego fateor me tardiorem esse quam ut intelligam) admittunt Christum pro omnibus mortuum sufficienter; atque hanc rem, sufficientiam ad omnes homines sese diffundentem, verbis aliquando valde exitollunt. Fatentur siquidem Christum pro omnibus hominibus, pro omnibus hominum ordinibus, statibus, generibus, imo etiam pro singulis hominibus quoad sufficientiam meritorum mortuum fuisse. Veteravitii in Judicio Dordracenae Synodo exhibito sic scribunt, Quando Christus dicitur pro omnibus mortuus, hoc intelligi potest de meriti sufficientia, seu pretii magnitudine. Mors quippe Filii Dei est unicum perfectum et sufficiens lytron expiandis et delendis omnibus totius mundi peccatis: meritum immensum justitiae, medicina catholica mortis, fons perennis vitae, etc. Paulo post, Haec sufficientia lytri, quantum ad reprobos, geminum habet finem, unum per se, alterum per accidens. Finis per se, ut Deus testatum faciat se non delectari perditione hominum, utpote qui Filium suum unigenitum dederit, ut omnis qui credit in eum non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Finis per accidens ut hac sufficientia lytri reddantur inexcusabiles. Hi enim non Christi sed sua culpa pereunt, quando per infidelitatem suam beneficia a Christo in Evangelio oblata repudiant. Hactenus illi. Hanc sufficientiam mortis Christi pro omnibus reconciliandis, nego recte concipi posse ex nuda sufficientia rei oblatae, nisi accedat ordinata sufficientia ex actu offerentis: Quod sic probari potest.

Quando dicimus Christum pro omnibus mortuum sufficienter, nihil aliud dicimus, quam pro omnibus fuisse oblatum sufficienter, vel pro omnibus dedisse se lytron sive redemtionis pretium sufficienter. Mori autem pro omnibus, vel offerri pro omnibus, vel dare semetipsum pro omnibus, designat actum morientis vel semetipsum offerentis ad omnes liberandos sub aliqua ordinatione terminatum. Ergo sola sufficientia lytri, absque animo et actu offerentis ad personas terminato, non potest veram reddere hanc assertionem, Christus pro omnibus mortuus est sufficienter. Sensus etenim communis respuit, ut pro omnibus sufficienter mortuus concedatur, qui pro aliquibus mortuus sive oblatus negatur. Stante autem et concessa intrinseca lytri sufficientia ad mille mundos redimendos, simul stare potest hoc idem lytron nondum esse pro multis hominibus ullatenus oblatum, nedum sufficienter oblatum. Nam sicuti ad liberandum quinque debitores qui singuli debent ducentas libras decem mille librarum satis superque sufficiunt; si tamen haec summa integra offeratur et persolvatur creditori nominatim pro duobus solummodo, reliquis tribus exclusis, sufficientia et superabundantia in se hujus lytri non efficiet ut pro illis tribus sufficienter datum et persolutum dicatur: sic in hac communi causa humani generis, licet pretiosus Christi sanguis sit lytron plusquam sufficiens ad omnium et singulorum debita dispungenda, tamen non inde pro illis sufficienter oblatum affirmaretur, qui in ipso actu offerentis discrete excluduntur. Non itaque tam interpretari quam ludificari videntur receptissimum hoc et verissimum Theologorum pronunciatum, Christus pro omnibus mortuus est sufficienter, qui terminum hunc sufficienter transferunt ab animo et actu morientis ad nudam sufficientiam sive intrinsecum valorem mortis in se consideratae; quasi sensus esset, Mors Christi in se sufficiens habet meritum et valorem ad delenda peccata omnium hominum, sed non fuit Christus pro omnibus oblatus sive mortuus: cum clarus sensus hujus dicti sit, Christum pro omnibus fuisse mortuum, et pro omnibus fuisse mortuum sufficienter, quamvis quod ille sufficienter pro omnibus obtulit propter interveniens infidelitatis obstaculum non omnibus efficaciter applicetur.

In hac distinctione Scholasticorum, quam nostri communiter admittunt, Christum scilicet pro omnibus mortuum sufficienter, pro praedestinatis efficaciter, vocabula illa sufficienter et efficaciter denotant quid in ipso modo oblationis fuit commune omnibus hominibus, tam electis quam non-electis, quid vero peculiare electis solis. Commune fuit utrisque, quod Christus pro illis fuerit sufficienter mortuus sive oblatus in hostiam Deo Patri. At quomodo prior hic terminus, sufficienter, ad electos et non-electos promiscue referetur, si nudam sufficientiam rei designet, exclusa ordinatione ejusdem rei ad personas quae oritur ex animo et actu offerentis? Aut quid opus est posteriore illo termino, efficaciter, ad constituendam distinctionem in modo oblationis sive in intentione offerentis quoad electos et non-electos, si nulla prorsus intentio fuit Christi seipsum offerentis nisi pro solis praedestinatis? Frivola et plane inepta est distinctio bimembris, ubi in re contradistincta utrumque membrum non praesupponitur. Observandum itaque est, sanctos Patres universalem mortis Christi sufficientiam urgentes, non haerere in nuda sufficientia rei, sed in actu, animo, et modo ipso offerendi. Sic passim Athanasius in tractatu De incarnatione Verbi. Apponam locum unum aureum: Christus Dei Filius, a nobis simili corpore mutuato, eo quod omnes morti obnoxii essemus, pro omnibus idipsum in mortem deditum Patri suo sacrificavit. Item: Post edita Divinitatis suae monumenta, reliquum jam erat ut pro omnibus sacrificium offerret, pro omnibus templum suum morti tradens, quo omnes liberos a veteri praevaricatione efficeret, etc. Videtis notam universalitatis non cum intrinseca sufficientia rei oblatae, sed cum animo et actu offerentis, qui ad omnes spectavit, esse conjunctam. Sic Augustinus: Christi sanguis sic in remissionem peccatorum omnium fusus est, ut ipsum etiam peccatum posset delere quo fusus est. Non dicit in sanguine effuso esse sufficientem valorem intrinsecum ad expianda omnium hominum peccata, quod in confesso est apud omnes qui sanguinem Dei rite aestimare norunt; sed modum et actum offerendi urget, in eoque hanc universalitatem constituit; Sic fusus est in remissionem peccatorum omnium. Aliud est dicere Christi sanguinem habere ex se et in se sufficientem valorem ad delenda omnium hominum peccata, aliud affirmare fusum esse ipso facto in remissionem peccatorum omnium, quod dixit Augustinus. Sed quid commemoro sanctos Patres? Sacrosancta Scriptura de Christi morte sic loquitur ut universalem ejus vim non referat ad nudam hostiae oblatae dignitatem, sed ad actum et animum offerentis, 1 Tim. ii. 6. Dedit semetipsum redemtionis pretium pro omnibus. Non dicit Apostolus, Hoc lytron in se et intrinseco suo valore sufficiens est pro omnibus redimendis, sed re vera datum est pro paucis, non pro omnibus; sed, Dedit semetipsum pro omnibus. Animus ergo et actus Christi dantis semetipsum omnes complectebatur. Sicut et Patris Filium mittentis; Sic Deus dilexit mundum, etc. Johan. iii. 16. Nuda igitur illa rei sufficientia non eo valet ut Christus pro omnibus sufficienter mortuus affirmetur, absque sufficientia ad omnes ex animo et actu offerentis ordinata.
english: 1. The mere sufficiency of Christ’s death, which is estimated from the intrinsic value alone of this lutron, without that ordained sufficiency which arises from the mind and act of offering, does not avail so far that Christ may truly be said to have died sufficiently for all. I thought this thesis should be added because of those who hold tightly that Christ died for the elect alone, and yet (I confess I am too slow to understand how) admit that Christ died sufficiently for all; and sometimes exalt this thing, a sufficiency spreading itself to all human beings, in very strong words. For they confess that Christ died for all human beings, for all orders, states, and kinds of human beings, indeed even for individual human beings as to the sufficiency of merits. The Contra-Remonstrants in the Judgment exhibited to the Synod of Dort write thus: When Christ is said to have died for all, this can be understood of the sufficiency of the merit, or the magnitude of the price. For the death of the Son of God is the one perfect and sufficient lytron for expiating and blotting out all the sins of the whole world: an immense merit of righteousness, a catholic medicine of death, a perennial fountain of life, etc. A little later: This sufficiency of the lytron, as to the reprobate, has a twin end, one of itself, the other by accident. The end of itself, that God may make it plain he does not delight in the destruction of human beings, inasmuch as he gave his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life ([[John 3:16 >> Bible:John 3:16]]). The end by accident, that by this sufficiency of the lytron they may be rendered inexcusable. For these perish not by Christ’s fault but by their own, when by their unbelief they repudiate the benefits offered by Christ in the Gospel. So far they. This sufficiency of Christ’s death for reconciling all, I deny can be rightly conceived from a bare sufficiency of the thing offered, unless an ordained sufficiency from the offerer’s act accompanies it. Which can be proved thus.

When we say that Christ died sufficiently for all, we say nothing else than that he was offered sufficiently for all, or that he gave himself as a lytron or price of redemption sufficiently for all. But to die for all, or to be offered for all, or to give oneself for all, designates the act of one dying or offering himself, terminated under some ordination to freeing all. Therefore the mere sufficiency of the lytron, without the mind and act of the offerer terminated to persons, cannot make true this assertion, Christ died sufficiently for all. For common sense refuses that one should be granted to have died sufficiently for all who is denied to have died or been offered for some. And while the intrinsic sufficiency of the lytron for redeeming a thousand worlds stands and is conceded, it can at the same time stand that this same lytron has not yet been offered in any way for many human beings, much less sufficiently offered. For just as for freeing five debtors who each owe two hundred pounds, ten thousand pounds are more than enough; yet if this whole sum is offered and paid to the creditor by name for two only, the other three excluded, the sufficiency and superabundance in itself of this lytron will not make it that it was sufficiently given and paid for those three: so in this common cause of the human race, although Christ’s precious blood is a lytron more than sufficient for canceling the debts of all and each, yet it would not thence be affirmed to have been sufficiently offered for those who are discretely excluded in the very act of offering. They seem therefore not so much to interpret as to mock this most received and most true pronouncement of the Theologians, Christ died sufficiently for all, who transfer this term sufficiently from the mind and act of the one dying to a bare sufficiency or intrinsic value of the death considered in itself; as if the sense were, Christ’s death in itself has sufficient merit and value for blotting out the sins of all human beings, but Christ was not offered or dead for all — when the clear sense of this saying is that Christ died for all, and died sufficiently for all, although what he sufficiently offered for all is not efficaciously applied to all because of the intervening obstacle of unbelief.

In this distinction of the Scholastics, which our men commonly admit — namely that Christ died for all sufficiently, for the predestinate efficaciously — those words sufficiently and efficaciously denote what in the very mode of oblation was common to all human beings, elect and non-elect alike, and what was peculiar to the elect alone. Common to both was that Christ was sufficiently dead or offered for them as a victim to God the Father. But how will this former term, sufficiently, be referred promiscuously to elect and non-elect, if it designates a bare sufficiency of the thing, excluding the ordination of the same thing to persons that arises from the offerer’s mind and act? Or what need is there of that latter term, efficaciously, to constitute a distinction in the mode of oblation or in the offerer’s intention as to elect and non-elect, if there was absolutely no intention of Christ offering himself except for the predestinate alone? A bimembral distinction is frivolous and plainly inept where both members are not presupposed in the thing distinguished. It is to be observed, then, that the holy Fathers, urging the universal sufficiency of Christ’s death, do not stick in a bare sufficiency of the thing, but in the act, mind, and very mode of offering. So repeatedly Athanasius in the treatise On the Incarnation of the Word. I will set down one golden place: Christ the Son of God, having borrowed a body like ours, because we all were liable to death, sacrificed to his Father that same body given over to death for all. Likewise: After the monuments of his Divinity had been displayed, it remained that he should offer a sacrifice for all, delivering his temple to death for all, that he might make all free from the old transgression, etc. You see that the note of universality is joined not with the intrinsic sufficiency of the thing offered, but with the mind and act of the offerer, which looked to all. So Augustine: Christ’s blood was so poured out for the remission of all sins that it could blot out even the very sin by which it was poured. He does not say that in the blood poured out there is a sufficient intrinsic value for expiating all human beings’ sins, which is confessed among all who know how to estimate God’s blood rightly; but he urges the mode and act of offering, and in that constitutes this universality: It was so poured for the remission of all sins. It is one thing to say that Christ’s blood has from itself and in itself a sufficient value for blotting out all human beings’ sins; another to affirm that it was poured by the very fact for the remission of all sins, which Augustine said. But why do I recall the holy Fathers? Holy Scripture so speaks of Christ’s death that it does not refer its universal force to the bare dignity of the victim offered, but to the act and mind of the offerer ([[1 Timothy 2:6 >> Bible:1 Timothy 2:6]]): He gave himself a price of redemption for all. The Apostle does not say, This lytron in itself and in its intrinsic value is sufficient for redeeming all, but was in truth given for a few, not for all; but, He gave himself for all. The mind and act, then, of Christ giving himself embraced all. So also of the Father sending the Son; So God loved the world, etc. ([[John 3:16 >> Bible:John 3:16]]). That bare sufficiency of the thing, then, does not avail so far that Christ may be affirmed to have died sufficiently for all, without a sufficiency ordained toward all from the offerer’s mind and act.

3. Christus pro omnibus hominibus eo sensu sufficienter mortuus agnoscitur, quo pro angelis lapsis mortuus negatur. Hoc clarum est et in confesso apud omnes orthodoxos, qui saepe hoc discrimen commemorant inter angelos malos et quosvis homines malos, saltem dum viatores sunt. Huc spectant illa verba Ambrosii, in illud Psalm. cxviii. Misericordia Domini plena est terra, Serm. 8: Mysticus Sol ille justitiae omnibus ortus est, omnibus venit, omnibus passus, omnibus resurrexit. Si quis autem non credit in Christum, a generali beneficio ipse se fraudat. Paulo post, Fortasse dicas, Qua ratione non dictum sit, MISERICORDIA DOMINI PLENUM EST COELUM? Quia sunt etiam spirituales nequitiae in caelestibus, sed non illae ad commune jus indulgentiae Dei remissionemque pertinent peccatorum. Ex quibus patet, Christum ita passum pro universo humano genere, ut omnes homines inde habeant commune jus indulgentiae obtinendae per fidem, quod daemones non habent, quia pro illis nullatenus mortuus est. Quidam ex nostris, qui pro restringenda Christi morte acriter depugnant, tamen hoc ultro largiuntur, Non esse eandem rationem hominum quorumcunque quae est diabolorum, quoad sufficientiam mortis Christi. Hominibus enim quibuscunque, non autem diabolis, satis idoneum solvebat lytron, si modo amplecti vellent. Dignum est observatione hoc discrimen in hujus lytri solutione: Ita Deo persolutum est ut diabolos non possit redimere, etiamsi supponantur credere; nempe quia pro illis non fuit persolutum: at ita Deo exhibitum et datum est ut quosvis homines possit redimere, si velint credere; unde hoc, nisi quia pro illis omnibus fuit oblatum et persolutum? Non enim valeret ad homines quoscunque liberandos, etiamsi crederent, nisi supponatur pro eisdem datum et oblatum Deo, in communi causa generis humani, etiam quando non credebant. Stabilito igitur hoc discrimine inter sufficientiam mortis Christi quoad homines et quoad daemones, quod Christi mors scilicet pro omnibus hominibus eo sensu sufficiens intelligitur quo pro angelis recte negatur, ab hac Majore propositione transeamus ad minorem. Dico igitur, si aliam sufficientiam in morte Christi quoad homines quoscunque redimendos non agnoscamus, nisi eam quam appellavimus sufficientiam meram, quaeque pendet ex intrinseco valore lutri, sublata ordinatione offerentis ad personas, nullum discrimen constitui inter tales personas et ipsos daemones quoad illud jus indulgentiae et remissionis obtinendae beneficio hujus lutri, quod ab Ambrosio supra commemoratum fuit, atque hominibus universim concessum, angelis exclusum. Patet; Quia valor passionis Christi aestimatur ex dignitate personae patientis. Habuit igitur in se et intrinseco suo pretio non modo sufficientiam, sed infinitam superabundantiam, etiamsi contra appendantur peccata non hominum modo universorum, sed angelorum. Danda est ergo respectu hominum, non modo sufficientia illa mera, quae pendet ex rei oblatae insita dignitate, sed illa ordinata, quae oritur ex animo et actu Christi ad omnes homines hanc suam passionem referentis, ad angelos non referentis. Hoc posito, Christus revera dicitur pro omnibus hominibus mortuus sufficienter, illa sufficientia quae in relatione ad angelos apostatas locum non habet, et de qua vere dicatur, Christus pro angelis lapsis neque efficaciter, neque sufficienter mortuus est.

Objicitur. Sed huic argumento occurat fortasse aliquis, atque asserat, Meram rei oblatae sufficientiam in se consideratam quoad homines efficere ut Christus recte dicatur passus pro omnibus hominibus sufficienter; non tamen efficere quoad Diabolos, quia sufficiens non est quod non est aptum, idoneum. Aptitudinis autem in Christo ad peccata humana tollenda pars magna fuit, quod similitudinem carnis peccatricis assumpsit. Cum igitur angelorum naturam non assumpserit, nec statum habuit idoneum, nec sufficientem passionem ad malorum angelorum tollenda peccata.

Solutio. Sed utrinque claudicat haec argutatio. Nam sufficientia illa mera, accedente aptitudine et congruentia quantalibet, si non accesserit ordinatio aliqua et actio offerendi ad personas relata, nondum efficit ut pro talibus personis Christus passus omnino dicatur, nedum ut passus sufficienter affirmetur. Frustra igitur obtenditur humanae naturae assumptio, ut inde deducatur Christum pro omnibus hominibus fuisse mortuum sive sufficienter sive insufficienter, ab iis qui pro solis electis illum fuisse mortuum contendunt. Ex altera etiam parte vacillat praedicta exceptio, quia licet inter Christum et Angelos non intercesserit ea naturae similitudo quae inter Christum et homines, tamen hoc impedire non potest quin lytron a Christo persolutum, hoc est, sanguis Dei, fuerit in se et valore suo sufficientissimum ad tollenda etiam peccata angelorum. Quod enim potest esse tantum crimen cujuscunque creaturae, cui expiando non sufficiat effusus sanguis Dei; qui valorem habet ex dignitate Divinae personae infinitum, ac proinde non obstante humanae naturae dissimilitudine, si Deus hoc jus in passionem Christi angelis indulgere dignatus esset, etiam ad angelos redimendos applicabilem. Voluit quidem Deus humani generis misereri, angelorum non misereri; voluit Redemtorem assumere non naturam angelicam, sed semen Abrahae: Hinc concludere possumus mortem Christi non esse lytron ordinatum pro redemtione angelorum, at non esse lytron in se sufficientis dignitatis, valoris et efficacitatis, si ordinatio haec fuisset, nec possumus concludere, nec debemus. Argumentum esse potest in contrariam partem, quod Christus, non obstante naturae dissimilitudine, est sufficiens et idoneum Caput ad influendam gratiam etiam angelis ipsis; unde dona gratiae et gloriae ipsis bonis angelis meruisse a Theologis doctissimis asseritur. Quod autem malis angelis non prosunt Christi merita, id non ad insufficientiam rei, sed ad solam voluntatem Dei est referendum: ac per consequens, si ponamus homines multos, ad quos passio et meritum Christi nullatenus ordinetur, quoad sufficientiam mortis Christi non alia erit horum ratio et conditio quam Diabolorum.
english: 3. Christ is acknowledged to have died sufficiently for all human beings in that sense in which he is denied to have died for the fallen angels. This is clear and confessed among all the orthodox, who often recall this discrimination between evil angels and any evil human beings, at least while they are wayfarers. To this look those words of Ambrose on that text of Psalm 118, The earth is full of the Lord’s mercy, Sermon 8: That mystical Sun of righteousness has risen for all, come for all, suffered for all, risen for all. But if anyone does not believe in Christ, he defrauds himself of the general benefit. A little later: Perhaps you may say, Why was it not said, THE HEAVEN IS FULL OF THE LORD’S MERCY? Because there are also spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places, but those do not pertain to the common right of God’s indulgence and the remission of sins. From which it is plain that Christ so suffered for the whole human race that all human beings thence have a common right of obtaining indulgence by faith, which the demons do not have, because he in no way died for them. Certain of our own, who fight hard for restricting Christ’s death, yet freely grant this: that there is not the same ratio for any human beings that there is for the diaboli, as to the sufficiency of Christ’s death. For to any human beings, but not to the diaboli, he paid a lytron apt enough, if only they were willing to embrace it. This discrimination in the payment of this lytron is worth observing: It was so paid to God that it cannot redeem the diaboli, even if they are supposed to believe — namely because it was not paid for them; but it was so exhibited and given to God that it can redeem any human beings, if they are willing to believe; whence this, unless because it was offered and paid for all of them? For it would not avail to free any human beings, even if they believed, unless it is supposed to have been given and offered to God for them, in the common cause of the human race, even when they did not believe. This discrimination between the sufficiency of Christ’s death as to human beings and as to demons being established — that Christ’s death is understood as sufficient for all human beings in that sense in which it is rightly denied for the angels — let us pass from this Major proposition to the minor. I say, then, that if we acknowledge no other sufficiency in Christ’s death for redeeming any human beings than that which we have called mere sufficiency, which depends on the intrinsic value of the lutron, the offerer’s ordination to persons being removed, no discrimination is set up between such persons and the demons themselves as to that right of obtaining indulgence and remission by the benefit of this lutron, which was recalled above from Ambrose and granted universally to human beings, excluded from angels. It is plain; because the value of Christ’s passion is estimated from the dignity of the suffering Person. It had therefore in itself and in its intrinsic price not only sufficiency but infinite superabundance, even if against it are weighed the sins not only of all human beings but of angels. There must therefore be granted, with respect to human beings, not only that mere sufficiency which depends on the inherent dignity of the thing offered, but that ordained one which arises from Christ’s mind and act referring this his passion to all human beings, not referring it to angels. This being posited, Christ is truly said to have died sufficiently for all human beings, by that sufficiency which has no place in relation to the apostate angels, and of which it is truly said, Christ died for the fallen angels neither efficaciously nor sufficiently.

Objection. But perhaps someone may meet this argument and assert that a mere sufficiency of the thing offered, considered in itself, as to human beings makes it that Christ is rightly said to have suffered sufficiently for all human beings; yet does not make it as to the Diaboli, because that is not sufficient which is not apt and suitable. But a great part of the aptitude in Christ for taking away human sins was that he assumed the likeness of sinful flesh. Since therefore he did not assume the nature of angels, he had neither a suitable state nor a sufficient passion for taking away the sins of evil angels. Solution. But this subtlety limps on both sides. For that mere sufficiency, even with aptitude and congruence however great added, if some ordination and action of offering related to persons has not accompanied it, does not yet make it that Christ is said to have suffered at all for such persons, much less that he is affirmed to have suffered sufficiently. In vain, then, is the assumption of human nature urged, so that from it those who contend he died for the elect alone may deduce that Christ died for all human beings, whether sufficiently or insufficiently. On the other side also the aforesaid exception wavers, because although between Christ and the Angels there did not intervene that likeness of nature which is between Christ and human beings, yet this cannot hinder the lytron paid by Christ — that is, the blood of God — from having been in itself and in its value most sufficient for taking away even the sins of angels. For what crime of any creature can be so great that the poured blood of God would not suffice to expiate it? — which has infinite value from the dignity of the Divine Person, and therefore, the dissimilarity of human nature notwithstanding, if God had deigned to indulge the angels this right in Christ’s passion, it would be applicable even to redeeming angels. God indeed willed to pity the human race, not to pity the angels; he willed the Redeemer to assume not an angelic nature but the seed of Abraham: From this we can conclude that Christ’s death is not a lytron ordained for the redemption of angels, but we neither can nor ought to conclude that it is not a lytron of sufficient dignity, value, and efficacy in itself, if that ordination had been. An argument can be made the other way: that Christ, nature’s dissimilarity notwithstanding, is a sufficient and suitable Head for pouring grace even into the angels themselves; whence the most learned Theologians assert that he merited gifts of grace and glory for the good angels themselves. But that Christ’s merits do not profit the evil angels is to be referred not to insufficiency of the thing but to the will of God alone: and consequently, if we posit many human beings to whom Christ’s passion and merit are in no way ordained, their ratio and condition as to the sufficiency of Christ’s death will be no other than that of the Diaboli.

source_text: 4. Probamus nudam rei oblatae in se sufficientiam non posse verum reddere illud pronunciatum Theologorum, Christus pro omnibus hominibus mortuus est sufficienter, idque ex confessione eorum qui mortem Christi toti humano generi impensam negant, et ad solos electos restringunt. Sic Piscator in Resp. Apologet. Sect. 87, Dici non potest, Christum pro omnibus mortuum sufficienter: sequeretur enim mortuum esse pro omnibus, cujus contrarium est demonstratum. Et eodem in loco, distinctio illa qua dicitur Christum pro omnibus mortuum esse sufficienter, pro solis electis efficaciter, inanis est, quia implicat contradictionem, etc. Revera implicat contradictionem apud illos qui nudam mortis sufficientiam quoad omnes admittunt, et ordinationem ejus universalem ad omnium hominum salutem procurandam pernegant. Tenentur igitur hanc distinctionem hactenus ab orthodoxis probatam explodere, aut nobiscum ordinatam mortis Christi ad omnes liberandos sufficientiam agnoscere. Doctissimus Pareus in hanc sententiam ire videtur, quando affirmat, Christum quoad sufficientiam meriti sui, pro omnibus et singulis mortuum esse, et mori voluisse. Ubi hanc sufficientiam non in eo solo constituit, quod mors Christi in suo valore intrinseco sufficiat ad omnes redimendos; sed in voluntate etiam Christi morientis, ac mortem suam ad omnes liberandos sufficienter ordinantis. Atqui hic obiter notandum est, falli eos qui arctant mortem Christi ad solos electos, ita ut pro illis solis mori voluisse statuant, et tamen obtendant, De sufficientia mortis Christi pro omnibus et singulis nullam esse quaestionem aut contentionem; controversiam vero omnem esse de actu hujus efficaciae. Nam posita illa sufficientia mortis in se ad mille mundos redimendos; et hoc etiam posito, quod mortis hujus efficacia non ad omnes sed ad certas quasdam personas de facto liberandas absolute et infallibiliter destinetur, tamen adhuc manet controversum, Utrum mors Christi intrinsecam sufficientiam ad omnes redimendos, sub hypothesi nempe conceptam, Si pro omnibus illud lytron offerre et solvere voluisset, non habeat, etiam conjunctam Dei ordinationem, juxta quam hoc lytron in se sufficiens, pro omnibus de facto oblatum fuit, atque inde omnibus ad salutem applicabile atque applicandum, si praedictae ordinationi parere ac sese subjicere voluerint. Talem ordinationem nos tuemur, etiam ad illos spectantem qui non servantur, quia non crediderunt in nomen unigeniti Filii Dei; atque hinc dicimus Christum pro omnibus sufficienter mortuum. Sed hic nonnulli ex illis qui Christum pro solis electis passum et mortuum acriter tenent, nihilo tamen minus videri volunt non nudam mortis Christi in se sufficientiam, sed illam ordinatam ex Dei intentione quam nos asserimus, defendere. Atque hanc ob causam, cum urgentur argumentis, voluntatis et intentionis Divinae mentionem facere non recusant.
