Quorum mens et sententia propius excutienda est, ne cum larvis luctari, aut de lana (quod aiunt) caprina pugnare videamur. Sic igitur doctus quidam vir hac de re scripsit, Quando fatemur Christum pro omnibus mortuum esse, phrasis illa, PRO OMNIBUS, a nostris propter sufficientiam et intentionem Dei, qua voluit ut sit sufficiens pro omnibus, admittitur. Sciendum tamen est impropriam hanc locutionem esse; non rejiciendam tamen, quia fundamentum aliquando in re ipsa habet, et apud Theologos est usu longe recepta. Alii in eandem sententiam aiunt, Consilium et decretum Dei Patris fuisse ut Christus passione et morte sua ejusmodi lytron persolveret, quod in se consideratum omnibus hominibus reconciliandis sufficeret. Videntur hi, praeter meram rei sufficientiam, addere sufficientiam ex intentione et consilio Dei ad omnes homines reconciliandos relatam et pertinentem. Videntur quidem sed revera non faciunt. Nam primo quod aiunt se agnoscere Christum pro omnibus mortuum sufficienter propter intentionem Dei, qua voluit ut mors ejus sit sufficiens pro omnibus, nullius momenti est. Mors siquidem Filii Dei non eget superveniente aliqua intentione ut sit sufficiens pro omnibus, cum in se sit valoris infiniti: eget tamen, ut sit pro omnibus data et acceptata ad eos liberandos, sub quacunque conditione. Sufficientia est intrinseca quaedam potentia et aptitudo rei: nec requiritur ad illam constituendam extrinsecus actus intendentis hanc sufficientiam; sed ordinatio ad personas quascunque liberandas, est actus voluntarius, et fluit ab intentione et consilio ordinantis. Frivolum itaque copulare intentionem Dei cum interna sufficientia rei; quae intentio aut omnino neganda fuit quoad Christum pro omnibus sufficienter mortuum; aut cum ordinatione mortis ad omnes pertinente fuit conjungenda. Secundo quod dicunt hanc phrasin, Christus pro omnibus mortuus est sufficienter, habere fundamentum in re, ex ipsorum sententia defendi non potest. Si dicerem, Christi mors est sufficiens lytron pro omnibus, est hujus dicti verum fundamentum in ipsa re, nempe in dignitate personae morientis: at si dicam, Christus est pro omnibus sufficienter mortuus vel oblatus in ara crucis (quae sunt aequipollentia), jam nullum est fundamentum in quo subsistit hujus dicti veritas, nisi primo ponam Christum pro omnibus passum et oblatum, dein et adjungam hujus passionis pro omnibus ex dignitate lytri sufficientiam. Forum unum qui negat, frustra in altero ejus dicti defensionem tentat. Concludamus ergo, quod neque Christus vere dici potest pro omnibus passus sive mortuus sufficienter, neque mors Christi vere agnosci universale remedium omnibus hominibus juxta ordinationem Dei applicabile, nisi praeter meram sufficientiam rei ex innata ejus dignitate fluentem, admittamus ex voluntate Dei hanc hostiam acceptantis et Christi eandem offerentis, stabile et fixum Dei decretum juxta quod omnibus et singulis haec mors Christi vitam aeternam possit apportare. Atque hactenus primum membrum thesis nostrae tractavimus: In quo ostendimus, nudam illam sufficientiam, quae in ipsa morte Christi per se considerata intelligitur, non ad hoc sufficere ut Christus pro omnibus mortuus dicatur, aut ut mors ejus universalis causa salutis respectu totius humani generis habeatur. Ostendamus porro quid illud sit quod ad hanc rem ultra requiratur. Huic rei illustrandae secunda haec thesis inserviet.
english: 4. We prove that a bare sufficiency of the thing offered in itself cannot make true that pronouncement of the Theologians, Christ died sufficiently for all human beings, and that from the confession of those who deny that Christ’s death was spent on the whole human race and restrict it to the elect alone. So Piscator in the Apologetic Response, section 87: It cannot be said that Christ died sufficiently for all: for it would follow that he died for all, whose contrary has been demonstrated. And in the same place, that distinction by which Christ is said to have died for all sufficiently, for the elect alone efficaciously, is empty, because it implies a contradiction, etc. It truly implies a contradiction among those who admit a bare sufficiency of the death as to all, and utterly deny its universal ordination for procuring the salvation of all human beings. They are therefore bound either to explode this distinction hitherto approved by the orthodox, or with us to acknowledge an ordained sufficiency of Christ’s death for freeing all. The most learned Pareus seems to go this way when he affirms that Christ, as to the sufficiency of his merit, died and willed to die for all and each. Where he does not constitute this sufficiency in that alone, that Christ’s death in its intrinsic value suffices for redeeming all; but also in the will of Christ dying and sufficiently ordaining his death to freeing all. And here it is to be noted in passing that those err who narrow Christ’s death to the elect alone, so as to establish that he willed to die for them alone, and yet plead that there is no question or contention about the sufficiency of Christ’s death for all and each; that the whole controversy is about the act of this efficacy. For even with that sufficiency of the death in itself for redeeming a thousand worlds posited; and this also posited, that the efficacy of this death is destined absolutely and infallibly not to all but to certain persons to be freed in fact — still it remains controversial whether Christ’s death has only an intrinsic sufficiency for redeeming all, conceived under the hypothesis, If he had willed to offer and pay that lytron for all, or also a conjunct Divine ordination according to which this lytron, sufficient in itself, was in fact offered for all, and thence is applicable and to be applied to all unto salvation, if they have been willing to obey and subject themselves to the aforesaid ordination. Such an ordination we defend, looking even to those who are not saved, because they did not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God; and hence we say that Christ died sufficiently for all. But here some of those who hold tightly that Christ suffered and died for the elect alone nevertheless wish to seem to defend not a bare sufficiency of Christ’s death in itself, but that ordained one from God’s intention which we assert. And for this reason, when they are pressed with arguments, they do not refuse to mention the Divine will and intention. Their mind and sense must be examined more closely, lest we seem to wrestle with ghosts, or to fight (as they say) about goat’s wool.

So a certain learned man wrote on this matter: When we confess that Christ died for all, that phrase, FOR ALL, is admitted by our men on account of the sufficiency and the intention of God, by which he willed that it be sufficient for all. Yet it is to be known that this locution is improper; not however to be rejected, because it sometimes has a foundation in the thing itself, and among Theologians is received by long use. Others say in the same sense that it was the counsel and decree of God the Father that by his passion and death Christ should pay such a lytron as, considered in itself, would suffice for reconciling all human beings. These seem, besides a mere sufficiency of the thing, to add a sufficiency related and pertaining from God’s intention and counsel to reconciling all human beings. They seem to, but in truth they do not. For first, that they say they acknowledge Christ to have died sufficiently for all on account of God’s intention by which he willed that his death be sufficient for all, is of no moment. For the death of the Son of God does not need some supervening intention in order to be sufficient for all, since in itself it is of infinite value: yet it does need, in order to be given and accepted for freeing them, under whatever condition. Sufficiency is a certain intrinsic power and aptitude of the thing: nor is an extrinsic act of one intending this sufficiency required to constitute it; but ordination to freeing any persons is a voluntary act, and flows from the intention and counsel of the one ordaining. It is therefore frivolous to couple God’s intention with the internal sufficiency of the thing; which intention was either to be denied altogether as to Christ having died sufficiently for all, or was to be joined with an ordination of the death pertaining to all. Second, that they say this phrase, Christ died sufficiently for all, has a foundation in the thing, cannot be defended on their own view. If I should say, Christ’s death is a sufficient lytron for all, the true foundation of this saying is in the thing itself, namely in the dignity of the dying Person: but if I say, Christ is sufficiently dead or offered on the altar of the cross for all (which are equipollent), there is now no foundation on which the truth of this saying stands, unless I first posit that Christ suffered and was offered for all, and then also add the sufficiency of this passion for all from the dignity of the lytron. He who denies the one forum vainly attempts to defend the saying in the other. Let us conclude, then, that neither can Christ truly be said to have suffered or died sufficiently for all, nor can Christ’s death truly be acknowledged as a universal remedy applicable to all human beings according to God’s ordination, unless besides a mere sufficiency of the thing flowing from its innate dignity we admit, from the will of God accepting this victim and of Christ offering the same, a stable and fixed decree of God according to which this death of Christ can bring eternal life to all and each. And thus far we have treated the first member of our thesis: in which we have shown that that bare sufficiency which is understood in Christ’s death itself considered by itself does not suffice for this, that Christ be said to have died for all, or that his death be held the universal cause of salvation with respect to the whole human race. Let us show further what that is which is required beyond this for the matter. This second thesis will serve to illustrate that point.

source_text: Christi mors ratione foederis Evangelici, cum omnibus hominibus per eam stabiliti, pro omnibus hominibus vere tolerata affirmatur, et Christus eodem respectu pro omnibus sufficienter mortuus asseritur. Pactum autem illud designamus cujus mentionem ante fecimus, Si credideris, salvus eris; vel, Quisquis crediderit salvus erit: Rom. x. 9. Quod hoc pactum de remissione peccatorum gratificanda, et de hominibus per fidem servandis, sit sanguine et morte Filii Dei sancitum, primo patet ex sacris Scripturis. In coenae Dominicae institutione inquit Christus ipse, Luc. xxii. 20, Hoc poculum est novum illud testamentum in sanguine meo, qui pro vobis effunditur. Quasi dixisset, Vinum est symbolum sanguinis Dominici, quo sanguine novum illud foedus de remissione peccatorum et justificatione nostra per fidem sancitur et stabilitur. Et Apostolus, Heb. ix. 22, Absque effusione sanguinis non est remissio. Foedus igitur illud cum hominibus initum, quo Deus se obstrinxit ad remittenda peccata credentium, habet in morte Christi suam firmitatem. Idem Apostolus, Rom. iii. 25, docet Deum proposuisse ut Christus esset placamentum per fidem in sanguine ipsius, ad declarandam justitiam suam per remissionem praecedentium peccatorum. In sanguine igitur sive morte Christi fundatum est hoc foedus Evangelicum, juxta quod per fidem remissio peccatorum, justificatio et salus aeterna hominibus confertur. Ne multus sim in re satis perspicua, cum hoc promissum conditionatum, Si credideris, salvus eris, ex gratioso Dei affectu in homines dimanet, non potest alibi suum fundamentum habere quam in morte et merito Christi Mediatoris, in quo omnes Dei promissiones gratuitae sunt Etiam et Amen, 2 Cor. i. 20. Neque enim tanti est ipse actus fidei ut possit sua dignitate aut suo merito a Deo impetrare remissionem peccatorum et salutem; sed tanti est mors et sanguis Filii Dei ut possit suo merito et virtute quemvis fidelem justificare et servare juxta tenorem foederis Evangelici. Per mortem igitur Christi hoc foedus stabilitum est. Sed restat secundo in loco illud quod plus habet scrupuli, Utrum scilicet hoc foedus Evangelicum, Si credideris, salvus eris, quod per mortem Christi stabilitum ostendimus, ad totum humanum genus, aut ad singulares solummodo et ad certas quasdam personas, ex Divina ordinatione pertineat. Nos cum toto humano genere firmatum defendimus. Quod constare potest. 1. Ex mandato et promisso ipsius Christi post mortem toleratam et devictam Apostolos suos in totum mundum mittentis, Marc. xvi. 15, 16. Dixit eis, Euntes in mundum universum praedicate evangelium omni creaturae. Qui crediderit et baptizatus fuerit, servabitur: qui vero non crediderit, condemnabitur. In quae verba promissionis recte annotavit doctissimus Calvinus, Hanc promissionem fuisse adjunctam, quae totum humanum genus ad fidem alliceret. Cum toto igitur humano genere stabilita intelligitur. Promissio enim nullam habet vim alliciendi ad actionem quamlibet nisi eos quibus facta praesupponitur. 2. Idem liquet ex praxi Apostolorum, et omnium Ministrorum Evangelicorum, Christi mandato et promisso conformi. Nam hi nullo habito respectu nationis aut praedestinationis omnibus et singulis, quos datur convenire, audacter remissionem peccatorum sub fidei conditione pollicentur, hoc ipso facto agnoscunt foedus de remissione peccatorum per fidem in sanguine Christi sancitum esse universale. Nam pactum conditionatum non potest serio illis proponi, et beneficium annexum sub conditione illis promitti, ad quos ex voluntate paciscentis ipsum pactum non extenditur. Exempli causa, si rex aliquis cum quibusdam certis personis hoc pactum ineat, Velle se illis admissum laesae majestatis crimen condonare, si supplices ab illo veniam petant; non inde liceret cuivis e famulis Regiis carcerem adire, et omnibus promiscue nuntiare veniam a Rege obtinendam, si modo ad genua ejus se supplices demiserint: quia hoc pactum non spectat ad eos solos quos Regium beneplacitum inclusos voluit? Perinde neque Dei Ministris liceret promiscue omnibus sub conditione fidei remissionem et salutem promittere, nisi certo illis constaret, ex voluntate Dei hoc pactum conditionatum cum omnibus initum et stabilitum. At hoc fecerunt Apostoli, hoc nos facimus: ergo agnoscimus hoc pactum cum omnibus et singulis, idest, cum toto humano genere, firmatum.
english: Christ’s death, by reason of the Evangelical covenant stabilized with all human beings through it, is affirmed as truly endured for all human beings, and Christ in the same respect is asserted to have died sufficiently for all. We designate that pact of which we made mention before: If you have believed, you will be saved; or, Whoever has believed will be saved ([[Romans 10:9 >> Bible:Romans 10:9]]). That this pact concerning granting remission of sins, and concerning human beings to be saved by faith, has been sanctioned by the blood and death of the Son of God, first appears from the sacred Scriptures. In the institution of the Lord’s Supper Christ himself says ([[Luke 22:20 >> Bible:Luke 22:20]]): This cup is that new testament in my blood, which is poured out for you. As if he had said, The wine is a symbol of the Lord’s blood, by which blood that new covenant concerning remission of sins and our justification by faith is sanctioned and stabilized. And the Apostle ([[Hebrews 9:22 >> Bible:Hebrews 9:22]]): Without shedding of blood there is no remission. That covenant therefore entered with human beings, by which God bound himself to remit the sins of believers, has its firmness in Christ’s death. The same Apostle ([[Romans 3:25 >> Bible:Romans 3:25]]) teaches that God set forth Christ to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, for declaring his righteousness through the remission of sins that were before. In Christ’s blood or death, then, this Evangelical covenant is founded, according to which by faith remission of sins, justification, and eternal salvation are conferred on human beings.

Not to be long in a matter clear enough: since this conditioned promise, If you have believed, you will be saved, flows from God’s gracious affection toward human beings, it cannot have its foundation elsewhere than in the death and merit of Christ the Mediator, in whom all God’s free promises are Yes and Amen ([[2 Corinthians 1:20 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 1:20]]). For the act of faith itself is not of such worth that by its own dignity or merit it could obtain from God remission of sins and salvation; but the death and blood of the Son of God are of such worth that by their merit and power they can justify and save any believer according to the tenor of the Evangelical covenant. Through Christ’s death, therefore, this covenant has been stabilized.

source_text: Sed fortasse dixerit aliquis, Utcunque hoc pactum sanguine Christi stabilitum non ad omnes homines promiscue, sed ad solos electos pertineat, potest tamen proponi et offerri omnibus remissio et salus sub hypothesi fidei, quia certum est solos electos perseveranter credituris: ac proinde nemo non-electorum poterit unquam causari hoc foedus conditionatum ex parte Dei fuisse falsum quoad ipsum aut violatum. Verum haec responsio nullius momenti est. Nam veritas cujuscunque propositionis conditionalis concipienda est ante positionem conditionis: imo licet conditio nunquam in actum ventura sit, tamen veritas propositionis conditionalis rite institutae debet consistere. Hic itaque propositio sive promissio conditionalis, Si credideris, peccata tibi remittentur, quoad Cainum aut Judam falsa est, nisi detur verum fundamentum connexionis, si contingeret eos credere. Nec quicquam refert ad veritatem conditionatae propositionis, sive illi sint credituri sive non credituri; cum in tali propositione spectetur ratio connexionis, non veritas aut falsitas partium separatarum. Si Petrus Christum abnegaverit, vitam aeternam obtinebit, est falsa propositio propter connexionis imbecillitatem, et tamen utraque pars separata vera fuit. Si Petrus non crediderit, non obtinebit vitam aeternam, est vera propositio, et tamen utraque pars seorsim sumta falsa fuit: Nam et credidit Petrus, et obtinuit vitam aeternam. Pari igitur ratione hoc conditionale pronunciatum, Si credideris, remissionem peccatorum et vitam aeternam obtinebis, esset falsum quoad quemvis non-electum, licet supponatur nunquam crediturus, si desit antecedanea ratio et causa connexionis: deest autem, nisi pactum illud conditionale cum omnibus et singulis hominibus stabilitum asseratur. Non enim sequitur, Deus in morte Christi sanciit foedus de servandis per fidem omnibus electis: Ergo si Cain crediderit, servabitur. Foedus itaque illud conditionatum cum toto humano genere stabilitur.
english: But there remains in the second place that which has more scruple: whether this Evangelical covenant, If you have believed, you will be saved, which we have shown stabilized through Christ’s death, pertains by Divine ordination to the whole human race, or only to singular and certain persons. We defend it as firmed with the whole human race. Which can stand clear. First, from the mandate and promise of Christ himself sending his Apostles into the whole world after death endured and overcome ([[Mark 16:15–16 >> Bible:Mark 16:15]]): He said to them, Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature. He who has believed and been baptized will be saved; but he who has not believed will be condemned. On which words of promise the most learned Calvin rightly annotated that this promise was joined on, which would allure the whole human race to faith. It is therefore understood as stabilized with the whole human race. For a promise has no force of alluring to any action except those to whom it is presupposed as made.

Second, the same is plain from the practice of the Apostles and of all Evangelical Ministers conforming to Christ’s mandate and promise. For these, with no respect had to nation or predestination, boldly promise remission of sins under the condition of faith to all and each whom it is given them to meet; by this very deed they acknowledge the covenant concerning remission of sins through faith in Christ’s blood to be universal. For a conditioned pact cannot seriously be proposed to them, and the annexed benefit promised to them under condition, to whom by the will of the one making the pact the pact itself does not extend. For example: if some king should enter this pact with certain persons, that he is willing to pardon them a crime of offended majesty if as suppliants they seek pardon from him; it would not thence be lawful for any of the King’s servants to go to the prison and announce promiscuously to all that pardon is to be obtained from the King if only they have cast themselves as suppliants at his knees — because this pact does not look to those alone whom the Royal good pleasure willed included? Likewise neither would it be lawful for God’s Ministers to promise promiscuously to all under the condition of faith remission and salvation, unless it were certain to them that by God’s will this conditioned pact was entered and stabilized with all. But this the Apostles did; this we do: therefore we acknowledge this pact firmed with all and each, that is, with the whole human race.

source_text:
3. Probamus hoc Evangelicum pactum in morte Christi stabilitum, de danda salute sub conditione fidei, esse universale, hanc ipsam rationem ulterius urgendo, idque ex concessis illorum qui videntur nobis adversari. Qui igitur mortem Christi vel maxime restringere conantur, concedunt tamen, merito mortis Christi esse viam aliquam et rationem constitutam, per quam quilibet infidelis possit meritam condemnationem evadere, nimirum si credat. Concedunt, mortem Christi abunde suffecturam ad servandos omnes homines, si quotquot sunt in toto orbe homines in eum crederent. Concedunt denique, indiscriminatim electis et non-electis verbum Evangelii de Christo crucifixo annunciari, omnesque in ipsum credere juberi, addita hac promissione, Fore ut omnes in ipsum credentes remissionem peccatorum consequantur. Hisce positis sic arguo: Si quotquot sunt in toto orbe homines, consequerentur remissionem peccatorum et salutem, si crederent, tum est firmatum Christi morte pactum universale de servando quolibet homine sub praedicta fidei conditione: At verum primum: Ergo et secundum. Ratio consequentiae haec est; Quia illa conditionalis, quam admittunt tam quoad non-electos quam electos, nempe, Si tu credideris, quisquis tandem es, salvus erit, non habet veritatem necessariam ex rei natura, sicut ista, Si ignis est, calidus est, vel, Si est homo, est animal: relinquitur ergo ut habeat veritatem suam fundatam in aliqua voluntaria Dei ordinatione, qua ipse sanxit ut quoad quemvis hominem, posito in esse antecedente, poneretur et consequens. Nullum siquidem tertium fundamentum assignari potest, quo nitatur praedictae conditionalis veritas. Ergo fatendum est, pactum illud Evangelicum esse universale ex ordinatione ipsius Dei, et ad omnes ac singulos homines ex aequo spectare.

Si quis hic objiciat, ipsum Evangelium nunquam fuisse omnibus hominibus annunciatum, ac proinde neque pactum illud Evangelicum totum humanum genus complecti, vel ad omnes et singulos pertinere, respondeo; non sequi, Pactum Evangelicum non annunciatur huic nationi, aut huic homini singulari, Ergo quoad eos non fuit sancitum aut stabilitum: Sed illud recte sequitur, Pactum Evangelicum non est ex se Annunciabile huic nationi, aut huic homini, Ergo ad eos nullo modo pertinet. Causae siquidem non annunciati Evangelii aliae subesse possunt, ut illud omnibus annunciabile fateamur; quas causas rimari non est praesentis instituti. Dicimus igitur, quovis saeculo, cuivis nationi, et cuivis homini vere annunciari potuisse remissionem peccatorum in morte redemptoris, sub fidei conditione. Sic tempore Veteris Testamenti Jobo alienigenae fuit revelatum hoc foedus. Sic nostro saeculo si Minister Evangelicus ad Antipodas veniret, non exspectaret quoad eos hujus conditionati foederis novam stabilitionem, sed illico pro stabilito agnoscens iisdem annunciaret. Atque hinc est quod Apostolus hunc sermonem Evangelii vocat mysterium absconditum a saeculis et aetatibus, nunc autem patefactum, etc. Col. i. 26. Agnovit igitur ab aeterno stabilitum cum humano genere, quamvis absconditum sive patefactum hisce aut illis pro beneplacito Divino. Vide Rom. xvi. 25, 26 et Eph. iii. 5 et 9.
english: But perhaps someone may say: Even if this pact stabilized by Christ’s blood pertains not promiscuously to all human beings but to the elect alone, yet remission and salvation can be proposed and offered to all under the hypothesis of faith, because it is certain that the elect alone will perseveringly believe; and therefore no one of the non-elect will ever be able to charge that this conditioned covenant was false on God’s part as to himself, or violated. But this reply is of no moment. For the truth of any conditional proposition is to be conceived before the positing of the condition: indeed, although the condition is never going to come into act, still the truth of a rightly instituted conditional proposition ought to stand. Here, then, the conditional proposition or promise, If you have believed, your sins will be remitted to you, is false as to Cain or Judas unless a true foundation of the connexion is given, if it should happen that they believe. Nor does it matter at all to the truth of a conditioned proposition whether they are going to believe or not; since in such a proposition the ratio of the connexion is looked to, not the truth or falsity of the parts taken separately. If Peter shall have denied Christ, he will obtain eternal life, is a false proposition because of the weakness of the connexion, and yet each part separately was true. If Peter shall not have believed, he will not obtain eternal life, is a true proposition, and yet each part taken apart was false: for Peter both believed and obtained eternal life. By like reason, then, this conditional pronouncement, If you have believed, you will obtain remission of sins and eternal life, would be false as to any non-elect person, even if he is supposed never going to believe, if the antecedent ratio and cause of the connexion is lacking: but it is lacking unless that conditioned pact is asserted stabilized with all and each human being. For it does not follow: God in Christ’s death sanctioned a covenant concerning saving all the elect by faith: Therefore if Cain shall have believed, he will be saved. That conditioned covenant is therefore stabilized with the whole human race.

3. We prove that this Evangelical pact stabilized in Christ’s death, concerning giving salvation under the condition of faith, is universal, by urging this same reason further, and that from the concessions of those who seem to oppose us. Those therefore who try most of all to restrict Christ’s death nevertheless concede that by the merit of Christ’s death there is some way and ratio constituted by which any unbeliever can escape merited condemnation, namely if he believes. They concede that Christ’s death would abundantly have sufficed for saving all human beings, if as many human beings as are in the whole world believed in him. They concede finally that the word of the Gospel concerning Christ crucified is announced indiscriminately to elect and non-elect, and all are commanded to believe in him, with this promise added, that all believing in him will obtain remission of sins. These things posited, I argue thus: If as many human beings as are in the whole world would obtain remission of sins and salvation if they believed, then there is firmed by Christ’s death a universal pact concerning saving any human being under the aforesaid condition of faith: But the first is true: Therefore also the second. The reason of the consequence is this: Because that conditional which they admit as much as to non-elect as to elect — namely, If you have believed, whoever at length you are, you will be saved — does not have necessary truth from the nature of the thing, as these do, If there is fire, it is hot, or, If it is a human being, it is an animal: it remains therefore that it have its truth founded in some voluntary ordination of God, by which he himself sanctioned that as to any human being, the antecedent being posited in being, the consequent also would be posited. For no third foundation can be assigned on which the truth of the aforesaid conditional rests. Therefore it must be confessed that that Evangelical pact is universal from God’s own ordination, and looks equally to all and each human being.

If anyone here objects that the Gospel itself was never announced to all human beings, and therefore neither does that Evangelical pact embrace the whole human race, or pertain to all and each, I reply: it does not follow, The Evangelical pact is not announced to this nation, or to this singular human being, Therefore as to them it was not sanctioned or stabilized: But this rightly follows, The Evangelical pact is not of itself Announceable to this nation, or to this human being, Therefore it pertains to them in no way. For other causes of the Gospel’s not being announced can underlie, while we still confess it announceable to all; which causes it is not of the present design to search out. We say therefore that in any age, to any nation, and to any human being, remission of sins in the Redeemer’s death under the condition of faith could truly have been announced. So in the time of the Old Testament this covenant was revealed to Job the foreigner. So in our age if an Evangelical Minister came to the Antipodes, he would not wait for a new stabilization of this conditioned covenant as to them, but at once, acknowledging it as stabilized, would announce it to them. And hence it is that the Apostle calls this word of the Gospel a mystery hidden from ages and generations, but now made manifest, and so on ([[Colossians 1:26 >> Bible:Colossians 1:26]]). He therefore acknowledged it stabilized from eternity with the human race, although hidden or made manifest to these or those according to the Divine good pleasure. See ([[Romans 16:25–26 >> Bible:Romans 16:25]]) and ([[Ephesians 3:5 >> Bible:Ephesians 3:5]]) and 9.

source_text:
Reliquum est, ut ratione hujus pacti universalis per mortem Christi cum toto humano genere stabiliti ostendamus, vero et sano sensu nos affirmare posse Christum passum fuisse, aut mortuum fuisse, pro omnibus hominibus: quod paucis expediemus.

Illud autem praemoneo, ad verificandam hanc loquendi formulam neque ex sensu Scripturarum, neque ex sensu Patrum, neque ex ipsa vi verborum esse absolute necessarium ut tueamur, illos omnes per infallibilem ordinem praedestinationis ad vitam aeternam beneficio mortis Christi esse perducendos pro quibus Christus fuisse crucifixus et mortuus affirmantur; quanquam de quibusdam servandis fuisse talem Christi morientis intentionem lubenter agnoscimus, et suo loco Scripturarum testimoniis et argumentis perspicuis confirmabimus.

Primo igitur, ex usu Scripturarum non semper aequipollent haec duo, Christus pro hisce hominibus mortuus est, et, Deus hosce homines per Christi mortem infallibiliter servandos praedestinavit: quia Scripturae saepe universim pronunciant, Christum pro omnibus mortuum; at nunquam universim affirmant, Deum praedestinasse omnes salvandos beneficio mortis Christi. Quorsum, quaeso, Spiritus Dei in morte Christi depredanda saepenumero uteretur terminis generalibus ad omnes illam extendentibus, in praedestinatione Divina celebranda semper uteretur terminis restrictivis ad paucos illam limitantibus, si mors Christi et praedestinatio Dei quoad homines aequalem ac eundem plane ambitum haberent? Secundo, Quia in sacris Scripturis eodem sensu dicitur Christus reconciliasse homines, dedisse semetipsum redemtionis pretium pro hominibus, quo mortuus fuisse pro hominibus; At dicitur reconciliasse et redemisse mundum, quatenus mundus habet in morte ejus constitutam et stabilitam universalem causam, qua per fidem apprehensa quivis mortalium potest actualiter Deo reconciliari et a reatu peccatorum liberari: Ergo etiam et recte mortuus pro omnibus concipitur, quatenus omnes in morte ejus habent vitam aeternam sibi expositam et per fidem parabilem. Sicut igitur cum dicitur Deus mundum in Christo reconciliasse, aut Christus dedisse se redemtionis pretium pro omnibus, non idcirco dicitur Deum omnes in Christo praedestinasse, ita nec ex eo quod pro omnibus crucifixus et mortuus affirmatur. Deinde sacrae Scripturae ad eos clare extendunt mortem Christi, tanquam beneficium applicabile ex Divina ordinatione, qui sua infidelitate illud sibi minime applicarunt. Extendunt ergo extra numerum electorum, ex quibus nemo est cui ad salutem non infallibiliter applicatur illud lytron. Huc faciunt illa loca Scripturarum in quibus increduli condemnandi pronunciantur, quia non crediderunt in nomen unigeniti Filii Dei, in mundum missi, ut servetur mundus per eum, Joh. iii. 17, 18; quia nolunt venire ad Christum, ut vitam habeant, Joh. v. 40; quia repellunt salutarem Dei sermonem, et seipsos vita aeterna indignos decernunt, Actor. xiii. 46; denique, quia propter incredulitatem derelicta promissione introeundi in requiem Dei, sua culpa fuerunt frustrati, Heb. iv. Haec omnia evincunt, ex sensu Scripturarum Christi mortem ac merita fuisse etiam ordinata in illorum usum qui eadem spreverunt et repulerunt: non autem fuisse talibus ordinata secundum infallibilem praedestinationis ordinem, ex eventu liquet: Ergo ad verificandum, quod Christus pro hisce aut illis hominibus mortuus dicatur secundum Scripturas, non requiritur necessario ut mortuus pro eis intelligatur cum absoluto proposito eosdem salvandi.
english: It remains that, by reason of this universal pact stabilized through Christ’s death with the whole human race, we show that in a true and sound sense we can affirm that Christ suffered, or died, for all human beings: which we will set out in few words.

But this I warn beforehand: for verifying this formula of speaking it is not absolutely necessary, neither from the sense of the Scriptures, nor from the sense of the Fathers, nor from the very force of the words, that we maintain that all those for whom Christ is affirmed to have been crucified and to have died are to be led through to eternal life by the infallible order of predestination by the benefit of Christ’s death; although concerning certain ones to be saved we gladly acknowledge that there was such an intention of Christ dying, and in its place we will confirm it with clear testimonies of the Scriptures and arguments.

First, then, from the usage of the Scriptures these two are not always equivalent: Christ died for these human beings, and, God predestined these human beings to be saved infallibly through Christ’s death: because the Scriptures often pronounce universally that Christ died for all; but they never affirm universally that God predestined all to be saved by the benefit of Christ’s death. To what end, I ask, would the Spirit of God in proclaiming Christ’s death so often use general terms extending it to all, and in celebrating Divine predestination always use restrictive terms limiting it to few, if Christ’s death and God’s predestination as to human beings had an equal and plainly the same ambit? Second, because in the sacred Scriptures Christ is said in the same sense to have reconciled human beings, to have given himself as the price of redemption for human beings, in which sense he is said to have died for human beings; yet he is said to have reconciled and redeemed the world inasmuch as the world has in his death a universal cause constituted and stabilized, which any mortal, apprehending it by faith, can be actually reconciled to God and freed from the guilt of sins: Therefore also he is rightly conceived dead for all, inasmuch as all in his death have eternal life exposed to them and obtainable by faith. Just as, then, when God is said to have reconciled the world in Christ, or Christ to have given himself as the price of redemption for all, God is not therefore said to have predestined all in Christ, so neither from this, that he is affirmed crucified and dead for all. Further, the sacred Scriptures clearly extend Christ’s death, as a benefit applicable by Divine ordination, even to those who by their unbelief applied it least to themselves. They therefore extend it outside the number of the elect, of whom there is no one to whom that lytron is not infallibly applied unto salvation. Here belong those places of the Scriptures in which unbelievers are pronounced to be condemned because they have not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God, sent into the world that the world might be saved through him ([[John 3:17–18 >> Bible:John 3:17]]); because they will not come to Christ that they may have life ([[John 5:40 >> Bible:John 5:40]]); because they thrust away the saving word of God and judge themselves unworthy of eternal life ([[Acts 13:46 >> Bible:Acts 13:46]]); finally, because through unbelief, the promise of entering into God’s rest being left, they were frustrated by their own fault ([[Hebrews 4 >> Bible:Hebrews 4]]). All these prove that, from the sense of the Scriptures, Christ’s death and merits were ordained also for the use of those who scorned and thrust them away: but that they were not ordained to such according to the infallible order of predestination is plain from the event: Therefore for verifying that Christ is said according to the Scriptures to have died for these or those human beings, it is not necessarily required that he be understood dead for them with an absolute purpose of saving the same.

source_text:
A Scripturis ad Patres descendamus. Manifestum est apud illos non perinde valere hanc propositionem, Christus pro hisce hominibus mortuus est, atque hanc, Christus hosce homines sua morte infallibiliter servabit. Pauculis testimoniis erimus contenti, quia res notissima est illis qui sunt in Patrum scriptis mediocriter versati. Ambrosius, in Psal. 118, affirmat, Christum pro omnibus passum, et tamen statim subjungit, Eos qui non credunt in Christum generali hoc beneficio se fraudare. Non igitur Ambrosio perinde sonant, Christum pati pro aliquo, et passione sua infallibiliter servandum decernere. Prosper, ad Capit. Gallor. resp. 6, Rectissime dicitur Salvator pro totius mundi redemtione crucifixus. Idem tamen affirmat, Sent. 9, Licet sanguis Christi sit pretium totius mundi, tamen ab hoc pretio extraneos esse qui delectati captivitate sua redimi noluerunt. Ita ut de hisce recte dicatur, Redemtor mundi dedit pro mundo sanguinem suum, et mundus redimi noluit, Ad cap. Gallor. resp. 9. Non igitur apud Prosperum haec duo censentur isodynamounta, Christus pro hisce crucifixus est, et Christus hosce infallibiliter servandos procurabit. Theophylactus in Heb. ii. 9, Deus Filium suum nobis dedit in mortem, non pro fidelibus tantum, sed pro universo terrarum orbe. Etsi enim non omnes sunt servati, ipse tamen quod sui officii erat implevit. Ex quibus verbis patet, Theophylacto non idem esse, si quis dixerit, Christus a Deo datus est ut moreretur pro omnibus, ac si dixisset, Christus ex absoluto Dei beneplacito omnes per mortem suam servabit. Pluribus testimoniis supersedeo.

Tandem illud adjungo. Ex sola vi horum verborum, Christus pro omnibus mortuus est, non posse inferri, Christum pro omnibus ita mortuum fuisse, ut absolute decreverit hac sua morte omnium salutem efficaciter et infallibiliter operari: quia sane vere et proprie pro aliquo mori is dicatur qui bono alterius procurando moritur, quamvis ille alter suo vitio nihil commodi inde percipiat. Particula enim pro denotat respectum ad alterum in voluntate et intentione morientis; sed non perpetuo et necessario talem respectum involvit ut pro alio mori nemo recte dicatur, nisi qui decreverit per mortem suam alterum absolute et infallibiliter a morte liberare. Quid enim si sub conditione aliqua reddat liberationem a morte hominibus reis possibilem, quae absque ejus morte fuit impossibilis? Annon hoc solo nomine vere pro illis mortuus asseratur? Asserit Ambrosius, qui scribit, Christum pro salute universorum advenisse, et omnium redemtionem suscepisse, quatenus appertuit remedium quo possent omnes evadere, quamvis multi sint qui mortis suae causas sibi adscribant, quia curari noluerunt. Non igitur negamus particulam pro in sacris Scripturis, cum de morte Christi agitur, aliquando specialem illam intentionem designare juxta quam liberatio a morte et translatio in vitam illis infallibiliter destinatur pro quibus mortuus asseritur: sed hoc ita perpetuum aut necessarium esse, ut non stet veritas hujus assertionis, Christus pro omnibus mortuus est, nisi ponatur habuisse intentionem illam absolutam omnes salvandi, id demum pernegamus. Videtis jam arcanum illud et absolutum beneplacitum de servandis hominibus, juxta inscrutabilem ordinem praedestinationis, non esse ad hoc necessarium, ut Christus recte et vere dicatur passus et mortuus pro omnibus.

Quid igitur necessarium est? Dicam paucis. Quandoquidem Christi mors duplicem respectum habet, unum ad Deum, cui oblatum et persolutum fuit hoc pretiosum lytron, alterum ad homines, pro quibus oblatum fuit et persolutum; Christus pro omnibus passus, oblatus sive mortuus dicatur, si morte et passione sua constiterit illum effecisse, ut Deus ipse ad vitam aeternam omnibus hominibus donandam aliter dispositus intelligatur, quam esset absque hac morte Christi; atque etiam si illud constiterit, quemvis hominem in remissionem peccatorum et vitam aeternam sibi vendicandam habere virtute mortis Christi aliquid juris, quod hac morte seclusa habere, aut vendicare nullo modo posset. Utrumvis horum luculente ostendit vim mortis Christi ad totum humanum genus se extendere, atque idcirco nos nec falso nec improprie loqui, quando dicimus Christum pro omnibus hominibus fuisse mortuum.

Quod attinet ad prius, Certum est, respectu mortis Christi voluntatem Dei aliter jam esse comparatam ad omnes et singulos homines quam esset absque ea: Nam hoc ipso quod Christus in natura sua humana mortem passus est, sine alio ullo medio interveniente, hoc saltem apud Deum effectum est, ut velit cuivis homini credenti et poenitenti reconciliari, peccata remittere, vitam aeternam conferre. Hinc Caino, si bene egerit et resipuerit, ex parte Dei parata est remissio, Gen. iv. 7. Hinc improbo cuicunque dicitur nomine ipsius Dei, Si conversus fuerit a peccatis suis, omnino vivet, non morietur, Ezek. xviii. 21. Tolle respectum mortis Christi menti Divinae obversantem, et humanum genus complectentem, hujusmodi promissionibus quoad non-electos nihil veri, solidi, aut seri subiisset. Conditionatae enim remissionis promissio eam in morte Christi habere debet suam veritatem, quam ipsa remissio quae praestita conditione indulgetur. Neque quicquam refert ad infringendam hanc universalem vim, quam apud Deum obtinuit mors Christi, quod nemo ex non-electis illam Evangelicam fidei et poenitentiae conditionem impleat; sufficit enim, quod vi mortis Christi, ac ordinationis Divinae per eam stabilitae, si conditio a quocunque homine impleretur, beneficium remissionis et vitae aeternae indubie sequeretur. Jam quod ad posterius spectat, illud quoque certum est, atque connexum; quemlibet hominem beneficio mortis Christi hoc juris sibi vendicare posse, ut, si crediderit, protinus omnia sua peccata deleantur, et ipse in haeredem vitae aeternae adoptetur. Quamvis enim, propter defectum impletae conditionis, multi non possunt de facto haec promissa bona vendicare, nemo tamen mortalium est, si conditio fuisset ab eo impleta, in quem ex vi mortis Christi non redundassent. Hoc conditionatum Dei decretum morte Christi stabilitum, et in Evangelio revelatum, ex quo intelligimus Deum virtute passionis Christi obligasse seipsum ad dandam remissionem peccatorum et vitam aeternam omni credenti, et ex quo accreverit jus universale non his aut illis singularibus personis, sed cuilibet humani generis individuo, ad remissionem sub praedicta conditione obtinendam, satis sufficit ad hoc ut Christus pro omnibus hominibus passus vere afferatur. Neque quasi res nihili contemnendum est hoc conditionatum decretum morte Christi firmatum et ad omnes extensum, quia infallibilis conditionis impletio ex alio arcano decreto dependet: cum illud arcanum decretum, quatenus has aut illas singulares personas complectitur, sit nobis prorsus incognitum; ac proinde haud cuiquam nominatim praedicandum; hoc autem conditionatum decretum, quod totum humanum genus comprehendit, sit omnibus et singulis annunciandum, utpote Evangelicae nostrae doctrinae solidissimum fundamentum, juxta illud Apostoli, Rom. x. 8, 9, 11. Hoc est verbum illud fidei quod nos praedicamus, nempe, Quod si confessus fueris ore tuo Dominum Jesum, et credideris in corde tuo quod Deus eum excitavit a mortuis, salvus eris. Dicit enim Scriptura, Quisquis credit in eum non pudefiet. Hoc beneficium virtute mortis Christi est sub conditione fidei omnibus hominibus expositum et parabile; et eo respectu Christus pro omnibus mortuus affirmatur.
english: From the Scriptures let us descend to the Fathers. It is plain among them that this proposition, Christ died for these human beings, does not avail in the same way as this, Christ will by his death save these human beings infallibly. We will be content with a few testimonies, because the matter is most well known to those who are even moderately versed in the Fathers’ writings. Ambrose, on Psalm 118, affirms that Christ suffered for all, and yet at once adds that those who do not believe in Christ defraud themselves of this general benefit. Therefore for Ambrose, Christ suffering for someone, and deciding by his passion that someone is to be saved infallibly, do not sound the same. Prosper, to the Chapters of the Gauls, reply 6: Most rightly is the Savior said to have been crucified for the redemption of the whole world. Yet the same affirms, Sentence 9, that although Christ’s blood is the price of the whole world, yet those are strangers from this price who, delighted with their captivity, were unwilling to be redeemed. So that of these it is rightly said, The Redeemer of the world gave his blood for the world, and the world was unwilling to be redeemed — to the Chapters of the Gauls, reply 9. Therefore with Prosper these two are not counted as of equal force: Christ was crucified for these, and Christ will procure that these be saved infallibly. Theophylact on ([[Hebrews 2:9 >> Bible:Hebrews 2:9]]): God gave his Son to us unto death, not for the faithful only, but for the whole circle of the lands. For although not all are saved, yet he fulfilled what was of his office. From which words it is plain that for Theophylact it is not the same if someone has said, Christ was given by God that he might die for all, as if he had said, Christ by God’s absolute good pleasure will save all through his death. I pass over more testimonies.

Finally I add this. From the mere force of these words, Christ died for all, it cannot be inferred that Christ died for all in such a way that he absolutely decreed by this his death to work the salvation of all efficaciously and infallibly: because truly and properly he is said to die for someone who dies for procuring another’s good, even if that other by his own vice perceives no advantage thence. For the particle for denotes a respect to another in the will and intention of the one dying; but it does not perpetually and necessarily involve such a respect that no one is rightly said to die for another unless he has decreed by his death to free the other absolutely and infallibly from death. For what if under some condition he renders liberation from death possible for guilty human beings, which without his death was impossible? Is he not by this alone truly asserted dead for them? Ambrose asserts it, who writes that Christ came for the salvation of all, and undertook the redemption of all, inasmuch as he opened a remedy by which all could escape, although there are many who ascribe the causes of their death to themselves, because they were unwilling to be cured. We do not therefore deny that the particle for in the sacred Scriptures, when Christ’s death is treated, sometimes designates that special intention according to which liberation from death and transfer into life is infallibly destined for those for whom he is asserted dead: but that this is so perpetual or necessary that the truth of this assertion, Christ died for all, does not stand unless it is posited that he had that absolute intention of saving all — that at last we utterly deny. You see now that that secret and absolute good pleasure concerning saving human beings, according to the inscrutable order of predestination, is not necessary for this, that Christ be rightly and truly said to have suffered and died for all.

What then is necessary? I will say in few words. Since Christ’s death has a double respect, one to God, to whom this precious lytron was offered and paid, the other to human beings, for whom it was offered and paid: Christ is said to have suffered, been offered, or died for all, if by his death and passion it is established that he effected that God himself is understood otherwise disposed toward giving eternal life to all human beings than he would be without this death of Christ; and also if it is established that any human being has, by the virtue of Christ’s death, some right of claiming for himself remission of sins and eternal life, which with this death shut out he could in no way have or claim. Either of these clearly shows that the force of Christ’s death extends itself to the whole human race, and therefore that we speak neither falsely nor improperly when we say that Christ died for all human beings.

As to the former: It is certain that, with respect to Christ’s death, God’s will is now otherwise compared toward all and each human being than it would be without it. For by this very thing, that Christ in his human nature suffered death, without any other medium intervening, this at least has been effected with God, that he wills to be reconciled to any human being believing and penitent, to remit sins, to confer eternal life. Hence for Cain, if he has done well and repented, remission is prepared on God’s part ([[Genesis 4:7 >> Bible:Genesis 4:7]]). Hence to any wicked person it is said in God’s own name, If he shall have turned from his sins, he shall altogether live, he shall not die ([[Ezekiel 18:21 >> Bible:Ezekiel 18:21]]). Take away the respect of Christ’s death present to the Divine mind and embracing the human race, and nothing true, solid, or serious would underlie promises of this kind as to the non-elect. For the promise of conditioned remission ought to have its truth in Christ’s death no less than the remission itself which is granted when the condition is performed. Nor does anything avail to break this universal force which Christ’s death obtained with God, that no one of the non-elect fulfills that Evangelical condition of faith and penitence; for it is enough that by the force of Christ’s death, and of the Divine ordination stabilized through it, if the condition were fulfilled by any human being, the benefit of remission and eternal life would doubtless follow.

Now as to what looks to the latter: that also is certain and connected, that any human being can claim for himself this right by the benefit of Christ’s death, that if he has believed, at once all his sins are deleted, and he himself is adopted as heir of eternal life. For although, because of defect of the fulfilled condition, many cannot in fact claim these promised goods, yet there is no mortal who, if the condition had been fulfilled by him, would not have had them redound upon him from the force of Christ’s death. This conditioned decree of God stabilized by Christ’s death, and revealed in the Gospel — from which we understand that God by the virtue of Christ’s passion has obliged himself to give remission of sins and eternal life to every believer, and from which there has accrued a universal right not to these or those singular persons, but to any individual of the human race, of obtaining remission under the aforesaid condition — sufficiently suffices for this, that Christ be truly asserted to have suffered for all human beings. Nor is this conditioned decree firmed by Christ’s death and extended to all to be despised as a thing of nothing because the infallible fulfillment of the condition depends on another secret decree: since that secret decree, inasmuch as it embraces these or those singular persons, is utterly unknown to us, and therefore is scarcely to be preached to anyone by name; but this conditioned decree, which comprehends the whole human race, is to be announced to all and each, as the most solid foundation of our Evangelical doctrine, according to that of the Apostle ([[Romans 10:8–9 >> Bible:Romans 10:8]], 11): This is that word of faith which we preach, namely, That if you shall have confessed with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and shall have believed in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For the Scripture says, Whoever believes in him will not be put to shame. This benefit by the virtue of Christ’s death is exposed and obtainable to all human beings under the condition of faith; and in that respect Christ is affirmed dead for all.

source_text:
Docuimus Christum pro omnibus hominibus mortuum, eo sensu quod per mortem Christi sit stabilitum foedus Evangelicum cum toto humano genere, juxta quod remissio peccatorum et vita aeterna omnibus hominibus sub possibili fidei conditione sit exposita. Quidam in solum praedestinationis et reprobationis arcanum animi sui oculos defigentes, capere non possunt, quomodo Christus, fides, remissio peccatorum, vita aeterna, aut quicquam boni spiritualis et salutiferi ullatenus aut sub ulla conditione possibili ad eos pertineat, qui in praedestinatorum numero haud inclusi fuerunt ante jacta mundi fundamenta, licet Christus in Evangelica praedicatione eis offerri, licet fides ab eis exigi, licet sub ipsa fidei conditione remissio et vita aeterna per Christum obtinenda illis promitti possit. Breviter itaque ostendemus, Hanc fidei conditionem, quae requiritur ad hoc ut Christi mors pro omnibus tolerata sit huic aut illi singulariter applicata, neque esse, neque a nobis concipi oportere, ut cuivis Viatori omnino impossibilem. Hic autem in memoriam revocandum est, quod ab initio monuimus, hanc possibilitatem fundari in auxilio supernaturali possibiliter, dum hic in via sumus, a quolibet recipiendo; juxta celebre illud dictum Prosperi Aquitanici, Hoc inter malos homines distat et daemones, quod hominibus etiam valde malis superest, si Deus misereatur, reconciliatio, Daemonibus autem nulla est in aeternum servata conversio, Object. Vincent. resp. 6.

Primo igitur, quando dicimus fidem sive credere, esse quid possibile cuivis viatori, respicimus non activam et formalem potentiam, quasi quivis viator posset pro libertate arbitrii sui hunc actum credendi elicere; sed passivam, quam vocant, et materialem, quia in quolibet viatore potest hoc a Deo effici ut convertatur et credat Evangelio. Nam posse aliquid dupliciter dicimur, ut bene observavit Aquinas, scilicet vel per potentiam quae in nobis est, sicut dicimus quod lapis potest moveri deorsum; vel per potentiam ex parte alterius consideratam, sicut dicimus lapidem posse moveri sursum, non per potentiam innatam, sed per potentiam projicientis. Ad hunc modum nos affirmamus quemlibet viatorem posse credere; vel fidei conditionem esse cuivis viatori possibilem, non per potentiam proximam in seipso residentem, sed per auxilium supernaturale, quod a Deo potest pro quolibet momento cuivis viatori suppeditari; juxta illud Johannis Baptistae, Luc. iii. 8, Dico vobis, Posse Deum etiam ex lapidibus istis excitare filios Abrahae. Ergo nullum cor tam obduratum et lapideum est, quod non possit a Deo emolliri, et ad fidem ac poenitentiam inflecti. Hoc illud est quod aliis verbis significavit Augustinus, quando scripsit, Posse habere fidem, naturae est hominum, habere autem, gratiae est fidelium, De Praedestinat. Sanctor. cap. 5. Huc etiam allusit idem Augustinus in Soliloquiis, lib. 1. cap. 1, ubi cum dixisset, Credamus, si hoc in nostra potestate est, mox subjicit, Potestas nostra ipse Deus est.
english: We have taught that Christ died for all human beings, in this sense: that through Christ’s death an Evangelical covenant has been stabilized with the whole human race, according to which remission of sins and eternal life is exposed to all human beings under a possible condition of faith. Certain persons, fixing the eyes of their mind only on the secret of predestination and reprobation, cannot grasp how Christ, faith, remission of sins, eternal life, or any spiritual and saving good can pertain in any way, or under any possible condition, to those who were not included in the number of the predestinate before the foundations of the world were laid — even though Christ may be offered to them in Evangelical preaching, faith may be required of them, and remission and eternal life to be obtained through Christ may be promised to them under that very condition of faith. Briefly, then, we will show that this condition of faith, which is required for this, that Christ’s death endured for all be singularly applied to this or that person, neither is, nor ought to be conceived by us as, utterly impossible for any wayfarer. Here it must be recalled to memory what we warned from the beginning: that this possibility is founded in a supernatural help possibly to be received by anyone while we are here on the way; according to that celebrated saying of Prosper of Aquitaine: This is the difference between bad human beings and demons, that for human beings, even very bad ones, reconciliation still remains, if God has mercy; but for demons no conversion is reserved forever (Objection of Vincent, reply 6).

First, then, when we say that faith, or believing, is something possible for any wayfarer, we look not to an active and formal power, as if any wayfarer could by the liberty of his own choice elicit this act of believing; but to a passive power, as they call it, and a material one, because in any wayfarer this can be effected by God, that he be converted and believe the Gospel. For we are said to be able to do something in two ways, as Aquinas well observed: namely either by a power that is in us, as we say that a stone can be moved downward; or by a power considered on another’s part, as we say that a stone can be moved upward, not by an innate power, but by the power of the one throwing it. In this manner we affirm that any wayfarer can believe; or that the condition of faith is possible for any wayfarer, not by a proximate power residing in himself, but by a supernatural help which can be supplied by God at any moment to any wayfarer; according to that of John the Baptist ([[Luke 3:8 >> Bible:Luke 3:8]]): I say to you that God is able even from these stones to raise up children of Abraham. Therefore no heart is so hardened and stony that it cannot be softened by God and bent to faith and penitence. This is what Augustine signified in other words when he wrote that being able to have faith is of the nature of human beings, but having it is of the grace of the faithful (On the Predestination of the Saints, chapter 5). To this the same Augustine also alluded in the Soliloquies, book 1, chapter 1, where when he had said, Let us believe, if this is in our power, he at once adds, Our power is God himself.

source_text: Secundo, quando hanc fidei habendae possibilitatem ad potentiam Dei activam referimus, et ad potentiam hominis receptivam, hoc intelligendum est non de potentia Dei absoluta tantummodo, sed de potentia Dei ordinaria. Nam apud Theologos quaedam dicuntur possibilia per potentiam Dei absolutam, quaedam per potentiam ordinariam. Quam distinctionem paucis explicatam dare non erit a proposito nostro alienum. Illud itaque dicitur possibile per potentiam Dei absolutam, quod ex natura rei non involvit contradictionem si fieret: illud, e contra, impossibile, quod involveret contradictionem. Atque sub hac consideratione, ut recte Thomas, quicquid habere potest rationem entis, censetur in hisce possibilibus absolutis: in impossibilibus autem, quod rationem entis habere non potest; quale est, quicquid implicat in se esse et non esse simul. Quod talia non subsunt Divinae omnipotentiae, haud arguit ullum defectum in Deo. Quia sicut non est defectus visivae potentiae, cum minime feratur in illud quod non est visibile; ita neque defectus est potentiae absolutae, quod minime terminetur ad illud quod id impossibile. Sufficit itaque ad omnipotentiam Dei stabiliendam, quod possit facere quicquid est factu possibile: de eis autem quae aliter se habent convenientius dicitur quod talia non possunt fieri, quam quod Deus talia non possit facere. Huc referunt nonnulli illud Luc. i. 37, Non erit impossibile apud Deum omne verbum, idest, Quicquid concipi potest sine implicatione contradictionis a quocunque intellectu, illud a Deo fieri potest. Norma itaque judicandi quid Deus possit facere de potentia absoluta, ab ipsa re sumi debet; quia ubi non est defectus possibilitatis ex parte rei, non est defectus potentiae ex parte Dei. Sed haec absoluta potentia non illa est quam proprie et proxime respicimus in thesi nostra, sed potius illa, quam ordinatam sive ordinariam appellamus. Ea autem accipitur in ordine ad legem aliquam communem datam et promulgatam a Deo, secundum quam aliquid intelligitur possibile fieri vel non fieri, aut etiam secundum communem cursum rerum naturalium vel moralium, ut recte Bannes. Hoc sensu affirmamus, utcunque nobis ignotum sit arcanum decretum Divinae voluntatis de danda fide aut non danda personis singularibus, tamen quia non est lex communis a Deo promulgata decernens oppositum, debere nos de quolibet viatore pronuntiare, Fidei et poenitentiae conditionem secundum ordinariam Dei potentiam esse illi possibilem: sicut e contra recte dicimus secundum potentiam ordinatam vel ordinariam fidem ac poenitentiam esse jam cuivis damnato impossibilem.
english: Second, when we refer this possibility of having faith to God’s active power, and to the human being’s receptive power, this is to be understood not of God’s absolute power only, but of God’s ordinary power. For among Theologians some things are called possible by God’s absolute power, some by ordinary power. It will not be foreign to our purpose to give this distinction explained in a few words. That, then, is called possible by God’s absolute power which from the nature of the thing does not involve a contradiction if it were done; that, on the contrary, is impossible which would involve a contradiction. And under this consideration, as Thomas rightly has it, whatever can have the ratio of a being is counted among these absolute possibles; but among impossibles, what cannot have the ratio of a being — such as whatever implies in itself to be and not to be at once. That such things are not subject to Divine omnipotence argues no defect in God. Because just as there is no defect of the power of sight when it is not directed to what is not visible, so neither is there a defect of absolute power because it is not terminated to what is impossible. It therefore suffices for establishing God’s omnipotence that he can do whatever is possible to be done: but of those things that are otherwise disposed it is more fittingly said that such things cannot be done, than that God cannot do such things. To this some refer that of ([[Luke 1:37 >> Bible:Luke 1:37]]): No word will be impossible with God — that is, Whatever can be conceived by any intellect without implication of contradiction, that can be done by God. The norm, then, for judging what God can do by absolute power ought to be taken from the thing itself; because where there is no defect of possibility on the thing’s part, there is no defect of power on God’s part.

But this absolute power is not the one we properly and proximately look to in our thesis, but rather that which we call ordained or ordinary. That is taken in relation to some common law given and promulgated by God, according to which something is understood as possible to be done or not done, or also according to the common course of natural or moral things, as Báñez rightly has it. In this sense we affirm that, however unknown to us the secret decree of the Divine will may be concerning giving or not giving faith to singular persons, yet because there is no common law promulgated by God deciding the opposite, we ought to pronounce concerning any wayfarer that the condition of faith and penitence is possible for him according to God’s ordinary power: just as, on the contrary, we rightly say that according to ordained or ordinary power faith and penitence are already impossible for any damned person.

source_text:
Possibilitas illa habendi fidem, quae viatorem quemvis respicit, triplici argumento confirmatur. 1. Primo a misericordia Divina ducto. Deus enim, ut loquitur Prosper, nemini (in via adhuc constituto) correctionis adimit viam, nec quemquam boni possibilitate despoliat. Quinetiam legem fixit de indulgenda remissione peccatorum et vita aeterna cuivis poenitenti et credenti, Nolo mortem impii, sed ut convertatur impius a via sua, et vivat, Ezek. xxxiii. 11. Ergo non solum juxta potentiam Dei absolutam, sed secundum potentiam ordinariam quivis incredulus et impius potest vera poenitentia et fide salutifera donari. De Judaeis incredulis vere dicit Apostolus Rom. xi. 23, Potest Deus rursus eos inserere. Et de omnibus contumacibus peccatoribus in Dei persona recte affirmatur illud Apoc. ii. 21, Dedi illis tempus ut poenitentiam agerent, et noluerunt poenitere. Qui hominibus ita concessit totum hujus vitae spatium ut in quolibet ejusdem momento conversio ad Deum possit illis esse salutifera, juxta illud celeberrimum Prophetae dictum Ezek. xviii. 21, 22, Si impius egerit poenitentiam ab omnibus peccatis suis, etc. omnium iniquitatum ejus non recordabor; idem et sibi reservavit ut secundum ordinatam suam potentiam possit cuivis nondum ad inferos damnato gratiam fidei et poenitentiae infundere. Hinc est quod neminem ponere debemus extra possibilem salutis statum, quem patientia Dei sinit vivere.

2. Secundo, idem ostendi potest argumento ducto a respectu Christi Capitis, ad quemvis viatorum. Nam quamvis Caput naturale non habeat potentiam influendi nisi in membra conjuncta et unita, tamen hoc Caput mysticum potest agere in membra separata, et influere illis gratiam vivificam, qua mediante sibi uniantur. Quo sensu non incommode statuit Aquinas, Part. 3. qu. 8. art. 1, Christum esse caput omnium hominum, sed secundum diversos gradus. Principaliter dicitur Caput eorum qui sibi uniuntur per gloriam, aut per gratiam actualiter communicatam; minus principaliter eorum qui secundum legem Dei ordinariam possunt sibi adhuc uniri, sive ea potentia sit in actum reducenda, sive non: Illorum autem qui non sunt in potentia ad recipiendum influxum Christi nullatenus Caput dici potest. Tales autem judicari debent omnes et soli damnati; quia secundum promulgatam Dei voluntatem ab inferis nulla est redemtio. Potentia igitur habendi fidem, quoad quemvis in hac vita adhuc constitutum, fundatur in sufficientissima virtute Christi Capitis ad influendum, et praedicta Dei misericordia, qui secundum legem communem totum hujus vitae spatium patere voluit ad recipiendum.

3. Ultimo in loco, poenitentiae et fidei conditionem, sub qua mors Christi est cuivis homini ad salutem applicabilis, esse dum hic vivitur possibilem, patet ex diversa conditione hominum, dum viatores sunt, et postquam ad terminum pervenerunt. Ex consensu omnium Theologorum voluntas cujuscunque viatoris est pro hoc statu in bonum flexibilis; sicut e contra voluntas damnatorum pro illo statu in malo immobiliter obfirmata. Utcunque clarum est. Post hanc vitam immobilem et plane immutabilem esse statum hominum malorum, nemo dubitat. Nam ut recte Damascenus, lib. 2. cap. 4, Quod est angelis casus, idem hominibus mors. Si ceciderit lignum, sive ad austrum, sive ad aquilonem, in quocunque loco ceciderit, ibi erit, Eccles. xi. 3. E contra, flexibilis est voluntas et mutabilis malitia hominum in hac mortali vita constitutorum, adeo ut de potentia Dei ordinaria quivis incredulus possit illuminari, quivis impoenitens converti, uno verbo, quivis impius justificari et salvari. Unde illud Apostoli 2 Tim. ii. 25, 26, Cum lenitate erudiendos esse eos qui contrario animo sunt affecti: siquando det eis Deus ut resipiscentes agnoscant veritatem, ac mentis recipiant sanitatem. Innuit igitur haec posse adhuc fieri, et debere a nobis sperari. Non dissimile est illud Petri, 2 Petr. iii. 9, Patiens est Dominus erga nos, nolens ullos perire, sed omnes ad resipiscentiam tendere. Morum corrigendorum nullus alius quam in hac vita locus, inquit Augustinus, Epist. 54. In hac autem vita dum sumus, nullum tempus aut serum aut citum nimis ad recuperandam animae sanitatem, ut vere Clemens Alexandrinus Strom. lib. 2. Quis accepturus sit a Deo fidem et poenitentiam antequam exeat e vita, quis non accepturus, arcanum est pendens ex ejus voluntate; sed ipsam potentiam ad fidem et poenitentiam manere ad extremum usque hujus vitae periodum, etsi quidem frustra hujusmodi potentia esset nisi in aliquibus ad actum reduceretur: quod autem in omnibus non reducatur, partim ad arcanam Dei voluntatem, partim ad manifestam hominum pravitatem est referendum. Utroque respectu, ex capacitate sive potentia ad fidem et salutem, quoad multos in actum minime reducta, consequitur Deus majorem misericordiae suae manifestationem erga electos, justitiae manifestationem clariorem erga impios incredulos et impoenitentes: atque idcirco talis potentia non frustra illis conceditur. Bene Alvarez De auxiliis, disp. 105, Ut aliqua potentia non sit frustra, non requiritur ut aliquando sit reducenda ad quemlibet actum quem producere potest; sed sufficit quod reducatur ad aliquem, vel aliquos. Sicut enim nemo vere dixerit potentiam ad percipiendas disciplinas Mathematicas esse frustra datam hominibus a natura, quamvis multi capaces harum disciplinarum non inveniant magistros qui illos actu instituunt in eisdem; ita nemo affirmaverit hanc potentiam ad credendum et poenitendum frustra adesse omnibus viatoribus ex fixa Dei lege, quamvis Deus non efficiat in omnibus ut credant, ut poeniteant.
english: That possibility of having faith, which looks to any wayfarer, is confirmed by a triple argument. First, one drawn from Divine mercy. For God, as Prosper speaks, takes from no one (still constituted on the way) the path of correction, nor strips anyone of the possibility of good. Moreover he has fixed a law concerning granting remission of sins and eternal life to any penitent and believing person: I do not will the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live ([[Ezekiel 33:11 >> Bible:Ezekiel 33:11]]). Therefore not only according to God’s absolute power, but according to ordinary power, any unbeliever and impious person can be gifted with true penitence and saving faith. Of the unbelieving Jews the Apostle truly says ([[Romans 11:23 >> Bible:Romans 11:23]]): God is able to graft them in again. And of all contumacious sinners it is rightly affirmed in God’s person ([[Revelation 2:21 >> Bible:Revelation 2:21]]): I gave them time that they might repent, and they were unwilling to repent. He who has so granted human beings the whole span of this life that in any moment of it conversion to God can be saving for them, according to that most celebrated saying of the Prophet ([[Ezekiel 18:21–22 >> Bible:Ezekiel 18:21]]), If the wicked shall have done penitence from all his sins, etc., I will not remember all his iniquities — the same has also reserved to himself that according to his ordained power he can infuse the grace of faith and penitence into anyone not yet damned to the underworld. Hence it is that we ought to put no one outside a possible state of salvation whom God’s patience allows to live.

Second, the same can be shown by an argument drawn from the respect of Christ the Head toward any of the wayfarers. For although a natural head does not have power of influencing except into members conjoined and united, yet this mystical Head can act upon separated members and pour into them vivifying grace by which they are united to him. In which sense Aquinas not inconveniently lays down (Part 3, question 8, article 1) that Christ is the head of all human beings, but according to diverse degrees. He is called Head principally of those who are united to him by glory, or by grace actually communicated; less principally of those who according to God’s ordinary law can still be united to him, whether that power is to be reduced into act or not: but of those who are in no potency to receive Christ’s influx he can in no way be called Head. Such, however, ought to be judged all and only the damned; because according to God’s promulgated will there is no redemption from the underworld. The power of having faith, then, as to anyone still constituted in this life, is founded in the most sufficient virtue of Christ the Head for influencing, and in the aforesaid mercy of God, who according to the common law willed the whole span of this life to lie open for receiving.

Last, that the condition of penitence and faith, under which Christ’s death is applicable to any human being unto salvation, is possible while we live here, is plain from the diverse condition of human beings while they are wayfarers and after they have come to the term. By the consent of all Theologians the will of any wayfarer is for this state flexible toward the good; just as, on the contrary, the will of the damned for that state is immoveably hardened in evil. However clear it is. That after this life the state of bad human beings is immobile and plainly immutable, no one doubts. For as Damascene rightly has it, book 2, chapter 4: What the fall is to angels, the same is death to human beings. If a tree shall have fallen, whether toward the south or toward the north, in whatever place it shall have fallen, there it will be ([[Ecclesiastes 11:3 >> Bible:Ecclesiastes 11:3]]). On the contrary, the will is flexible and the malice of human beings constituted in this mortal life is mutable, so far that by God’s ordinary power any unbeliever can be illuminated, any impenitent converted — in a word, any impious person justified and saved. Whence that of the Apostle ([[2 Timothy 2:25–26 >> Bible:2 Timothy 2:25]]): Those who are affected with a contrary mind are to be instructed with gentleness: if at some time God may give them that repenting they may acknowledge the truth and receive soundness of mind. He therefore hints that these things can still be done, and ought to be hoped for by us. Not unlike is that of Peter ([[2 Peter 3:9 >> Bible:2 Peter 3:9]]): The Lord is patient toward us, not willing that any perish, but that all tend to repentance. There is no other place for correcting morals than in this life, says Augustine, Letter 54. But in this life while we are, no time is either too late or too early for recovering the soul’s health, as Clement of Alexandria truly has it in the Stromata. Who is going to receive faith and penitence from God before he exits life, who is not going to receive, is a secret hanging from his will; but that the very power unto faith and penitence remains to the extreme period of this life — although such a power would indeed be in vain unless in some it were reduced to act; but that it is not reduced in all is to be referred partly to God’s secret will, partly to the manifest wickedness of human beings. Under both respects, from a capacity or power unto faith and salvation least reduced into act as to many, there follows for God a greater manifestation of his mercy toward the elect, a clearer manifestation of justice toward the impious unbelieving and impenitent: and therefore such a power is not granted them in vain. Alvarez well, On Helps, disputation 105: For some power not to be in vain, it is not required that it sometime be reduced to every act it can produce; but it suffices that it be reduced to some, or several. For just as no one would truly say that the power of perceiving the mathematical disciplines is given to human beings by nature in vain, although many capable of these disciplines do not find masters who actually instruct them in the same; so no one will have affirmed that this power of believing and repenting is present in vain to all wayfarers by God’s fixed law, although God does not effect in all that they believe, that they repent.

source_text:
Objicitur et illud, quod majorem scrupulum videtur injicere, Deum ab aeterno non solum praescivisse sed praedestinasse quibus infallibiliter daturus est fidem, remissionem et vitam aeternam, quibus non daturus: Non potest autem Deus in tempore alia aut aliter agere quam ab aeterno praescivit et decrevit se facturum. Hoc argumento olim nixus Abailardus audacter asseruit, Deum non posse aliquid facere praeter ea quae fecit aut facturus est. Si hoc obtineat, cum certum sit quoad majorem hominum partem Deum nec praescivisse fidem in illis producendam, nec decrevisse, non est quod dicamus hanc fidei conditionem esse ullo modo possibilem quoad non-electos in hac vita etiamnum constitutos.

Deum absque aeterno decreto et aeterna praescientia antecedente nihil agere aut permittere, verissimum est. Sed si quis inde concludat Deum non posse facere juxta potentiam ordinariam quicquam praeter ea quae praescivit et decrevit facienda, falsissimum est. Nam ut recte Halensis noster, Part. 1. qu. 21. art. 4. memb. 2, Divina potentia nec voluntate nec praescientia Dei limitatur, quamvis egressum Divinae potentiae in actum semper praescientia ejus et voluntas concomitetur. Rationem hujus rei satis idoneam reddit Aquinas, nempe, Quia ipsum facere subjacet praescientiae et ordinationi facientis; non autem ipsum posse quod est naturale. Ideo enim Deus aliquid facit quia vult, non tamen ideo potest quia vult, sed quia potens est natura sua, Part. 1. qu. 25. art. 5. ad 1. Idem Aquinas praedictae objectioni in forma respondet, Quaest. Disp. De Potentia Dei art. 5. Resp. ad 1, cujus verba apponam, Haec locutio, Deus NON POTEST FACERE NISI QUOD PRAESCIT SE FACTURUM, est duplex: quia particula exceptiva NISI refertur vel ad potentiam quae importatur per verbum POTEST, vel ad actum qui importatur per verbum FACERE. Si primo modo, tunc locutio est falsa: Plura enim potest facere Deus quam praesciat se facturum. Si secundo modo, tum sensus est, quod non potest esse quod aliquid fiat a Deo, et non sit a Deo praescitum: sic locutio est vera; sed hic sensus nihil facit ad propositum. Hactenus ille. Verum quia nonnulli ita toti incumbunt huic aeternae et arcanae voluntatis praescientiaeque contemplationi, ut nihil fere aliud in animos suos admittant, ostendemus breviter, neque Scripturas, neque Patres, neque ipsam rationem permittere ut secundum arcana haec et aeterna decreta praedestinationis statuatur a nobis quid possibile sit Deo, aut impossibile secundum ordinariam ejus potentiam.

Ordiamur a Scripturis: quae non artare solent Dei potentiam secundum arcana decreta voluntatis ejus, sed eam extendere secundum infinitas Dei vires, et secundum regulam in verbo revelatam. Matth. iii. 9, Potens est Deus de lapidibus istis suscitare filios Abrahae. Matth. xix. 26, Omnia possibilia sunt apud Deum.
