Et Matth. xxvi. 53, An non possum rogare Patrem, et exhibebit mihi plusquam duodecim legiones angelorum? Marc. xiv. 36, Omnia tibi possibilia sunt: transfer calicem hunc a me. Sic etiam loquitur Apostolus, de Judaeis refractariis, Potens est Deus iterum inserere illos, Rom. xi. 23. Et de quovis homine lapso, Tu quis es qui judicas alienum servum? Domino suo stat aut cadit. Stabit autem: Potens est enim Deus statuere eum, Rom. xiv. 4. denique de quolibet viatore Verum est illud, Potens est Deus omnem gratiam abundare facere in eo, 2 Cor. ix. 8. Pluribus supersedeo. Ex hisce satis liquet, de potentia Dei ex arcanis ejus decretis minime esse judicandum: Non enim decrevit ex lapidibus excitare filios Abrahae, non Christum liberare e manibus Judaeorum, non quemvis lapsum erigere et statuminare, non gratiae suae copiam in quosvis effundere: imo decrevit et praescivit se haec omnia minime facturum, quae tamen (si sacras Scripturas audire velimus) non idcirco pro impossibilibus habentur.

Augustinus in hanc sententiam, Omnipotens Deus multa potest facere quae nec vult nec facit. Instat etiam idem Pater in ipso Juda, extra controversiam reprobo, Dominus, inquit, qui Lazarum suscitavit in corpore, non potuit Judam suscitare in mente? Potuit quidem, sed noluit. Quod de Juda non veretur affirmare Augustinus, id nos de quovis viatore intrepide affirmemus, non obstante arcana Dei voluntate aut praescientia de eodem, nempe posse Deum quemvis in mente suscitare, id est, poenitentia et fide ac gratia salutifera donare; quia de nullo particulari homine revelavit se hoc nolle, et de quolibet revelavit se per potentiam ordinariam hoc posse facere, dum est in via adhuc constitutus. Huic voluntati nos oportet incumbere, et de possibilitate aut impossibilitate rerum ex voluntate nobis prorsus incognita minime hariolari.
english: That also is objected which seems to cast a greater scruple: that God from eternity not only foreknew but predestined to whom he will infallibly give faith, remission, and eternal life, and to whom he will not: But God cannot in time act otherwise, or otherwise than he from eternity foreknew and decreed that he would do. On this argument Abelard once boldly asserted that God cannot do anything beyond those things which he has done or is going to do. If this holds, since it is certain that as to the greater part of human beings God neither foreknew faith to be produced in them nor decreed it, there is no ground for our saying that this condition of faith is in any way possible as to the non-elect still constituted in this life.

That God does or permits nothing without an antecedent eternal decree and eternal foreknowledge is most true. But if anyone thence concludes that God cannot do by ordinary power anything beyond those things which he foreknew and decreed to be done, that is most false. For as our Halensis rightly has it, Part 1, question 21, article 4, member 2: Divine power is limited neither by God’s will nor by his foreknowledge, although the egress of Divine power into act is always accompanied by his foreknowledge and will. Aquinas renders a reason of this matter fit enough, namely: Because the very doing is subject to the foreknowledge and ordination of the one doing; but not the very being-able, which is natural. For God therefore does something because he wills; yet he can not therefore because he wills, but because he is powerful by his nature (Part 1, question 25, article 5, to the first). The same Aquinas answers the aforesaid objection in form in the Disputed Questions On the Power of God, article 5, reply to 1, whose words I will set down: This locution, God CANNOT DO EXCEPT WHAT HE FOREKNOWS HE WILL DO, is twofold: because the exceptive particle EXCEPT is referred either to the power which is imported by the verb CAN, or to the act which is imported by the verb DO. If in the first way, then the locution is false: For God can do more things than he foreknows he will do. If in the second way, then the sense is that it cannot be that something is done by God and is not foreknown by God: so the locution is true; but this sense does nothing for the purpose. Thus far he. But because some so wholly lean on this contemplation of the eternal and secret will and foreknowledge that they admit almost nothing else into their minds, we will show briefly that neither the Scriptures, nor the Fathers, nor reason itself permit that according to these secret and eternal decrees of predestination it be established by us what is possible for God, or impossible, according to his ordinary power.

Let us begin from the Scriptures: which are accustomed not to restrict God’s power according to the secret decrees of his will, but to extend it according to God’s infinite strength, and according to the rule revealed in the word. ([[Matthew 3:9 >> Bible:Matthew 3:9]]): God is able from these stones to raise up children of Abraham. ([[Matthew 19:26 >> Bible:Matthew 19:26]]): All things are possible with God. And ([[Matthew 26:53 >> Bible:Matthew 26:53]]): Can I not ask the Father, and he will exhibit to me more than twelve legions of angels? ([[Mark 14:36 >> Bible:Mark 14:36]]): All things are possible to you: transfer this cup from me. So also the Apostle speaks of the refractory Jews: God is able to graft them in again ([[Romans 11:23 >> Bible:Romans 11:23]]). And of any fallen human being: Who are you who judge another’s servant? To his own Lord he stands or falls. But he will stand: for God is able to make him stand ([[Romans 14:4 >> Bible:Romans 14:4]]). Finally of any wayfarer that is true: God is able to make all grace abound in him ([[2 Corinthians 9:8 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 9:8]]). I pass over more. From these it is plain enough that God’s power is least to be judged from his secret decrees: For he did not decree to raise children of Abraham from stones, nor to free Christ from the Jews’ hands, nor to raise and establish any fallen person, nor to pour the abundance of his grace into any and all: indeed he decreed and foreknew that he would least do all these things, which yet (if we are willing to hear the sacred Scriptures) are not therefore held for impossibles.

Augustine to this sense: Almighty God can do many things which he neither wills nor does. The same Father also presses the point in Judas himself, a reprobate beyond controversy: The Lord, he says, who raised Lazarus in the body — could he not raise Judas in the mind? He could indeed, but he was unwilling. What Augustine does not fear to affirm of Judas, let us intrepidly affirm of any wayfarer, the secret will or foreknowledge of God concerning the same notwithstanding: namely that God can raise anyone in the mind, that is, gift him with penitence and faith and saving grace; because of no particular human being has he revealed that he wills not this, and of each he has revealed that by ordinary power he can do this while he is still constituted on the way. On this will we ought to lean, and least to divine about the possibility or impossibility of things from a will utterly unknown to us.

source_text: Denique ipsa ratio docet Divinam potentiam ordinariam non artari per arcana decreta aeternae praedestinationis. 1. Quia nos homunculi sentimus potentiam nostram non constringi juxta placita voluntatis nostrae. Qui firmissime decrevit apud se huic homini singulari non dare eleemosynam, haud inde amittit potestatem dandi: et e contra, qui decrevit dare alteri, haud inde adimit sibi potestatem non dandi. Sicut enim libere voluit unum oppositorum, cum potuisset velle alterum; ita et libere facit unum, non amissa potentia faciendi alterum. Si res sic se habeat in homine, cujus potentia est mutabilis et amissibilis, quanto magis in Deo, cujus potentia est immutabilis, aeterna et semper eadem. 2. Quia si ponamus ordinariam Dei potentiam aeternis et occultis ejus decretis alligatam et quasi circumscriptam, nihil possemus a Deo petere cum certa fide, non dicam quod velit, sed quod possit nobis subvenire: Verbi causa, si sensero me ab ipso Satana gravi aliqua tentatione pulsatum, non possum cum fide certitudine ad Deum recurrere, quasi potentem me liberare, quia mihi incertum est quid hac de re ab aeterno decreverit. Pari ratione non possemus Deum orare ut quosvis infideles ad fidem convertat, ut quosvis impios ad poenitentiam reducat, cum plena persuasione quod possit facere illud quod rogamus; quia nos latet quid in occulto ante jacta mundi fundamenta hisce de rebus Deo decretum sit. 3. Denique quia si nihil aliud judicetur possibile fieri, praeter ea quae Deus decrevit facienda, sequeretur Divinam potentiam non esse infinitam. Finita est enim illa potentia quae finitis effectis adaequatur, et in totum suum actum educitur. Potentia siquidem infinita, ut recte Halensis, Part. 1. qu. 21, Potest educi in actum, sed non in totum. Potest igitur Deus multa facere quae non vult, puta hanc personam singularem quamcunque fide donare, justificare, salvare. Imo, potest multa velle quae non vult, et tamen ejus voluntas (ut recte Lombardus, Lib. 1. Dist. 43. Littera E) Nec nova, nec mutabilis aliquo modo potest esse. Quod etsi possit velle quod nunquam voluit, non tamen aliter, nec nova voluntate, sed sempiterna tantum voluntate velle potest. Potest enim velle quod ab aeterno potest voluisse: habet enim potentiam volendi, et nunc, et ab aeterno, quod tamen nec modo vult nec ab aeterno voluit. Hactenus ille. Paulo fusius haec edisserenda putavimus, ut clarius constet Christi mortem esse cuivis viatori applicabilem, quia Fidei et poenitentiae conditio est cuivis viatori possibilis, arcano praedestinationis aut praeteritionis decreto hanc potentiam sive ex parte Dei sive ex parte hominum nullatenus perimente aut coarctante. Parum igitur considerate faciunt, qui universalitatem mortis Christi, ad homines quoscunque sub Evangelici pacti tenore pertinentem, per occultae electionis et praeteritionis decreta conantur evertere. Tantum est de secunda nostra thesi: pergamus ad tertiam.
english: Finally reason itself teaches that ordinary Divine power is not restricted by the secret decrees of eternal predestination. First, because we little humans sense that our power is not constrained according to the decrees of our will. He who has most firmly decreed with himself not to give alms to this singular human being does not thence lose the power of giving: and on the contrary, he who has decreed to give to another does not thence take from himself the power of not giving. For just as he freely willed one of opposites, when he could have willed the other, so also he freely does the one, the power of doing the other not lost. If the matter so stands in a human being, whose power is mutable and losable, how much more in God, whose power is immutable, eternal, and always the same. Second, because if we posit God’s ordinary power bound to his eternal and occult decrees and as it were circumscribed, we could ask nothing from God with sure faith — I do not say that he wills, but that he can help us. For example: if I sense myself struck by Satan himself with some heavy temptation, I cannot with the certainty of faith flee back to God as able to free me, because it is uncertain to me what he decreed from eternity about this matter. By like reason we could not pray God to convert any unbelievers to faith, to bring any impious persons back to penitence, with full persuasion that he can do what we ask; because what was decreed to God in secret before the foundations of the world about these things is hidden from us. Third, finally, because if nothing else is judged possible to be done besides those things which God decreed to be done, it would follow that Divine power is not infinite. For that power is finite which is equaled to finite effects and is educed into its whole act. But infinite power, as Halensis rightly has it, Part 1, question 21, Can be educed into act, but not into the whole. God can therefore do many things which he does not will — for example, gift any singular person whatever with faith, justify, save. Indeed, he can will many things which he does not will, and yet his will (as Lombard rightly has it, Book 1, Distinction 43, Letter E) Can be neither new nor mutable in any way. Which, although he can will what he never willed, yet not otherwise, nor by a new will, but only by a sempiternal will can he will. For he can will what from eternity he can have willed: for he has the power of willing, both now and from eternity, what yet he neither now wills nor from eternity willed. Thus far he.

We thought these things should be set out a little more fully, that it may stand clearer that Christ’s death is applicable to any wayfarer, because the condition of Faith and penitence is possible for any wayfarer, the secret decree of predestination or preterition in no way destroying or coarcting this power either on God’s part or on human beings’ part. Therefore those act with little consideration who try to overturn the universality of Christ’s death, pertaining to any human beings under the tenor of the Evangelical pact, by the decrees of occult election and preterition. So much for our second thesis: let us go on to the third.

source_text:
CAPUT V. Thesis tertia proponitur, illustratur, confirmatur.

Has priores nostras theses jam absolvimus, in quibus explicatum est quo sensu mors Christi universalis humanae salutis causa sit agnoscenda; illudque etiam ostensum, eos haud recte intelligere receptissimum Theologorum pronunciatum, Christus pro omnibus mortuus est sufficienter, pro electis efficaciter, qui nudam rei in se consideratae sufficientiam admittunt, atque interim excludunt ordinatam ejusdem sufficientiam, ex voluntate Dei ad omnes et singulos homines, juxta tenorem Evangelici pacti, sub possibili fidei conditione pertinentem. Jam vero, quia ex altera parte reperti sunt nonnulli, qui hanc universalem vim et ordinationem mortis Christi consideratam, hoc ipso solo quod Christus in ara crucis pro omnibus sese obtulit, plus aequo extendunt, erit nobis tertia thesis adjungenda, quae limites statuat ad quos se porrigat, et extra quos se minime diffundat haec universalis vis mortis Christi, quae humanum genus complectitur, et ex ipsa passione Christi, absque ullo alio medio considerata, exoritur. Ea autem erit hujusmodi.

Mors sive passio Christi, ut universalis causa salutis humanae, Deum Patrem ipso facto oblationis eatenus reddidit placatum et reconciliatum humano generi, ut vere nunc dicatur paratus quemvis hominem in gratiam recipere, simulac in Christum crediderit; neminem tamen, saltem ex adultis, praedicta Christi mors reponit in statum gratiae, actualis reconciliationis, sive salutis, antequam credat.

Sunt hujus thesis duo membra, quae seorsim tractabimus et argumentis confirmabimus, ubi de vocabulo reconciliationis ad clariorem totius rei intelligentiam paucula fuerint praemissa. Sciendum ergo est, Deum hominis peccato offensum non modo destituisse eum paterno suo favore, et aeternae morti adjudicasse, sed insuper decrevisse firmiter, quicquid, per nos unquam aut faceremus, aut pateremur, sub nulla conditione in aeternum nobis reconciliari. Sicuti offensa Dei hisce duobus quasi gradibus continebatur, ita reconciliatio nostra duobus aliis, hisce quasi ex adverso respondentibus, peragitur. Prior gradus reconciliationis tum procuratus intelligitur, quamprimum, etsi non a nobis, tamen nostro nomine id factum est, quo Divina voluntas inclinatur ut jam velit nobiscum sub certa aliqua conditione praestanda in gratiam redire, ac remissionem peccatorum, et vitam aeternam impertire. Hunc reconciliationis gradum, sine ullo alio medio, ipsa vi et ipso merito passionis Dominicae omnibus hominibus partum affirmamus. Atque hinc est (uti supra annotavimus) quod mors Christi redemtio sive reconciliatio totius mundi perhibetur: Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi, 2 Cor. v. 19. In quam sententiam Prosper, Ad Capit. Gallor. obj. 9. Redemtor mundi dedit pro mundo sanguinem suum, etc. Vide Augustinum, Epist. 159, 171, 173. Haec igitur reconciliatio mundi est quasi primus gradus ad actualem singulorum hominum reconciliationem; quorum nemini patuisset aditus ad hanc gratiam Divinam sub fidei conditione, absque hoc esset, quod Deus morte Christi aliquatenus reconciliatus humano generi exstitisset. Posterior gradus reconciliationis in eo situs est, atque tum acquisitus judicatur huic aut illi singulari personae, quando praestita fidei in Christum conditione in gratiam Dei paternam recipitur, justificatur et hereditario ad aeternam vitam jure donatur. Ad hunc posteriorem gradum nemo pervenit solo opere ipsius Christi semetipsum in cruce Deo Patri offerentis, sed accedat oportet, priusquam hanc actualem reconciliationem impetret, actus sive opus ipsius hominis credentis in Christum redemtorem, ac fide meritum mortis ejus sibi singulariter applicantis. Huc referri potest illud Johan. viii. 24. Nisi credideritis me eum esse, moriemini in peccatis vestris. Mors igitur Christi non eripit a morte, neque actualiter reconciliat Deo, hanc aut illam singularem personam, nisi credentem.
english: Chapter 5. The third thesis is proposed, illustrated, and confirmed.

We have already finished our prior theses, in which it was explained in what sense the death of Christ is to be acknowledged as a universal cause of human salvation; and it was also shown that those do not rightly understand the most received saying of the theologians, Christ died for all sufficiently, for the elect efficaciously, who admit a bare sufficiency of the thing considered in itself, and meanwhile exclude an ordered sufficiency of the same, belonging from the will of God to all and each human beings according to the tenor of the Evangelical pact, under a possible condition of faith. Now indeed, because on the other side some have been found who stretch this universal force and ordination of the death of Christ considered, by this alone that Christ offered himself on the altar of the cross for all, beyond what is equal, a third thesis will have to be added by us, which may set the limits to which this universal force of the death of Christ extends itself, and beyond which it by no means diffuses itself — this force which embraces the human race and arises from the passion of Christ itself, considered without any other medium. It will be of this sort.

The death or passion of Christ, as a universal cause of human salvation, has by the very fact of the oblation rendered God the Father so far placated and reconciled to the human race that he may truly now be said ready to receive any human being into grace as soon as he has believed in Christ; yet the aforesaid death of Christ places no one, at least of adults, into the state of grace, of actual reconciliation, or of salvation, before he believes.

There are two members of this thesis, which we will treat separately and confirm with arguments, when a few things have first been premised about the word reconciliation for a clearer understanding of the whole matter. It must therefore be known that God, offended by the sin of man, not only stripped him of his paternal favor and adjudged him to eternal death, but further firmly decreed never to be reconciled to us under any condition by anything we would ever do or suffer. Just as the offense of God was contained in these two quasi-grades, so our reconciliation is carried through in two other grades answering these as it were from the opposite side. The prior grade of reconciliation is understood as procured as soon as — although not by us, yet in our name — that was done whereby the Divine will is inclined so that it already wills to return into grace with us under some certain condition to be performed, and to impart remission of sins and eternal life. This grade of reconciliation we affirm procured for all human beings by the very force and the very merit of the Lord’s passion, without any other medium. And hence it is (as we annotated above) that the death of Christ is set forth as the redemption or reconciliation of the whole world: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself (2 Cor. 5:19). Into which sense Prosper, Against the chapters of the Gauls, objection 9: The Redeemer of the world gave his blood for the world, etc. See Augustine, Epistles 159, 171, 173. This reconciliation of the world, therefore, is as it were the first grade toward the actual reconciliation of singular human beings; to none of whom would access to this Divine grace under the condition of faith have lain open, unless it were that God by the death of Christ had somehow stood reconciled to the human race. The posterior grade of reconciliation is situated in this, and is then judged acquired for this or that singular person, when, the condition of faith in Christ having been performed, he is received into the paternal grace of God, is justified, and is gifted with a hereditary right to eternal life. No one arrives at this posterior grade by the sole work of Christ himself offering himself on the cross to God the Father, but there must accede, before he obtains this actual reconciliation, an act or work of the human being himself believing in Christ the Redeemer and by faith applying the merit of his death to himself singularly. To this that of John 8:24 can be referred: Unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins. The death of Christ therefore does not snatch from death, nor actually reconcile to God, this or that singular person, except as believing.

source_text:
Posita hac vocabuli reconciliationis sive distinctione sive explicatione, jam revertamur ad thesin propositam, cujus prius membrum priore loco a nobis confirmandum, sic se habuit, Ipso facto mortis Christi Deus eatenus reconciliatus est cuivis homini, ut vere dicatur paratus quemvis in gratiam, imo ad vitam aeternam, admittere, si modo crediderit. Eo paucioribus hanc rem expediemus, quod quae de universali pacto, per mortem Christi sub conditione fidei stabilito, disputavimus, huc spectant omnia: nonnulla tamen adjiciemus.

Primo igitur ipse tenor praedicationis nostrae Evangelicae hoc demonstrat. Quid enim aliud praedicamus hominibus impiis et adhuc incredulis, quam morte Christi effectum esse, ut Divina voluntas longe aliter jam erga humanum genus se habeat quam habuisset seclusa hac morte Christi? Nimirum quod Deus ille justus, qui absque sanguine Mediatoris nil aliud quam iram et mortem spirasset adversus nos omnes et singulos, jam placatus sanguine redemtoris veniam vitamque omnibus et singulis paratus sit indulgere, modo supplices atque in Mediatorem credentes sese praebeant. Deus nunquam juberet Ministros hoc promiscue hominibus praedicare, nisi reapse ita esset animo comparatus. Evangelium siquidem est sermo veritatis, Coloss. i. 5. quod nihil falsum aut vanum peccatoribus annunciat. Pronunciat autem promittitque Deum eatenus placatum et reconciliatum merito et efficacia sanguinis Christi in cruce suffusi ut paratus sit ad quemlibet peccatorem amplexandum, quandocunque poenituerit et crediderit: Ergo, seposita electionis et reprobationis importuna speculatione, quoad omnes et singulos praedicta Christi mortis efficacia agnosci debet, et promiscue depraedicari.

Secundo, actualis illa reconciliatio cujuscunque personae singularis, quae promittitur et exhibetur cuivis credenti propter meritum Christi crucifixi, praesupponit illam priorem gradum reconciliationis, quo Deus ita Christi morte placatus intelligitur, ut velit jam sub fidei conditione praestita cum quolibet peccatore redire in gratiam. Qui igitur fatentur quemvis hominem, quantumvis peccatis onustum, simulac crediderit, propter Christi mortem meritumque in gratiam recipi, negare non debeat Christi morte hoc effectum esse quoad omnes et singulos, ut habeant Deum paratum, imo obligatum, ad beneficium hoc reconciliationis sub praedicta conditione cuivis concedendum. Confirmatur antecedens. Quia ne cogitare quidem possumus actum reconciliationis sive remissionis perpetui quasi lege exeuntem et terminatum ad quamlibet personam credentem, eo ipso momento quo vera fide Mediatorem apprehenderit, nisi simul cogitemus et agnoscamus, Divinam voluntatem morte Christi ita esse quasi praeparatam et praedispositam ut propendeat in hunc favorem exhibendum cuivis homini, modo crediderit. Hanc propensionem sive prontitudinem Divinae voluntatis ad veniam et gratiam cuivis homini indulgondam, simulac fidei conditionem praestiterit, a nonnullis placabilitatis sive reconciliabilitatis vocabulo expressam animadverto: Quam placabilitatem sive reconciliabilitatem, ipsa passione Christi in se considerata impetratam, cur quidam Theologi tam superciliose rejiciant ego non intelligo. Deus etenim non esset actu placatus et reconciliatus cuivis homini, simulac crederet, hoc est, praestita fidei conditione, nisi esset placabilis et reconciliabilis cuivis homini antequam crederet, id est, sub praestanda fidei conditione.

Hic nobis objiciunt quidam Theologi, Ergo ex nostra sententia Deus non erit reconciliatus et placatus homini peccatori per et propter mortem Christi, sed tantum reconciliabilis et placabilis: homo item per mortem Christi non reconciliatus Deo, sed reconciliabilis sub certa quadam conditione, nempe fidei.
english: With this distinction or explanation of the word reconciliation set down, let us now return to the proposed thesis, whose prior member, to be confirmed by us in the prior place, stood thus: By the very fact of the death of Christ God is so far reconciled to any human being that he may truly be said ready to admit any into grace, even to eternal life, if only he has believed. We will dispatch this matter with fewer words, because the things we disputed about the universal pact, stabilized by the death of Christ under the condition of faith, all look toward this: yet we will add some things.

First, therefore, the very tenor of our Evangelical preaching demonstrates this. For what else do we preach to impious human beings and those still unbelieving, than that by the death of Christ it has been effected that the Divine will now stands toward the human race far otherwise than it would have stood with this death of Christ shut out? Namely, that that just God who without the blood of the Mediator would have breathed nothing other than wrath and death against us all and each, now placated by the blood of the Redeemer is ready to indulge pardon and life to all and each, provided they present themselves as suppliants and as believing in the Mediator. God would never order Ministers to preach this promiscuously to human beings unless he were in fact so disposed in mind. For the Gospel is a word of truth (Colossians 1:5), which announces nothing false or vain to sinners. But it pronounces and promises that God is so far placated and reconciled by the merit and efficacy of the blood of Christ poured out on the cross that he is ready to embrace any sinner whenever he has repented and believed: Therefore, the importunate speculation of election and reprobation set aside, the aforesaid efficacy of the death of Christ ought to be acknowledged toward all and each, and promiscuously proclaimed.

Second, that actual reconciliation of any singular person which is promised and exhibited to any believer because of the merit of crucified Christ presupposes that prior grade of reconciliation whereby God is understood so placated by the death of Christ that he already wills, under the condition of faith performed, to return into grace with any sinner. Whoever therefore confesses that any human being, however burdened with sins, as soon as he has believed is received into grace because of the death and merit of Christ, ought not to deny that by the death of Christ this has been effected toward all and each, that they have God ready, even obligated, to grant this benefit of reconciliation under the aforesaid condition to any. The antecedent is confirmed. Because we cannot even think the act of reconciliation or of perpetual remission going out as it were by law and terminated to any believing person at the very moment when he has apprehended the Mediator by true faith, unless we simultaneously think and acknowledge that the Divine will by the death of Christ is so prepared and predisposed that it leans toward exhibiting this favor to any human being, provided he has believed. This propensity or readiness of the Divine will to indulge pardon and grace to any human being as soon as he has performed the condition of faith I notice expressed by some with the word placability or reconciliability: which placability or reconciliability, obtained by the passion of Christ considered in itself, I do not understand why certain theologians reject so superciliously. For God would not be actually placated and reconciled to any human being as soon as he believed — that is, the condition of faith performed — unless he were placable and reconciliable to any human being before he believed — that is, under the condition of faith to be performed.

Here certain theologians object against us: Therefore on our view God will not be reconciled and placated to the sinful human being through and because of the death of Christ, but only reconciliable and placable: likewise the human being through the death of Christ is not reconciled to God, but reconciliable under a certain condition, namely of faith.

source_text:
Sol. Respondeo, vitiosum esse consequentiam; Deus est cuivis homini credituro reconciliabilis per mortem Christi: Ergo credenti cuivis non est reconciliatus per Christum, sed erit etiamnunc reconciliabilis. Imo profitemur Deum esse reconciliabilem cuivis homini credituro per et propter Christum; esse etiam reconciliatum cuivis homini credenti per et propter Christum; dedisse denique hanc fidei conditionem, qua interveniente actualis reconciliatio acquiritur per et propter eundem Christum. Frustra igitur et invalide ab universalis beneficii positione, nempe reconciliabilitatis sub praestandae fidei conditione, arguunt ad remotionem sive negationem particularium beneficiorum, puta reconciliationis et salutis; cum utraque a Christi morte et merito arcessantur; quamvis illa generalia absque ullo actu nostro interveniente, illa particularia non sine actu aliquo nostro, quamvis non propter aliquem nostrum actum, peragantur.

Obj. 2. Secundo, objicitur et illud (quod majoris momenti esse videtur) Si morte Christi ponamus Deum ita cuivis homini factum placabilem et reconciliabilem, ut quemvis paratus sit recipere in gratiam, si credat; nemini autem actu reconciliatum esse antequam credat; tum videmur ponere virtutem mortis Christi secundum se pari momento praestare omnibus, Deum etiam ipsum indifferenter se habere ad omnes, et quasi exspectare inferioris causae determinationem, ut mors Filii sui hominibus sive fructuosa, sive infructuosa evadat: quod nihil aliud est, quam cum Semipelagianis singulorum hominum salutem sive perditionem ex proprio uniuscujusque arbitrio, Christum per fidem sive apprehendente sive repellente, suspendere.

Respondeo, Ut sumatur, per mortem Christi Deum humano generi eatenus factum placatum aut placabilem, ut quemvis, si crediderit, nullo personarum discrimine, in gratiam sit recepturus (quae est ipsissima vox Evangelii) tamen non inde consequitur, hoc ipsum discrimen credentium et non-credentium, reconciliatorum et non-reconciliatorum, servatorum denique et perditorum ad incertam humani arbitrii aleam esse revocandum. Qui enim promulgavit hoc universale decretum Evangelicum, Quisquis crediderit salvus erit, reservavit nihilominus sibi speciale privilegium donandi fidem aliquibus pro singulari sua misericordia, non donandi aliis pro liberrima et justissima sua voluntate, atque istorum manifesta indignitate. Virtute mortis Christi Deus se obligavit ad reconciliationem ineundam cum quolibet homine, si crediderit; at non se obligavit ad infundendam eam gratiam efficacem cuilibet homini, qua infallibiliter efficiatur ut credat. Utrumque ergo tenemus, nempe et Deum Christi morte eatenus placatum, ut jam paratus sit quosvis in gratiam recipere, si poenitentiam agant et credant in Christum; atque eundem Deum, qui sub conditione fidei paratus est omnibus ex aequo remissionis gratiam indulgere, non tamen esse ita comparatum, ut ex aequo se habeat erga omnes quoad hanc fidei conditionem in illis producendam. Mercator paratus dicitur ad vendendas merces suas, si quis velit eas emere: quod autem uno nolente alius velit emere, non ipse mercator efficit, sed ex uniuscujusque libero arbitrio dependet. Non ita se res habet inter Deum et nos. Nam etsi virtute mortis Christi jam paratus sit ad dandam remissionem et reconciliationem ineundam cum quovis homine, si velit in Christum credere, tamen hoc peculiare habet Deus, quod ipse inspirat omnibus credentibus hanc ipsam voluntatem credendi. Non ergo Semipelagianis suffragamur, sed dicimus cum Arausicanis Patribus, Can. 6. Si quis sine gratia Dei credentibus, volentibus, desiderantibus, et pulsantibus nobis misericordiam dicit conferri, non autem Divinitus, ut credamus et velimus, per infusionem et inspirationem Sancti Spiritus in nobis fieri confitetur, resistit Apostolo dicenti, Gratia Dei sum quod sum. Haec de primo thesis nostrae membro.

Accedo ad alterum membrum, quod hunc in modum efformatur.

Christi mors considerata ut generalis causa salutis humanae, neminem ex adultis a reatu et pondere peccatorum suorum liberat, neminem Deo actualiter reconciliatum constituit, uno verbo neminem collocat in statu gratiae et salutis, ante fidem Evangelio adhibitam.
english: Solution. I answer that the consequence is vicious; God is reconciliable through the death of Christ to any human being about to believe: Therefore he is not reconciled through Christ to any believer, but will still be only reconciliable. Rather we profess that God is reconciliable to any human being about to believe through and because of Christ; that he is also reconciled to any believing human being through and because of Christ; and finally that he has given this condition of faith, by whose intervening actual reconciliation is acquired through and because of the same Christ. In vain therefore and invalidly do they argue from the position of a universal benefit, namely of reconciliability under the condition of faith to be performed, to the removal or negation of particular benefits, for example of reconciliation and salvation; since both are fetched from the death and merit of Christ; although those general ones are carried through without any intervening act of ours, those particular ones not without some act of ours, although not because of any act of ours.

Objection 2. Second, this also is objected (which seems to be of greater moment): If by the death of Christ we posit God made so placable and reconciliable to any human being that he is ready to receive any into grace if he believes, yet actually reconciled to no one before he believes; then we seem to posit that the virtue of the death of Christ according to itself stands equally for all, that God himself also stands indifferently toward all, and as it were waits for the determination of a lower cause, so that the death of his Son may turn out for human beings either fruitful or fruitless: which is nothing other than, with the Semipelagians, to suspend the salvation or perdition of singular human beings from the proper free choice of each one, either apprehending or repelling Christ by faith.

I answer: Let it be granted that by the death of Christ God was made so far placated or placable to the human race that he will receive any into grace if he has believed, with no discrimination of persons (which is the very voice of the Gospel); yet it does not thence follow that this very discrimination of believers and non-believers, of the reconciled and the non-reconciled, finally of the saved and the lost, is to be recalled to the uncertain dice of human free choice. For he who promulgated this universal Evangelical decree, Whoever has believed will be saved, nonetheless reserved to himself the special privilege of giving faith to some by his singular mercy, of not giving it to others by his freest and most just will, and by their manifest unworthiness. By the virtue of the death of Christ God obligated himself to enter into reconciliation with any human being if he has believed; but he did not obligate himself to pour into every human being that efficacious grace by which it is infallibly effected that he believe. We therefore hold both: namely both that God is so far placated by the death of Christ that he is already ready to receive any into grace if they do penitence and believe in Christ; and that the same God who under the condition of faith is ready to indulge the grace of remission to all equally is nonetheless not so disposed that he stands equally toward all as to producing this condition of faith in them. A merchant is said ready to sell his wares if someone wills to buy them: but that, one being unwilling, another wills to buy, the merchant himself does not effect, but it depends on the free choice of each one. The matter does not so stand between God and us. For although by the virtue of the death of Christ he is already ready to give remission and to enter into reconciliation with any human being if he wills to believe in Christ, yet God has this peculiar thing, that he himself inspires in all believers this very will of believing. We do not therefore vote with the Semipelagians, but we say with the Fathers of Orange, Canon 6: If anyone says that mercy is conferred on us believing, willing, desiring, and knocking without the grace of God, and does not confess that it is done Divinely in us by the infusion and inspiration of the Holy Spirit that we believe and will, he resists the Apostle saying, By the grace of God I am what I am. So much concerning the first member of our thesis.

I come to the other member, which is formed in this manner. The death of Christ considered as a general cause of human salvation frees none of adults from the guilt and weight of their sins, constitutes none actually reconciled to God — in a word, places none in the state of grace and salvation — before faith applied to the Gospel.

source_text:
Ad explicationem hujus propositionis paucula haec praemittam.

Primum est, Nos, per mortem Christi generaliter consideratam ut humanae salutis causam, nil aliud denotare, quam considerationem Dominicae passionis in effectu suo immediato, quod producit per se sine concursu aliquo actuum humanorum. Immediatam hanc effectionem, quae producitur sine ullis mediis ex parte nostra requisitis affirmamus esse reconciliabilitatem in actum venturam, quamprimum credimus, non autem actualem reconciliationem, aut collocationem in statu adoptionis et salutis antequam credimus.

Alterum quod praemittendum putavimus, spectat ad discrimen quoddam hic in re inter adultos et infantes observandum. Dictum est enim neminem ex adultis absque actu fidei reconciliari Deo, aut a reatu peccatorum suorum liberari: (quod mox probabitur) Unde perspicuum est, nos admittere quosdam ex infantibus virtute mortis Christi a peccatis absolvi et in statum salutis reponi, absque ullo actu voluntatis suae. Nam quia non possunt per fidem Christi sanguinem animis suis purgandis applicare, Deus misericors per arcanam Spiritus sui operationem eorum animas Christi sanguine quasi conspergit et vivificat. Hoc bene annotatum est ab Aquinate, Quaest. disp. de Justific. art. 3. Quia pueri, inquit ille, non habent unde possint se convertere ad causam justificantem, ipsa causa justificans, scilicet passio Christi, applicatur eis in baptismo, et ex hoc justificantur.

Ultimum est, Per statum gratiae et salutis, quem negamus competere ulli adultorum antequam fidei actu mediatorem apprehenderit, intelligere nos talem statum qualem descripsit Psalmista, Psal. xxxii. Quando pronunciat beatos quorum remissae sunt iniquitates, et quorum tecta sunt peccata; talem qualem depinxit Apostolus Coloss. i. 12. 14. Ubi dicit eos liberatos a potestate tenebrarum, et translatos in regnum Filii Dei dilecti, habere jam redemtionem per sanguinem ipsius, nempe remissionem peccatorum.

Hanc thesin sic explicatam probare oportet, tum contra eos, qui homines universos statuunt ipso merito passionis Christi in statum gratiae et salutis receptos, tum contra illos qui electos saltem ab aeterno reconciliatos, justificatos ac remissione peccatorum suorum donatos arbitrantur. Priorem opinionem Remonstrantibus tribuunt nonnulli: Sed, ut mihi videtur, utcunque ambigue et obscure loquantur, tamen ab hoc errore alieni sunt. Dicunt quidem, Colloq. Hagienst. p. 9. Christum omnibus per mortem crucis promeritum esse reconciliationem et remissionem peccatorum. Sed addunt, ita tamen ut nemo remissionis hujus particeps fiat reipsa praeter credentes. Sic alibi dicunt, pag. 131. Christum per mortem crucis impetrasse omnibus reconciliationem et remissionem peccatorum. Sed illico attexunt hanc glossam, Realem participationem hujus impetratae reconciliationis et remissionis esse credentium propriam. Denique pag. 162. et 163. expresse rejiciunt illud dogma quod iis a nonnullis tribuitur, nempe, omnes homines per mortem Christi restitutos esse ex lapsu, et repositos in statum gratiae; nec per impetratam omnibus remissionem aliud denotant quam medium et modum morte Christi jam esse paratum et stabilitum, quo, per fidem adhibito et applicato, omnes et singuli possunt obtinere remissionem peccatorum, pag. 186. Sic leniunt et exponunt quae suspiciosius dicta videbantur, in Colloquio Hagiensti: Fatendum tamen est, aliquos istorum hac in re aliquanto longius progressos. Borreus, apud Arminium tuetur, Deum universum genus humanum in reconciliationis gratiam assumpsisse, Resp. ad artic. 13. 14. Arnoldus contra Tilenum videtur etiam idem sentire, pag. 232. et 261. Huberus et Puccius (quorum scripta fateor me nondum vidisse) infamulantur passim quod docuerint Christi morte omnes et singulos homines justificatos, atque in sinum et gratiam Dei restitutos. Jam quod attinet ad posteriorem opinionem, non memini me quenquam ex nostris legisse qui eam expresse tueatur. Thomsonus tamen noster in sua Diatriba, cap. 24. pag. 92. et 99. quosdam commemorat, qui electorum peccata ab aeterno condonata ex dignitate et efficacia meritorum Christi probare conantur. Quo concesso, sequeretur eosdem ante fidem in Christum esse justificatos, reconciliatos Deo, ac in statum gratiae et salutis restitutos, quod falsissimum est. Probatio thesis nostrae erit utriusque erroris refutatio. Illam igitur Scripturarum testimoniis primo in loco confirmabimus.
english: For the explanation of this proposition I will premise these few things.

The first is: that we, by the death of Christ generally considered as a cause of human salvation, denote nothing other than a consideration of the Lord’s passion in its immediate effect, which it produces of itself without any concurrence of human acts. This immediate effecting, which is produced without any media required from our side, we affirm to be reconciliability about to come into act as soon as we believe, not however actual reconciliation, or placement in the state of adoption and salvation before we believe.

The second thing which we thought should be premised looks to a certain discrimination to be observed here in the matter between adults and infants. For it has been said that none of adults is reconciled to God, or freed from the guilt of their sins, without an act of faith (which will shortly be proved). Whence it is clear that we admit that some of infants are by the virtue of the death of Christ absolved from sins and placed in the state of salvation, without any act of their will. For because they cannot by faith apply the blood of Christ for purging their souls, merciful God by the secret operation of his Spirit as it were sprinkles and vivifies their souls with the blood of Christ. This was well annotated by Aquinas, Disputed questions on Justification, article 3. Because children, he says, do not have whence they can convert themselves to the justifying cause, the justifying cause itself, namely the passion of Christ, is applied to them in baptism, and from this they are justified.

The last is: By the state of grace and salvation, which we deny belongs to any of adults before he has apprehended the mediator by an act of faith, we understand such a state as the Psalmist described, Psalm 32, when he pronounces blessed those whose iniquities have been remitted and whose sins have been covered; such as the Apostle painted, Colossians 1:12, 14, where he says they have been liberated from the power of darkness and translated into the kingdom of the beloved Son of God, already having redemption through his blood, namely remission of sins.

This thesis so explained must be proved, both against those who posit all human beings by the very merit of the passion of Christ received into the state of grace and salvation, and against those who think the elect at least reconciled from eternity, justified, and gifted with remission of their sins. Some attribute the former opinion to the Remonstrants: but, as it seems to me, however ambiguously and obscurely they speak, they are nonetheless alien from this error. They do indeed say, Hague Colloquy, page 9, that Christ by the death of the cross merited for all reconciliation and remission of sins. But they add, yet so that no one becomes a partaker of this remission in fact except believers. So elsewhere they say, page 131, that Christ by the death of the cross obtained for all reconciliation and remission of sins. But immediately they weave on this gloss, that the real participation of this obtained reconciliation and remission is proper to believers. Finally, pages 162 and 163, they expressly reject that dogma which is attributed to them by some, namely that all human beings by the death of Christ were restored from the fall and replaced in the state of grace; nor by remission obtained for all do they denote anything other than that a medium and mode has already been prepared and stabilized by the death of Christ whereby, faith applied, all and each can obtain remission of sins, page 186. So they soften and explain what seemed spoken more suspiciously in the Hague Colloquy: yet it must be confessed that some of them progressed somewhat further in this matter. Borreus, with Arminius, defends that God assumed the whole human race into the grace of reconciliation, Response to articles 13 and 14. Arnoldus against Tilenus seems also to sense the same, pages 232 and 261. Huberus and Puccius (whose writings I confess I have not yet seen) are everywhere charged with having taught that by the death of Christ all and each human beings were justified and restored into the bosom and grace of God. Now as concerns the latter opinion, I do not remember that I have read anyone of ours who expressly defends it. Yet our Thomson in his Diatriba, chapter 24, pages 92 and 99, commemorates some who try to prove the sins of the elect forgiven from eternity from the dignity and efficacy of the merits of Christ. Which granted, it would follow that the same were justified before faith in Christ, reconciled to God, and restored into the state of grace and salvation, which is most false. The proof of our thesis will be the refutation of both errors. We will therefore confirm it first in place by the testimonies of the Scriptures.

source_text:
Primo, ex ipsa Christi passione non immediate fluere remissionem peccatorum ad homines universos absque ullo actu nostro interveniente, probant illa omnia Scripturarum testimonia quae poenitentiae actum expresse praerequirunt. Qualia sunt, Ezek. xviii. 21. Si impius egerit poenitentiam ab omnibus peccatis suis, vita vivet, et non morietur. Lucae xxiv. 46, 47. Oportuit Christum pati et resurgere a mortuis, et praedicari in ejus nomine poenitentiam et remissionem peccatorum. 1 Johann. i. 9. Si confiteamur peccata nostra, fidelis est et justus ut remittat nobis peccata nostra, et emundet nos ab omni iniquitate. Ex quibus patet, quamvis Christus pro omnibus mortuus sit, tamen non omnes illico vivere per hanc mortem Christi, sed omnes vivere quamprimum resipuerint; quamvis in nomine Christi offeratur remissio peccatorum, tamen non omnes promiscue fieri hujus beneficii participes, sed solos poenitentes; eadem lege, ut poenitentia praecedat remissionem; Denique quamvis virtute mortis Christi Deus obligetur ad remittenda peccata, ita tamen ut neque fidelitas neque justitia Dei poscat hanc remissionem cuiquam indulgeri, nisi sub hac conditione, Si confiteatur peccata sua.

Secundo, idem evincitur ex illis locis, quae antequam justificati aut Deo reconciliati esse possumus, fidem a nobis praerequirunt, tanquam instrumentum quo apprehendimus gratiam justificationis, et tanquam conditionem reconciliationis obtinendae, in ipso Evangelico pacto nobis imperatam. Hujusmodi sunt, Actor. xvi. 31. Crede in Dominum Jesum Christum, et salvus eris. Johan. vi. 40. Haec est voluntas Patris mei, qui misit me, ut omnis qui videt Filium, et credit in eum, habeat vitam aeternam. Johan. xx. 31. Haec scripta sunt ut credatis, et ut credentes vitam habeatis in nomine ejus. Rom. iii. 22. Justitia Dei per fidem Jesu Christi, in omnes et super omnes qui credunt. et vers. 25. Quem proposuit Deus ut esset placamentum per fidem, etc. Gal. ii. 16. Scimus quod non justificatur homo nisi per fidem Jesu Christi; et nos in Christum Jesum credimus, ut justificemur ex fide Christi. Mitto alia innumera. Ex hisce abunde liquet, Remissionem peccatorum, et Justificationem, sive reconciliationem nostram cum Deo non esse beneficium tale, quod ex ipsa passione Christi, absque omnibus mediis, ad quemvis hominem redundet; sed eos pro quibus Christus mortuus est, sive sufficienter sive efficaciter, non posse habere salutiferum fructum ejusdem mortis sibi applicatum, nisi per fidem praeeuntem.

Tertio, hoc etiam colligi potest ex illis dictis Scripturarum, in quibus, morte Christi praesupposita, nihilominus diserte affirmatur homines quoslibet sub reatu mortis et ira Divina jacere, tantisper dum vera fide Mediatorem apprehenderint. Huc spectant illa: Marc. xvi. 16. Praedicate Evangelium omni creaturae. Qui crediderit, servabitur: qui vero non crediderit, condemnabitur. Et Johan. iii. 36. Qui incredulus est Filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum. Johan. viii. 24. Si non credideritis quia ego sum, moriemini in peccatis vestris. Denique non obstante quod Christus pro nobis mortuus est dixit Apostolus Eph. ii. 3. Nos omnes nasci filios irae. Frustra igitur sunt qui somniant ipsa morte Christi omnes homines, absque ullo actu ex parte nostra interveniente, esse in sinum gratiae Divinae et statum salutis restitutos.

Quarto, ne quis dicat praedicta testimonia ad solos non-electos pertinere, electos autem omnes ipso merito mortis Christi stare justificatos, et reconciliatos Deo antequam crediderint, audiantur in contrarium haec Scripturarum clara testimonia, Ephes. ii. 11, 12, 13. Mementote vos quondam fuisse absque Christo, alienos a republ. Israelis, et extraneos a pactis promissionis, spem non habentes, et Deo expertes in mundo. At nunc in Christo Jesu vos, qui olim eratis procul, propinqui facti estis per sanguinem Christi, etc. Alloquitur eos quos cap. i. vers. 4. praesumit electos ante jacta mundi fundamenta; eo usque tamen extraneos a pactis promissionis, et a Deo alienatos mansisse docet, dum per fidem, quasi manum spiritualem, opes Divinae gratiae in Christo congestas ad se pertraxissent, uti promptum est colligere ex vers. 7 et 8 hujus secundi capitis. In eandem sententiam sonant illa verba ejusdem Apostoli Rom. v. 1. Justificati fide pacem habemus erga Deum per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum. Mors igitur Christi in se considerata, donec fides ex parte nostra accesserit, hanc aut illam singularem personam neque justificat, neque in sinum gratiae reponit. Denique, Apostolus Paulus extra omnem controversiam fuit unus ex electis, non tamen idcirco aut justificatus, aut in statum gratiae et salutis restitutus, dum blasphemus mansit in Christum et persecutor Ecclesiae, sed tum demum, postquam Christum agnosceret, et in Christum totus recumberet, 1 Tim. i. 16. Misertus est mei Jesus Christus, ut in me ostenderet omnem clementiam, ut essem exemplo credituris ipsi in vitam aeternam. Remissio igitur peccatorum in Christi sanguine non anticipat fidem et poenitentiam, ne in electis quidem. Hactenus Scripturarum expressis testimoniis pugnavimus; jam rationes aliquot iisdem Scripturis fundatas attexemus.
english: First, that remission of sins does not flow immediately from the passion of Christ itself to all human beings without any intervening act of ours is proved by all those testimonies of the Scriptures which expressly prerequire an act of penitence. Such are Ezekiel 18:21: If the impious man has done penitence from all his sins, he will live with life and will not die. Luke 24:46, 47: It was necessary that Christ suffer and rise from the dead, and that penitence and remission of sins be preached in his name. 1 John 1:9: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to remit our sins to us and to cleanse us from every iniquity. From which it is plain that although Christ died for all, yet not all immediately live through this death of Christ, but all live as soon as they have come to their senses; although remission of sins is offered in the name of Christ, yet not all promiscuously become partakers of this benefit, but only the penitent; by the same law, that penitence precede remission; Finally, although by the virtue of the death of Christ God is obligated to remit sins, yet so that neither the faithfulness nor the justice of God demands that this remission be indulged to anyone except under this condition, If he confess his sins.

Second, the same is shown from those places which, before we can be justified or reconciled to God, prerequire faith from us, as an instrument by which we apprehend the grace of justification, and as a condition of obtaining reconciliation, commanded to us in the Evangelical pact itself. Of this sort are Acts 16:31: Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved. John 6:40: This is the will of my Father who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life. John 20:31: These things have been written that you may believe, and that believing you may have life in his name. Romans 3:22: The righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all who believe; and verse 25: Whom God set forth to be a propitiation through faith, etc. Galatians 2:16: We know that a human being is not justified except through faith in Jesus Christ; and we believe in Christ Jesus that we may be justified from the faith of Christ. I pass over innumerable others. From these it abundantly appears that Remission of sins, and Justification, or our reconciliation with God, is not such a benefit as overflows from the passion of Christ itself, without all media, to any human being; but that those for whom Christ died, whether sufficiently or efficaciously, cannot have the saving fruit of the same death applied to themselves except through faith going before.

Third, this can also be gathered from those sayings of the Scriptures in which, the death of Christ presupposed, it is nonetheless expressly affirmed that any human beings lie under the guilt of death and Divine wrath so long as they have not apprehended the Mediator by true faith. To this those look: Mark 16:16: Preach the Gospel to every creature. He who has believed will be saved; but he who has not believed will be condemned. And John 3:36: He who is unbelieving toward the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. John 8:24: If you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sins. Finally, notwithstanding that Christ died for us, the Apostle said Ephesians 2:3 that we are all born children of wrath. Vain therefore are those who dream that by the death of Christ itself all human beings, without any intervening act from our side, have been restored into the bosom of Divine grace and the state of salvation.

Fourth, lest anyone say that the aforesaid testimonies pertain only to the non-elect, but that all the elect by the very merit of the death of Christ stand justified and reconciled to God before they believed, let these clear testimonies of the Scriptures be heard to the contrary, Ephesians 2:11, 12, 13: Remember that you were once without Christ, aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world. But now in Christ Jesus you who formerly were far off have been made near by the blood of Christ, etc. He addresses those whom chapter 1, verse 4, he presupposes elect before the foundations of the world were cast; yet he teaches that they remained strangers from the covenants of promise and alienated from God until by faith, as a spiritual hand, they had drawn to themselves the riches of Divine grace heaped up in Christ, as it is ready to gather from verses 7 and 8 of this second chapter. In the same sense sound those words of the same Apostle, Romans 5:1: Justified by faith we have peace toward God through our Lord Jesus Christ. The death of Christ therefore, considered in itself, until faith has acceded from our side, neither justifies this or that singular person nor places him in the bosom of grace. Finally, the Apostle Paul beyond all controversy was one of the elect, yet was not therefore either justified or restored into the state of grace and salvation while he remained a blasphemer against Christ and a persecutor of the Church, but then at last, after he acknowledged Christ and wholly leaned upon Christ, 1 Timothy 1:16: Jesus Christ had mercy on me, that in me he might show all clemency, that I might be an example to those who would believe in him unto eternal life. Remission of sins in the blood of Christ therefore does not anticipate faith and penitence, not even in the elect. Thus far we have fought with the express testimonies of the Scriptures; now we will attach some reasons founded in the same Scriptures.

source_text: Rat. 1. Quamvis concedamus mortem Christi in ratione causae meritoriae esse sufficientissimam ad expianda peccata omnium hominum, eosque in statum gratiae cum Deo restituendos, tamen non potest actu constituere justificatum et reconciliatum, nisi aliquo modo conjungatur, coaptetur, et uniatur illi, qui per eam justificandus et reconciliandus supponitur. Nam quod Philosophi dicere solent, Omnis actio est per aliquem contactum, id etiam valet in hac supernaturali actione, quae non fit absque contactu aliquo supernaturali. Fide autem tangimus Christum, et per fidem eidem conjungimur et quasi coaptamur. Habitat enim Christus in nobis per fidem. Absque fide igitur, sive ante fidem, nulla nobis actualis conjunctio cum Christo, ac proinde ex merito mortis ejus nulla remissio peccatorum, nulla justificatio, nulla cum Deo Patre reconciliatio. Doctissimus Calvinus hoc observavit in Rom. viii. 4. Suam justitiam nullis communicat Christus, nisi quos Spiritus sui vinculo sibi conjungit. Quicquid igitur latet in aeterno Dei decreto de justificandis, et sibi reconciliandis, eademque salvandis omnibus electis, quicquid in pretioso Christi sanguine sufficientiae, aut efficaciae sit ad homines redimendos, et Deo reconciliandos, tamen in effectum actualis reconciliationis minime exire solet, nisi per fidem prius hominibus conjungatur, quia tam meritoria quam naturalis causa conjungi illi debet in quod influit et virtutem suam salutiferam transfundit.
english: Ratio 1. Although we grant that the death of Christ, considered as a meritorious cause, is most sufficient to expiate the sins of all human beings and to restore them into the state of grace with God, yet it cannot actually constitute anyone justified and reconciled unless it is somehow joined, fitted, and united to the one who is supposed to be justified and reconciled by it.

For what the philosophers commonly say — that every action is through some contact — holds also in this supernatural action, which does not take place without some supernatural contact. By faith we touch Christ, and through faith we are joined to him and as it were fitted to him. For Christ dwells in us through faith (Ephesians 3:17).

Without faith, then, or before faith, we have no actual conjunction with Christ; and therefore from the merit of his death there is no remission of sins, no justification, no reconciliation with God the Father.

Most learned Calvin observed this on Romans 8:4: Christ communicates his own righteousness to none except those whom he joins to himself by the bond of his Spirit. Whatever therefore lies hidden in God’s eternal decree concerning those who are to be justified, reconciled to him, and likewise all the elect who are to be saved; whatever sufficiency or efficacy there is in the precious blood of Christ for redeeming human beings and reconciling them to God — still it does not customarily pass into the effect of actual reconciliation unless it is first joined to human beings through faith, because a meritorious cause no less than a natural one must be joined to that into which it flows and into which it pours its saving power.

source_text: Rat. 2. Secundo arguitur a proportione inter Adamum autorem mortis et condemnationis, et Christum autorem vitae et justificationis. Sicut igitur Adamus neminem constringit reatu mortis, neminem subdit irae Divinae et condemnationi, nisi fiat quasi membrum ejus per generationem naturalem; ita Christus neminem liberat a morte, neminem in gratiam Divinam restituit, justificat et Deo reconciliat, nisi fiat membrum ejus per regenerationem supernaturalem. At hoc non fit ante fidem inspiratam cordibus nostris: Johan. i. 12. 13. Quotquot eum exceperunt, dedit eis potestatem ut filii Dei fierent, nempe iis qui credunt in nomen ejus: Qui non ex sanguine, &c. sed ex Deo geniti sunt. Nemo igitur sive praeteritorum sive electorum ipsa Christi morte stat reconciliatus et justificatus coram Deo, sed tum demum, cum Christo incorporatur, et per regenerationem quasi membrum huic Capiti mystico supponitur, justitiam Christi et pacem apud Deum obtinet.
english: Ratio 2. Second, the argument is drawn from the proportion between Adam, the author of death and condemnation, and Christ, the author of life and justification.

Just as Adam binds no one with the guilt of death, and subjects no one to the divine wrath and condemnation, unless that one becomes as it were his member by natural generation: so Christ frees no one from death, restores no one into divine grace, justifies and reconciles no one to God, unless that one becomes his member by supernatural regeneration.

But this does not happen before faith is inspired into our hearts: John 1:12–13: As many as received him, to them he gave power to become the sons of God, namely to those who believe in his name: who were born not of blood, and so on, but of God.

No one therefore — whether among those passed by or among the elect — stands reconciled and justified before God by Christ’s death itself; but only then, when he is incorporated into Christ and through regeneration is set as it were as a member under this mystical Head, does he obtain the righteousness of Christ and peace with God.

source_text: Rat. 3. Si ipso merito mortis Christi omnia peccata hominibus condonata essent, antequam illi in Christum crederent, atque sic omnes essent in statum gratiae et reconciliationis restituti ipso facto, sequeretur neminem nasci filium irae, quod est e diametro contrarium verbis Apostoli modo allegatis, ex Ephes. ii. 3. Porro, cum Christi meritum in acceptatione Dei habeat efficaciam infinitam et aeternam, illud etiam incommodi sequeretur, Peccata hominum prius remitti quam committi, prius expiari quam perpetrari, si absque ulla media actione nostra, ex solo merito Christi, remissio peccatorum et actualis hominum reconciliatio nasceretur. Sed hoc plane impossibile est. Nam sicuti pharmacum, quod quantum ad insitam suam efficaciam et virtutem potest lepram sanare, tamen non actu sanat hunc aut illum hominem, nisi jam factum leprosum, et praedictum pharmacum sumentem; ita sanguis Christi, qui sanare potest quemvis hominem, non actu tamen quenquam sanat, purgat aut Deo reconciliat, nisi jam contaminatum peccato, et credentem. Nullo igitur modo audiendi sunt, sive qui omnes homines promiscue reconciliatos, et in statum gratiae repositos ipsa Christi passione philosophantur, sive qui contendunt omnes Electos virtute sola ejusdem passionis habere omnia sua peccata ab aeterno sibi condonata; cum nulla sit condonatio peccatorum nisi commissorum, neque commissorum ulla ullis speranda nisi credentibus. Optime et verissime reverendus ac piae memoriae Sarisburiensis, Futurorum peccatorum facta jam remissio credi non debet. Quamquam enim Deo quidem tanquam jam facta sint, quae ille ut fiant omni ab aeternitate disposuit, nobis tamen non aliter accipienda sunt, nisi secundum modum illum dispensationis, quo ab aeterno decreta, et in tempore complenda nobis, et in actum perducenda sunt. Hactenus ille. Nobis igitur non est somnianda remissio peccatorum, aut reconciliatio obtenta, nisi secundum modum dispensationis a Deo decretae: id est, nisi prius vere poeniteamus, et in Mediatorem credamus.
english: Ratio 3. If by the very merit of Christ’s death all sins had been forgiven to human beings before they believed in Christ, and so all had been restored into the state of grace and reconciliation by the mere fact itself, it would follow that no one is born a child of wrath — which is diametrically contrary to the Apostle’s words just alleged from Ephesians 2:3.

Further: since the merit of Christ, in God’s acceptation, has infinite and eternal efficacy, this inconvenience would also follow — that the sins of human beings are remitted before they are committed, and expiated before they are perpetrated — if without any intervening act of ours, from the merit of Christ alone, the remission of sins and the actual reconciliation of human beings were to arise. But this is plainly impossible.

For just as a medicine which, as to its implanted efficacy and virtue, can heal leprosy, yet does not actually heal this or that human being unless he has already become a leper and takes the medicine named: so the blood of Christ, which can heal any human being, yet does not actually heal, cleanse, or reconcile anyone to God unless that one is already contaminated by sin and is believing.

In no way, then, are they to be heard who either philosophize that all human beings promiscuously are reconciled and placed in the state of grace by the passion of Christ itself, or contend that all the elect, by the sole power of that same passion, have all their sins forgiven them from eternity — since there is no forgiveness of sins except of sins committed, and no forgiveness of committed sins is to be hoped for by any except believers.

Most excellently and truly the reverend of pious memory, the Bishop of Salisbury: An already-made remission of future sins ought not to be believed. For although to God they are as already done which he from all eternity disposed should be done, yet for us they are not to be received otherwise than according to that mode of dispensation by which, decreed from eternity, they are to be completed for us in time and brought into act. Thus far he. We therefore must not dream of a remission of sins, or of a reconciliation already obtained, except according to the mode of dispensation decreed by God: that is, unless we first truly repent and believe in the Mediator.

source_text: Rat. 4. Tota vis et efficacia meriti ejus, quod Christus morte sua in bonum humani generis comparavit, quoad effluxum et derivationem in alias personas, pendet a voluntate Patris illud ordinante et acceptante. Quis enim ausit Christi meritum ad se rapere alio modo, aut alia lege, quam Deus ipse illud hominibus communicandum, et eorum nomine acceptilandum ordinavit? Sane si quis hoc facere conetur, frustra fecerit: Nam meritum Christi tantum bonum est nobis, pro quanto acceptabatur a Deo, ut Scotus hoc nostro sensu haud incommode docuit, l. 3. dist. 19. qu. unic. pag. 74. At a Deo minime acceptatum est, ut pareret actualem remissionem peccatorum, et reconciliationem cuiquam mortalium ante poenitentiam, fidem, et insertionem in Christum: Ergo non actu justificat, aut Deo reconciliat nisi poenitentes et credentes. Non fuisse autem ita acceptatum ut quenquam reconciliaret ante fidem, patet argumento a Scripturis negative, hoc modo. Nullum verbum occurrit in Sacris Scripturis ex quo colligi potest, ipsa vi et efficacia mortis Christi omnes homines in statum gratiae promiscue reponi, aut ullum hominem, sive electum sive non-electum, ante poenitentiam et fidem, obtinere virtute sanguinis Christi in cruce fusi, remissionem peccatorum aut actualem reconciliationem cum Deo: Ergo temerarium est hoc asserere. Neque est quod quis rejiciat hujusmodi argumentum ductum ab autoritate Scripturarum negative: Quia licet in rebus mediocrioribus, quae summam salutis nostrae non spectant, infirma sit argumentatio, Hoc non est positum in Scripturis, Ergo falsum est aut illicitum, tamen in rebus ad salutem factu aut cognitu necessariis, quale est modus impetrandae remissionis et reconciliationis cum Deo, optime sequitur, Hoc in Scripturis non docetur, Ergo non est a nobis credendum. Cum ergo Scripturae nullibi doceant, Christi morte cuiquam singulari personae remissionem peccatorum, aut reconciliationem actualem conferri, priusquam poenituerit, et in Christum crediderit, sub praetextu amplificandi dignitatem mortis Christi, aut quocunque alio minime est admittendum.
english: Ratio 4. The whole force and efficacy of that merit which Christ by his death prepared for the good of the human race, as regards its outflow and derivation into other persons, depends on the will of the Father who ordains and accepts it.

For who would dare snatch the merit of Christ to himself in another manner, or under another law, than that by which God himself ordained it to be communicated to human beings and accepted in their name? Indeed if anyone tries to do this, he will have done it in vain: for the merit of Christ is so great a good to us as it was accepted by God — as Scotus taught not inconveniently in this our sense (Sentences book 3, distinction 19, unique question, p. 74).

But it was by no means accepted by God so as to produce actual remission of sins and reconciliation for any mortal before penitence, faith, and insertion into Christ. Therefore it does not actually justify, or reconcile to God, anyone except the penitent and the believing.

That it was not so accepted as to reconcile anyone before faith is clear from an argument drawn negatively from the Scriptures, in this way. No word occurs in the Sacred Scriptures from which it can be gathered that by the very force and efficacy of Christ’s death all human beings are promiscuously placed in the state of grace, or that any human being — whether elect or non-elect — before penitence and faith obtains, by the virtue of Christ’s blood poured out on the cross, remission of sins or actual reconciliation with God. Therefore it is rash to assert this.

Nor is there any reason for rejecting an argument of this kind drawn from the authority of the Scriptures negatively. For although in more middling matters, which do not concern the summit of our salvation, the reasoning is weak — This is not set down in the Scriptures; therefore it is false or illicit — yet in matters necessary to do or to know for salvation, such as the mode of obtaining remission and reconciliation with God, it follows most soundly: This is not taught in the Scriptures; therefore it is not to be believed by us. Since therefore the Scriptures nowhere teach that by the death of Christ remission of sins, or actual reconciliation, is conferred on any singular person before he has repented and believed in Christ, it is by no means to be admitted under pretext of amplifying the dignity of Christ’s death, or under any other pretext.

source_text:
Post firmamenta Scripturarum & argumentorum pondera, Patrum etiam suffragia apponemus, sed paucissima.

Ambrosius, De Fide ad Gratian. lib. 4. c. 1. Si non credis, non descendit tibi, non tibi passus est. Quae verba hunc sensum habent, Nullum fructum redemtionis ex Christo incarnato & passo pervenire ad hanc aut illam singularem personam, donec credat in Christum. Non enim negare vult Ambrosius Christum descendisse & passum esse pro hominibus, sive illi credant, sive non credant; sed docere vult, utilitatem sive vim salutiferam hujus passionis tum vivificare & reconciliare homines quando credunt. In hac igitur formula loquendi sequitur notas regulas Jurisconsultorum, qui dicere solent, Non esse, & esse, sed inutiliter esse pro paribus habentur. Quae absque effectu comperiuntur, possunt dici quasi nulla. Christus igitur pro non credentibus incarnatus & mortuus negatur; quia illorum vitio pro illis inutiliter & absque effectu incarnatus & passus intelligitur. Hoc plane arguit ex mente Ambrosii, eo solo quod Christus mortuus est pro credentibus, neminem collocari in statu reconciliationis & salutis ante fidem Evangelio adhibitam.
english: After the firm foundations of the Scriptures and the weight of the arguments, we will also set down the Fathers’ suffrages — but very few.

Ambrose, On the Faith to Gratian, book 4, chapter 1: If you do not believe, he did not descend for you; he did not suffer for you. Those words have this sense: no fruit of redemption from Christ incarnate and having suffered reaches this or that singular person before he believes in Christ.

For Ambrose does not mean to deny that Christ descended and suffered for human beings, whether they believe or do not believe; he means to teach that the usefulness, or saving force, of this passion then vivifies and reconciles human beings when they believe.

In this manner of speaking, then, he follows the known rules of the jurisconsults, who are accustomed to say that not-being, and being but uselessly, are held for equals. Things found without effect may be called as if nothing. Christ is therefore denied to have been incarnate and to have died for unbelievers, because by their vice he is understood to have been incarnate and to have suffered for them uselessly and without effect.
This plainly argues from Ambrose’s mind that by this alone — that Christ died for believers — no one is placed in the state of reconciliation and salvation before faith is applied to the Gospel.

source_text: Ambrosium subsequetur Augustinus, qui sic scribit, in resp. ad artic. sibi falso imposit. resp. 1. Qui hoc saeculum sine fide Christi, & sine regenerationis sacramento pertranseunt, redemtionis alieni sunt. Paulo post, Redemtionis proprietas penes illos est, de quibus princeps hujus mundi missus est foras. Tandem addit, Passio sive mors Christi habet in se ut omnibus prosit; sed si non bibitur, non proficit. Quae omnia Ambrosianam illam sententiam, Si non credis, tibi passus non est, aliis atque aliis verbis enunciant. Nam illud, redemtionis alieni sunt, nil aliud innuit, quam minime participes esse remissionis peccatorum, & reconciliationis cum Deo, qui nondum crediderunt. Sic etiam redemtionis proprietas acquisitum & quasi possessum fructum redemtionis denotat, eundemque penes solos credentes & regeneratos esse declarat. Denique illa Augustini verba, si non bibitur, non proficit, plane evincunt, utilitatem ex morte Christi redundantem non nisi bibendo, id est, credendo, ad singulares personas derivari. Haec omnia & singula evertunt illorum sententiam qui statuunt, sive omnes homines promiscue, sive praedestinatos speciali quasi privilegio, hoc ipso solo quod Christus in cruce passus est pro illis, in statum gratiae, & actualis reconciliationis apud Deum restitui.
english: Augustine will follow Ambrose. He writes thus in the reply to the article falsely imposed on him, reply 1: Those who pass through this age without the faith of Christ, and without the sacrament of regeneration, are aliens to redemption. A little later: The property of redemption is with those from whom the prince of this world has been cast out. At length he adds: The passion or death of Christ has in itself that it profits all; but if it is not drunk, it does not profit.

All of which utter that Ambrosian sentence — If you do not believe, he did not suffer for you — in still other words. For that phrase, they are aliens to redemption, hints at nothing else than that those who have not yet believed are by no means sharers of the remission of sins and of reconciliation with God.

So also the property of redemption denotes the acquired and as-it-were possessed fruit of redemption, and declares that same fruit to be with believers and the regenerate alone. Finally those words of Augustine — if it is not drunk, it does not profit — plainly prove that the usefulness overflowing from Christ’s death is derived to singular persons only by drinking, that is, by believing.

These things, all and each, overturn the sentence of those who state that either all human beings promiscuously, or the predestinate by a special quasi-privilege, by this alone — that Christ suffered on the cross for them — are restored into the state of grace and of actual reconciliation with God.

source_text:
Tertio in loco prodeat Theodoretus, scribens in illa verba Apostoli, Rom. iii. 25. Quem proposuit Deus ut esset propitiatorium per fidem in sanguine ipsius, &c. Dominus Christus, inquit, propitiatorium est, & suo sanguine nostram salutem procuravit, solam a nobis fidem exigens. Ex quibus verbis colligimus, Christum cum morte meritisque suis omnibus sic constitutum esse causam universalem redemtionis, reconciliationis & salutis nostrae, ut priusquam fructus redemtionis & salutis hujus per Christum procuratae a quoquam participetur, oporteat, hanc causam universalem ad singulos specialiter applicari. Jam vero ut fiat haec fructuosa applicatio, quod bene monuit Theodoretus, Deus a nobis fidem exigit. Dum igitur abest fides, Christi mors in se considerata nemini confert statum actualis reconciliationis, gratiae & salutis.

Cyrillus etiam in eadem sententia est constitutus, qui lib. 2. cap. 74. explicans illa verba Servatoris nostri, Johan. iii. 36. Qui credit in Filium habet vitam aeternam; qui autem incredulus est Filio, non videbit vitam, sic colligit, Vivificat igitur Christus credentes in se, quia cum secundum naturam vita sit, habitat in omnibus fidelibus per fidem. Utcunque ergo Christus sit ipsa vita, tamen non vivificat nisi credentes, quod optima & validissima ratione confirmavit Cyrillus, nimirum, quia non habitat in hominibus nisi credentibus. Quasi dixisset, Fons vitae non actu vivificat nisi sibi conjunctos, conjuncti autem habentur soli fideles. Male igitur arguunt, qui sive a morte, sive ab ipsa vita Christi colligunt aut omnes aut ullos homines in statu vitae, gratiae & salutis constitutos, priusquam hoc vinculo fidei Christo uniantur.
english: Third in place let Theodoret come forth, writing on those words of the Apostle (Romans 3:25): Whom God set forth to be a propitiatory through faith in his blood, and so on. The Lord Christ, he says, is the propitiatory, and by his blood procured our salvation, requiring from us faith alone.

From which words we gather that Christ, with his death and all his merits, has been so constituted the universal cause of our redemption, reconciliation, and salvation, that before the fruit of this redemption and salvation procured through Christ is participated by anyone, this universal cause must be applied specially to individuals.
