Now that this fruitful application may happen, as Theodoret well warned, God requires faith from us. Faith being absent, Christ’s death considered in itself confers on no one the state of actual reconciliation, grace, and salvation.

Cyril also stands in the same sentence. Explaining those words of our Savior (John 3:36) — He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who is unbelieving toward the Son will not see life — he gathers thus (book 2, chapter 74): Therefore Christ vivifies believers in himself, because, since according to nature he is life, he dwells in all the faithful through faith.

However much, then, Christ is life itself, yet he does not vivify anyone except believers — which Cyril confirmed by an excellent and most valid reason, namely because he does not dwell in human beings except in believers. As if he had said: the fountain of life does not actually vivify except those joined to himself, and the joined are held to be the faithful alone. Badly, therefore, do they argue who from either the death or the very life of Christ gather that either all or any human beings are constituted in the state of life, grace, and salvation before they are united to Christ by this bond of faith.

source_text: Ultimo proferam testimonium venerabilis Bedae expressissimum, quod habetur in Commentariis ejus supra 2 Cor. v. Per fidem mundus reconciliatur Deo, cum credit in Christum, qui missus est a Deo. Dixerat Apostolus Deum in Christo mundum reconciliasse sibi, id est, Christum ex Dei ordinatione illud λυτρον Patri dependisse, quo effectum est ut Deus non a nobis exposcat satisfactionem pro peccatis nostris, antequam nobiscum redeat in gratiam, sed hoc solo contentus, paratus sit quemlibet in gratiam recipere. Si adhuc quaeras, numquid soluto hoc pretio ipso facto solutionis universi homines statim reconciliantur, respondet Beda, Minime illud quidem; sed unusquisque tum reconciliatur Deo, cum ipse credit in Christum, qui missus est a Deo. Eandem habent mentem & illa verba ejusdem autoris in Luc. xv. Tum unicuique nostrum occiditur Christus, cum credit occisum. Occisus fuit ab origine mundi in acceptatione Divina; occisus etiam, adveniente plenitudine temporis, in ipsa cruce; tibi tamen ac mihi, id est, unicuique homini singulari, tum occisus, cum credit in occisum. Quod perinde est ac si dixisset, Occisi sive mortui Christi beneficium tum ad nos pertinere cum incipimus in eum credere.
english: Last I will bring forward the most express testimony of the Venerable Bede, found in his Commentaries on 2 Corinthians 5: Through faith the world is reconciled to God, when it believes in Christ who was sent by God.

The Apostle had said that God in Christ reconciled the world to himself — that is, that Christ by God’s ordination paid that ransom to the Father, whereby it was effected that God does not exact from us satisfaction for our sins before he returns into grace with us, but, content with this alone, is ready to receive anyone into grace.

If you still ask whether, this price having been paid, by the very fact of the payment all human beings are at once reconciled, Bede answers: By no means that; but each one is then reconciled to God when he himself believes in Christ who was sent by God.

Those words of the same author on Luke 15 have the same mind: Then for each of us Christ is slain, when he believes him slain. He was slain from the origin of the world in the Divine acceptation; slain also, when the fullness of time came, on the cross itself; yet for you and for me — that is, for each singular human being — then slain when he believes in the slain. Which is just as if he had said: the benefit of the slain or dead Christ then pertains to us when we begin to believe in him.

source_text: Ab orthodoxa ergo antiquitate desciverunt, qui statuunt ipsa passione Christi omnes homines in statum gratiae repositos; nec minus illi, qui docent ipsos praedestinatos in hac morte Christi consecutos remissionem peccatorum suorum, sive justificationem & reconciliationem cum Deo, ab aeterno: cum haec justificatio sive actualis reconciliatio (ut vere & scite Bernardus) tam absque consensu non potest esse recipientis, quam absque gratia dantis. Atque sic accepistis sententiam nostram confirmatam, atque enervatam contrariam.
english: From orthodox antiquity, therefore, they have departed who state that by the very passion of Christ all human beings are placed in the state of grace; nor less those who teach that the predestinate themselves, in this death of Christ, obtained the remission of their sins, or justification and reconciliation with God, from eternity — since this justification or actual reconciliation (as Bernard truly and skillfully) cannot belong to the receiver without consent any more than without the grace of the giver.
And thus you have received our sentence confirmed, and the contrary enervated.

source_text:
Jam quae objici possunt ab adversariis, in medium afferantur, & paucis dissipentur.

Pro sententia Huberiana, quae ponit omnes homines, hoc ipso quod Christus pro hominibus mortuus est, in statum gratiae & salutis esse restitutos, hujusmodi argumenta afferuntur.
english: Now let us bring forward the objections our adversaries can raise, and briefly dispose of them.
In defence of Huber's position—that every human being is already restored to the state of grace and salvation simply because Christ died for humankind—arguments of the following kind are advanced.

source_text: Christi mors aut sufficiens fuit λυτρον ad dispungenda peccata humani generis, omnesque homines in statum gratiae & reconciliationis reponendos, aut insufficiens. Si statuatur insufficiens, gratiam Divinam extenuamus, & meritum Christi indigne conculcamus. Si agnoscatur sufficiens, tum posita causa sufficienti in actu, nihil aliud requiritur ad effectum inducendum. Ex ipso igitur actu Christi seipsum Deo offerentis statim sequatur universalis liberatio omnium hominum a reatu peccatorum suorum, & universalis reconciliatio, sive receptio omnium hominum in gratiam Divinam.
english: Either Christ's death was a sufficient ransom to wipe away the sins of the human race and put every human being back into grace and reconciliation, or it was insufficient. Call it insufficient, and we diminish divine grace and trample Christ's merit. Grant that it was sufficient, and then—once that sufficient cause has been put into act—nothing else is required to bring about the effect. From Christ's very act of offering himself to God, therefore, there would follow at once the universal liberation of all people from the guilt of their sins, and a universal reconciliation: that is, the reception of everyone into divine grace.

source_text: Agnoscimus plenissimam lytri sufficientiam, imo infinitam ejusdem superabundantiam: sed respondemus, Hoc meritum Christi in se solo consideratum operari quidem sufficienter, ut causam salutis humanae universalem; universalis autem causa non producit effectus in singularibus ante singularem applicationem. Ipsa igitur morte Christi instituta est causa universalis sufficientissima, ex qua (ut loquitur Aquinas) possent quaecunque quorumcunque peccata expiari; sed priusquam haec causa vim suam exserat expiatoriam ad liberationem & reconciliationem singulorum, oportet eam applicari singulis per fidem. Quod ipse Apostolus perspicue docuit Rom. iii. 25. Quem proposuit Deus propitiatorium per fidem in sanguine ipsius, &c. Quamvis ergo haec mors Christi sit sufficiens satisfactio pro peccatis humani generis, cum tamen per modum remedii nos purget a peccatis, est unicuique prius applicanda, quam possit effectum reconciliationis & sanitatis producere: Applicatio autem non fit nisi per fidem.
english: We acknowledge the fullest sufficiency of the ransom—indeed its infinite superabundance. Our answer, however, is this: Christ's merit, considered in itself alone, does operate sufficiently as a universal cause of human salvation; yet a universal cause does not produce effects in particular persons before it is applied to each one. By Christ's death itself, therefore, a most sufficient universal cause was instituted, from which (as Aquinas says) any sins of any persons could be expiated. But before that cause puts forth its expiatory power for the liberation and reconciliation of individuals, it must be applied to each by faith. The Apostle himself teaches this clearly in Romans 3:25: "Whom God set forth as a propitiatory through faith in his blood," and so on.

So although Christ's death is a sufficient satisfaction for the sins of the human race, it cleanses us by way of a remedy: it must first be applied to each person before it can produce the effect of reconciliation and healing. And that application is made only through faith.

source_text:
Si post acceptatum λυτρον sufficiens Deus non recipiat omnes in gratiam, Christo injurius esset, quia non gratificatur hominibus quod Christus moriendo pro illis meruit: cum hominibus etiam injuste ageret, quia eos peccatis, quasi debitis, constrictos adhuc tenet, quorum omnia debita Christus suo sanguine dispunxit.

Neutri infertur injuria. Non Christo, quia ipse noluit satisfactionem a se praestitam pro peccatis humani generis valere ad actualem reconciliationem hominum singularium, nisi interveniente fide eorundem, ut supra probatum est. Esset igitur Christo contumeliosum, si in societatem & participationem actualem hujus gratiae quilibet admitteretur, nondum credens in Autorem salutis & Redemtorem nostrum Jesum Christum. Neque hominibus infertur injuria, eo quod non recipiantur illico in favorem Dei propter ipsum actum Christi morientis, quia hoc neque debitum fuit hominibus, neque promissum. Non possumus enim ex morte Christi vendicare nobis ullum beneficium contra, aut praeter ordinem ac pactum a Deo Christoque constitutum, nobisque in Evangelio patefactum. Est autem hic ordo stabilitus, haec conditio expresse posita in Evangelio, quod reconciliationis gratia & beneficium vitae aeternae ad peccatores ex morte Christi redundaret, si crederent; sin minus, manerent obstricti peccatis, & perirent in sua infidelitate: Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam aeternam; qui vero non obtemperat Filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum, Joh. iii. 36.
english: Suppose that after accepting a sufficient ransom God still does not receive everyone into grace. Then, the objection says, he would wrong Christ, because he would not grant to human beings what Christ merited for them by dying. He would also deal unjustly with human beings, because he would still hold them bound by sins as by debts, even though Christ wiped out all those debts with his blood.

Neither side is injured. Not Christ: he himself did not will that the satisfaction he offered for the sins of the human race should avail for the actual reconciliation of particular persons unless their faith intervened, as we proved above. It would therefore be an insult to Christ if anyone were admitted into the actual fellowship and share of this grace while still not believing in Jesus Christ, the Author of salvation and our Redeemer. Nor are human beings injured when they are not received at once into God's favor simply on account of Christ's dying act, for that was neither owed to them nor promised. We cannot claim from Christ's death any benefit against or beyond the order and covenant established by God and by Christ and opened to us in the Gospel.

That order stands fixed, and the Gospel expressly sets this condition: the grace of reconciliation and the gift of eternal life overflow to sinners from Christ's death if they believe; if they do not, they remain bound by sins and perish in their unbelief. "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; but whoever does not obey the Son will not see life, and the wrath of God remains on him" (John 3:36).

source_text: Non fuit major vis in peccato Adami ad constringendos omnes homines reatu aeternae mortis, quam in morte ac merito Christi ad omnes expiandos, Deo reconciliandos, & in statum gratiae ac salutis revocandos: Sed ipse actus Adami peccantis constrinxit omnes homines reatu, atque irae Divinae subjecit: Ergo ipse actus Christi morientis debet omnes a morte liberare, Deo reconciliare, atque in statum gratiae & salutis reponere.
english: Adam's sin, they argue, did not have greater force to bind every human being under the guilt of eternal death than Christ's death and merit have to expiate all, reconcile them to God, and call them back into grace and salvation. Yet Adam's very act of sinning did bind everyone with guilt and subject them to divine wrath. Therefore Christ's very act of dying ought to free everyone from death, reconcile them to God, and restore them to the state of grace and salvation.

source_text:
In hoc argumento involvitur falsa suppositio. In majore enim propositione quasi pro concesso sumitur, Efficaciam sive virtutem causae alicujus majorem semper aut minorem aestimandam, prout ad plura aut pauciora subjecta sese extendat: quod falsissimum est. Aestimanda enim est causae efficacia, sive excellentia, ex natura ipsa & excellentia effectorum, potius quam ex multitudine. Exempli causa, majoris virtutis atque excellentiae argumentum est, si quis uni homini caeco oculos restituat, quam si mille hominibus oculos effodiat; si unicum mutilatum & morbidum sanet, quam si mille homines sanos & integros mutiliet, aut veneno inficiat; uno verbo, si unum hominem ad vitam revocet, quam si mille neci dederit. Pari ratione major & efficacior est vis Christi morte sua vel unum hominem servantis, quam Adami peccato suo totum humanum genus perdentis. Ad Minorem etiam responderi potest, ipsum actum Adami peccantis non constringere ullum hominem reatu mortis, aut obnoxium reddere irae Divinae, nisi exinde quod ab Adamo peccante per generationem naturalem propagetur: atque ad eundem plane modum actus Christi morientis non eripit ullum hominem e statu mortis, neque ab ira Divina liberat, nisi in quantum a Christo per regenerationem supernaturalem derivetur. Utrobique igitur par conditio, si instituatur justa comparatio. Omnes ab Adamo generati naturaliter gratiam Dei ac vitam perdiderunt: Omnes a Christo regenerati supernaturaliter gratiam Dei ac vitam recuperant. Nullus vitio Adami peccantis morti aut irae Divinae subjicitur, nisi ab eo traxerit originem naturalem: Nullus merito Christi morientis a morte aut ira Divina eximitur, nisi ab eo traxerit caelestem nativitatem. Prudenter & docte hoc ab Aquinate explicatur, Contra Gentil. lib. 4. cap. 55. ubi haec habet, Effectus peccati primi parentis pervenit ad unumquemque per carnis originem: sic effectus mortis Christi pertingit ad unumquemque per spiritualem regenerationem. Oportet per Christi Spiritum regenerari, qui cupit Christi meritum in se operari. Si quis adhuc urgeat, Ab Adamo propagari, unde ira consequitur & mortis reatus, est hominibus universis commune; cur per Christum regenerari, unde dependet reconciliatio & salus nostra, non eodem modo omnibus commune statuitur? Nihil aliud est quod respondeam quam, Deum ipsum noluisse, ea quae per modum gratiae ad homines fluunt, ita esse communia omnibus, atque sunt ea quae per modum naturae ad homines derivantur. Voluit gratiam suam discernere homines ab hominibus, ac proinde noluit eam ex aequo communem facere omnibus hominibus. Notavit hoc Augustinus, De Praedest. Sanctor. cap. 5. quem per otium inspicite. Nemo igitur contra Deum obmurmuret, quod specialis gratiae operatione quosdam regeneret, & per fidem in Christum inserat; nemo quaerat cur illum potius quam hunc liberet: quia ad obstuenda ora quorumcunque sufficit hic illud responsum ipsius Dei, Matth. xx. 15. Licet mihi de meo facere quod volo, &c. illud Apostoli, Rom. ix. 18. Misereatur cujus vult. Videte etiam Augustinum, De bono persev. c. 8. Quamvis igitur quantum ad sufficientiam mortis Christi aequaliter se habeat ad omnes, tamen quantum ad efficaciam ex Divina electione pendet, quod effectus meritorum Christi quibusdam misericorditer applicentur, dum propria sua infidelitate impediente aliis non applicentur.

Hactenus responsum est illis qui pugnant pro universali eademque actuali omnium & singulorum hominum reconciliatione: Jam audiamus quid ab illis afferri possit, qui electos ipsos efficacia mortis Christi ab aeterno justificatos, & Deo reconciliatos, statuunt.
english: This argument smuggles in a false assumption. Its major premise treats it as conceded that the efficacy or virtue of a cause is always to be rated greater or lesser according as it reaches more or fewer subjects. That is quite false. A cause's efficacy—or excellence—must be judged from the nature and excellence of its effects, not from how many subjects it touches. Restoring sight to one blind person shows greater virtue than gouging out the eyes of a thousand; healing one mutilated and sick person shows more than mutilating or poisoning a thousand who are healthy and whole; in a word, recalling one human being to life shows more than handing a thousand over to slaughter. By the same measure, Christ's power in saving even one human being by his death is greater and more efficacious than Adam's power in destroying the whole human race by his sin.

To the minor premise one may also reply that Adam's very act of sinning binds no one with the guilt of death, and makes no one liable to divine wrath, except insofar as that person is propagated from sinful Adam by natural generation. In exactly the same way, Christ's dying act snatches no one out of the state of death, and frees no one from divine wrath, except insofar as that person is derived from Christ by supernatural regeneration. On both sides, then, the condition is equal if the comparison is just. All who are generated from Adam by nature lost God's grace and life; all who are regenerated from Christ by grace recover God's grace and life. No one is subjected to death or divine wrath by Adam's fault unless he has drawn natural origin from Adam; no one is exempted from death or divine wrath by Christ's merit unless he has drawn heavenly birth from Christ.

Aquinas explains this prudently and learnedly in Against the Gentiles, book 4, chapter 55: the effect of the first parent's sin reaches each person through the origin of the flesh; so the effect of Christ's death reaches each through spiritual regeneration. Anyone who wants Christ's merit to work in himself must be regenerated by Christ's Spirit. If someone still presses the point—propagation from Adam, from which wrath and the guilt of death follow, is common to all; why then is regeneration through Christ, on which our reconciliation and salvation depend, not made common to all in the same way?—I have nothing else to answer than this: God himself did not will that what flows to human beings by way of grace should be common to all in the same way as what comes by way of nature. He willed his grace to distinguish one person from another, and therefore did not will to make it equally common to all. Augustine noted this in On the Predestination of the Saints, chapter 5; read him at leisure. Let no one murmur against God, then, because by the working of special grace he regenerates some and grafts them into Christ through faith; let no one ask why he frees that one rather than this. To stop every mouth it is enough that God himself answers (Matthew 20:15), "Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with what is mine?" and so on; and that the Apostle says (Romans 9:18), "He has mercy on whom he wills." See also Augustine, On the Good of Perseverance, chapter 8. So although, as to sufficiency, Christ's death stands equally related to all, as to efficacy it depends on divine election: the effects of Christ's merits are mercifully applied to some, while others, hindered by their own unbelief, do not receive that application.

So far we have answered those who contend for a universal and likewise actual reconciliation of all human beings, each and every one. Now let us hear what can be urged by those who hold that the elect themselves, by the efficacy of Christ's death, were justified from eternity and reconciled to God.

source_text: Obj. 1. Qui statuunt Deum ipsis electis ante fidem illorum & paenitentiam placabilem solummodo & reconciliabilem, non autem actu reconciliatum & placatum, illi videntur in Deo ponere actus & potentias, & admittere Deum posse esse quod non est: At Deus est purus actus & prorsus immutabilis; Impossibile est igitur illum nunc esse quod ante non fuit: Si ergo reconciliatus est Petro aut Paulo postquam illi paenitere & credere cognoscuntur, fuit utique illis reconciliatus ab aeterno. Secus enim videri posset dari in Deo, qui purissimus est actus, & usquequaque immutabilis, aliqua est variatio; Quod tamen a Natura Divina omnimodae mutabilitatis experte alienissimum esse nemo sanus non fatebitur: maxime cum non solum rectae rationis dictatis consonum, saniorisque Philosophiae placitis consentaneum esse videatur, quae docet, quod idem qua idem semper facit idem, hoc est, idem eodem modo se habens eundem semper producit effectum; verum etiam non paucis, iisque disertissimis sacrae Scripturae locis confirmari ac stabiliri possit; illo utique testimonio ex Prophetia Malachiae c. 3. v. 6. Ego enim Dominus & non mutor (secundum Junium, Ego Jehovah non mutor), item Numerorum c. 23. 19. Non est Deus quasi homo, ut mentiatur: nec ut filius hominis, ut mutetur. Quibus consimilis plane locus suffragatur ex Epist. sancti Apostoli Jacobi, c. 1. v. 17. Omnis donatio bona, & omne perfectum munus est superne descendens a Patre luminum, apud quem non inest transmutatio, aut conversionis obumbratio: tantum abest ut in Deo sit mutatio quaevis, ut in eo ne minime quidem sit conversionis obumbratio. Quod si de Deo affirmari possit, quod modo placabilis sit, modo placatus, modo reconciliabilis tantum, modo reconciliatus, dubitari sane, nec immerito, potest, an Deus semper sui similis existat, atque eodem plane modo semper se habeat. Placabilitas enim praeviam quandam tantum dispositionem, & ad futuram placationem inclinationem, innuere videtur, ut & reconciliabilitas, facilitatem & propensionem in Deo ad reconciliationem, quae hominibus demum credentibus ex potentia in actum elicitur.
english: Objection 1. Those who say that toward the elect themselves, before their faith and repentance, God is only placable and reconciliable—not actually reconciled and placated—seem to put acts and potencies in God, and to admit that God can be what he is not. But God is pure act and altogether immutable. It is therefore impossible that he should now be what he was not before. So if he is reconciled to Peter or Paul after they are known to repent and believe, he was already reconciled to them from eternity. Otherwise some variation would seem to be given in God, who is purest act and altogether immutable. Yet no sane person will deny that such variation is utterly alien to the divine nature, which is free of mutability on every side—especially since that conclusion agrees not only with the dictates of right reason and with the sounder philosophy (which teaches that the same, as the same, always does the same: that is, what remains the same way always produces the same effect), but can also be confirmed and settled by not a few, and those the clearest, places of sacred Scripture: by Malachi’s prophecy (Malachi 3:6), “For I the Lord do not change” (Junius: “I Jehovah do not change”); likewise by Numbers (Numbers 23:19), “God is not as a human that he should lie, nor as a son of man that he should change.” A plainly similar place gives support from the Epistle of James (James 1:17): “Every good giving and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of turning.” So far is any change from belonging in God that in him there is not even the least shadow of turning. But if one may say of God that he is now placable, now placated, now only reconciliable, now reconciled, one may fairly and not without cause doubt whether God always remains like himself and always holds himself in exactly the same way. Placability seems to suggest only a prior disposition and an inclination toward a future placating; reconciliability likewise suggests a readiness and propensity in God toward reconciliation—which at last, when human beings believe, is drawn out from potency into act.

source_text: Deum esse reconciliabilem huic aut illi electo ante fidem & paenitentiam ejus, & esse actu reconciliatum eidem post fidem & paenitentiam ejusdem, non magis arguit in Deo mutationem ab actu ad potentiam, quam hunc hominem minime esse justificatum donec credat, & esse actu a Deo justificatum postquam credat, arguat eandem in Deo mutabilitatem; aut hujus peccata esse remissibilia, & esse post paenitentiam actu a Deo remissa, probet essentiae aut voluntatis Divinae mutationem temporalem a potentia ad actum. Nemo autem recte dixerit, ex eo quod Paulus nunc justificatus est in Christum credens, qui minime fuit justificatus dum fuit in Christum blasphemus, Deum ipsum subire aliquam mutationem; ergo neque ex eo quod modo reconciliabilis Deo, modo actu reconciliatus statuitur: cum esse justificatum, & esse Deo reconciliatum, aut plane eadem sunt, aut saltem inseparabiliter connexa. Sed ut hunc scrupulum magis aperte eximamus, sciendum est, Utcunque nullum absolutum potest de novo advenire Deo sine ejus mutatione, tamen infinitas relativas denominationes posse de novo, & secundum differentiam temporis de Deo aliquando praedicari, aliquando non praedicari, Divina essentia & voluntate interea manente absque omni umbra mutationis. Quae enim mutabiliter & temporaliter de Deo affirmantur, non sic affirmantur propter mutationem aliquam Deo advenientem, sed secundum mutationem creaturae advenientem. Verbi causa, Adamus est a Deo creabilis vere dici potuit, quando vere dici non potuit, Adamus est a Deo creatus. Pari ratione, Adamus est a Deo justificabilis, vel Adamus est Deo reconciliabilis, potuit dici ante paenitentiam ejus actualem; at Adamus est actu justificatus & Deo reconciliatus, non potuit. Neque tamen in Deo ponimus actus & potentias, aut mutabilitatem qualemcunque; quia haec praedicantur de Deo diversimode, non per mutationem sui in seipso, sed per mutationem creaturae quae est ab ipso.
english: That God is reconciliable to this or that elect person before that person’s faith and repentance, and is actually reconciled to the same person after faith and repentance, no more proves a change in God from act to potency than this does: that a human being is not justified at all until he believes, and is actually justified by God after he believes. Nor does it prove a temporal change of the divine essence or will from potency to act that someone’s sins are remissible and, after repentance, are actually remitted by God. No one will rightly say that because Paul is now justified as a believer in Christ—though he was not justified at all while he blasphemed against Christ—God himself undergoes some change. So neither does it follow from saying that a person is now reconciliable to God and now actually reconciled. To be justified and to be reconciled to God are either plainly the same, or at least inseparably joined.

To clear the scruple more openly, this must be known: although nothing absolute can newly arrive to God without a change in him, yet countless relative names can newly be predicated of God—at one time, and not at another—according to differences of time, while the divine essence and will remain without any shadow of change. What is affirmed of God in a mutable and temporal way is not affirmed because some change has come upon God, but because a change has come upon the creature. For example, one could truly say “Adam is creatable by God” when one could not yet truly say “Adam is created by God.” By the same measure, one could say before Adam’s actual repentance, “Adam is justificable by God,” or “Adam is reconciliable to God”; but one could not say, “Adam is actually justified and reconciled to God.” Even so we do not put acts and potencies in God, or any mutability at all. These things are said of God in different ways not by a change of God in himself, but by a change of the creature that comes from him.

source_text: Nam, ut docet Albertus, in illis quae agunt per essentiam, agens uno modo semper se habet: Non dicitur Agens nunc, & non prius, nisi quatenus actum nunc est, & non prius. Neque in ipsa Dei voluntate cogitamus novum aut temporaneum actum, quando ponimus fide adveniente illum fieri actu reconciliatum huic aut illi homini, cui ante fidem fuit tantum reconciliabilis: quia Deus non tunc incipit velle ut hic credens sit ei actualiter reconciliatus, qui fuit ante conceptam fidem reconciliabilis, sed ab omni aeternitate voluit ut hoc ipso momento & credens esset, & actu reconciliatus. In volente igitur non sunt mutationes succedaneae, sed in volito, eaedemque secundum unam, aeternam ac constantissimam Dei voluntatem.
english: As Albert teaches, in things that act through essence the agent always holds himself in one way: he is not called “agent now and not before,” except insofar as the act now is and was not before. Nor do we invent a new or temporal act in God’s will itself when we say that, once faith has come, he becomes actually reconciled to this or that human being to whom, before faith, he was only reconciliable. God does not then begin to will that this believer should be actually reconciled to him—after having been only reconciliable before faith was conceived. From all eternity he willed that at this very moment the person both would believe and would be actually reconciled. Succession of changes is not in the willer, then, but in the thing willed—and those changes follow one eternal and most constant will of God.

source_text:
Obj. 2. Deus est illi actu reconciliatus, quem actu diligit. At diligit omnes electos ab aeterno: Ergo ab aeterno est illis actu reconciliatus: Ergo illi sunt etiam actu reconciliati & justificati ab aeterno.

Solut. Distinguendum est cum Aquinate. Deus enim dicitur diligere dupliciter, secundum propositum communicandi bonitatem suam, & secundum ipsum actum communicationis, In 3. Sent. dist. 19. Amor ille secundum aeternum propositum, quem Theologi appellant amorem aeternae benevolentiae, non facit ut qui hunc in modum ametur, actu justificatus, aut actu reconciliatus a Deo habeatur, sed ut inter infallibiliter justificandos & reconciliandos censeatur. Est igitur diversa ratio illorum vocabulorum quae actus in Deo immanentes, & quae actus a Deo ad nos transeuntes denotant. Priora, qualia sunt Dilectio, Electio, Praedestinatio, sunt aeterni & interni actus ipsius Dei; atque ab illis homines dicuntur Dilecti, Electi, Praedestinati, propter arcanum beneplacitum Divinae voluntatis in seipso conceptum & absconditum. Posteriora, qualia sunt Vocatio, Justificatio, Reconciliatio, Glorificatio, sunt actus externi ad creaturam existentem terminati, & in eam quasi recepti; atque ab illis nemo proprie dicitur Vocatus, Justificatus, Reconciliatus, Glorificatus, ex solo illo arcano & aeterno Divinae voluntatis proposito, sed ex facta exsecutione ejusdem propositi, & producto effectu in hominibus. Fatemur ergo in Deo voluntatem aeternam justificandi & sibi reconciliandi omnes electos: negamus tamen eos ab aeterno justificatos aut reconciliatos dici oportere: Sicut agnoscimus fuisse in Deo aeternam voluntatem creandi mundum, & tamen negamus mundum fuisse ab aeterno creatum. Quod Zanch. dixit de remissione actuali peccatorum, id nos dicimus de actuali reconciliatione Electorum: Est quidem illa certissima in destinatione Divina ab aeterno, at actu non datur ex parte Dei, neque actu recipitur ex parte hominis, donec resipiscat & credat. Thomson, Diatr. pag. 96.
english: Objection 2. God is actually reconciled to whoever he actually loves. He loves every elect person from eternity. So, the objection runs, he has been actually reconciled to them from eternity—and they have been actually reconciled and justified from eternity.

Solution. Follow the distinction in Aquinas. God loves in two senses: by the purpose to communicate his goodness, and by the very act of communicating it (Sentences, book 3, distinction 19). The love that tracks the eternal purpose—theologians call it the love of eternal benevolence—does not already count the beloved as actually justified or actually reconciled. It only ranks that person among those who will infallibly be justified and reconciled. Words for acts that stay inside God, and words for acts that pass from God to us, therefore do different work. Dilection, Election, and Predestination name eternal, inward acts of God; people are called Beloved, Elect, and Predestined from the hidden good pleasure of the divine will conceived and kept in God himself. Calling, Justification, Reconciliation, and Glorification name outward acts that terminate on a creature who already exists and are as it were received into that creature. No one is properly Called, Justified, Reconciled, or Glorified from the hidden eternal purpose alone, but from the finished execution of that purpose and the effect it produces in human beings. We gladly grant that God has an eternal will to justify every elect person and reconcile each to himself. We still refuse to say they were justified or reconciled from eternity. In the same way we grant God an eternal will to create the world, yet deny that the world was created from eternity. What Zanchi said of the actual remission of sins fits the elect's actual reconciliation: it is most certain in the divine destination from eternity, yet it is not actually given on God's side, nor actually received on the human side, before the person repents and believes (Thomson, Diatribe, p. 96).

source_text:
Obj. 3. Efficacia mediorum in quibusdam hominibus potius quam in aliis non ex discrimine liberi arbitrii oritur, sed exinde quod Deus est reconciliatus electis omnibus in Christo ante jacta mundi fundamenta, aliis haud reconciliatus: Non igitur negare debemus electos omnes esse Deo actualiter reconciliatos ante conversionem suam ac fidem; quandoquidem ipsa dispensatio tam efficacium mediorum ad producendam in illis fidem & paenitentiam, ex aeterna illa & antecedanea eorundem reconciliatione traxit suam originem.

Solut. Efficacitatem infallibilem mediorum ad salutem ordinatorum non ab humana voluntate pendere, sed ex aeterno & speciali quodam Dei erga electos suos amore, lubenter confitemur. At hunc amorem nil aliud esse dicimus, quatenus respicit homines adhuc infideles & inconversos, quam gratuitum propositum providendi iisdem quo in futurum convertantur, justificentur, Deo reconcilientur, & ad aeternam vitam infallibiliter perducantur. Aeque male igitur ab hoc amore aeterno infertur aeterna justificatio, & aeterna reconciliatio electorum, atque aeterna glorificatio eorundem, cum colligere inde solummodo oporteat certam et infallibilem eorundem justificationem, reconciliationem et glorificationem: quae certitudo sive infallibilis efficacia mediorum ad salutem tendentium ex praedicto amore Dei, non ex virtute liberi arbitrii nascitur. Hunc amorem aeternum, unde pendet certitudo conversionis et reconciliationis in tempore producendae, si lubet alicui vocare actualem reconciliationem, eo quod ipse Deus vocet ea quae non sunt tanquam sint, Rom. iv. 17. nihil impedio, modo simul fateatur se rei faciendae propositum rei factae nomine indigitare: Quia in Dei praedestinatione fixum erat quod suo tempore futurum erat, ut loquitur Augustinus, De Civit. Dei, lib. 12. cap. 16.
english: Objection 3. Why do the means work in some people and not in others? Not, they say, from any difference of free choice, but because God is already reconciled to all the elect in Christ before the world's foundations were laid, and is not reconciled to the rest. So we must not deny that every elect person is actually reconciled to God before conversion and faith—since the very dispensing of means powerful enough to produce faith and repentance in them sprang from that eternal, prior reconciliation.

Solution. We gladly admit that the infallible efficacy of means ordained to salvation does not hang on the human will. It hangs on a certain eternal and special love of God for his elect. But so far as that love regards people who are still unbelieving and unconverted, it is nothing but a free purpose to supply them with what will later convert them, justify them, reconcile them to God, and lead them without fail to eternal life. Inferring from that eternal love an eternal justification, an eternal reconciliation of the elect, and an eternal glorification of them is therefore just as bad a leap. What follows is only their certain and infallible justification, reconciliation, and glorification. That certainty—the infallible efficacy of means that tend toward salvation—is born from the love of God just named, not from free choice's power. If someone wants to label this eternal love (the ground of the certainty that conversion and reconciliation will be produced in time) "actual reconciliation," because God himself "calls the things that are not as though they were" (Romans 4:17), I will not stop him—provided he also admits he is using the name of a finished deed for the purpose of a deed still to be done. For God's predestination had already fixed what would come in its own time, as Augustine puts it (City of God, book 12, chapter 16).

source_text:
Proferri etiam possunt ex Scripturis loca nonnulla quae videntur quoad electos actualem cum Deo reconciliationem, eamque aeternam, asserere; ante fidem & paenitentiam eorundem.

Ephes. i. 4. Deus dicitur eos elegisse ante mundi constitutionem, & versu 6. acceptos habuisse in dilecto suo Filio: Fuerunt igitur electi, & jam actu justificati & reconciliati ab aeterno: neque reconciliatio illorum ex parte Dei post fidem Evangelio adhibitam facta est, sed potius tum incepit manifestari & revelari, quod factum fuit ante jacta mundi fundamenta.
english: Some Scripture places can also be brought forward that seem, as to the elect, to assert an actual reconciliation with God—and an eternal one—before their faith and repentance.

Ephesians 1:4 says God elected them before the world’s foundation, and verse 6 that he had them accepted in his beloved Son. So, the objection runs, they were elect, and already actually justified and reconciled from eternity. Their reconciliation on God’s side was not made after faith was applied to the gospel; rather, what had already been done before the world’s foundations were laid then began to be manifested and revealed.

source_text: Resp. Aliud est eligere aliquem ad vitam ante constitutionem mundi, aliud actu justificare & reconciliare eundem sibi ante constitutionem mundi. Electio dicit in Deo aeternam voluntatem justificandi, reconciliandi & salvandi personam electam, sed justificandi, reconciliandi & salvandi suo tempore per fidem. Ipsa igitur actualis justificatio, reconciliatio, sanctificatio hominis electi fluit ab aeterna electione, sed non est eidem coaeterna. Facile est hoc colligere ex toto discursu Paulino in illo primo capite ad Ephesios. Affirmat nos electos ante jacta mundi fundamenta, vers. 4. sed non dicit proinde nos sanctificatos ante jacta mundi fundamenta, sed electos ut essemus sancti & inculpati coram eo per charitatem. Neque virtute aeternae electionis docet nos ab aeterno fuisse justificatos aut reconciliatos, sed in pleni temporis dispensatione, postquam patefacto Evangelio fidem adhibuimus, vers. 9, 10, &c.
english: Response. Electing someone to life before the world’s foundation is one thing; actually justifying and reconciling that same person to himself before the world’s foundation is another. Election names in God an eternal will to justify, reconcile, and save the elect person—but to justify, reconcile, and save him in his own time through faith. So the elect person’s actual justification, reconciliation, and sanctification flow from eternal election; they are not coeternal with it. That is easy to gather from Paul’s whole argument in Ephesians 1. He affirms that we were elect before the world’s foundations were laid (Ephesians 1:4), yet he does not say we were therefore sanctified before those foundations were laid. He says we were elect so that we might be holy and blameless before him in love. Nor does he teach, by the power of eternal election, that we were justified or reconciled from eternity. He teaches that this happened in the dispensation of the fullness of time, after we applied faith to the gospel that had been opened (Ephesians 1:9–10 and following).

source_text: Neque obstat illud, Acceptos nos habuit in dilecto suo Filio: Nam Graecum verbum ἐχαρίτωσεν potius ad praesentem statum electorum jam regeneratorum quam ad aeternum Dei propositum referri videtur. Unde Beza vertit, gratis efficit sibi gratos, nempe gratis nunc justificavit & in statum actualis reconciliationis admisit ipsos credentes; Quod si quis illam acceptationem de aeterno Dei amore interpretetur, quo electos nondum natos complectitur, acceptatio illa propositum communicandi bonitatem suam, non ipsum actum communicationis denotabit, ut ex Aquinate supra responsum est. Beza etiam in Commentariis suis ad vers. 5. recte observavit Electos suo tempore sapientiam, justitiam, sanctificationem, redemptionem gratis per fidem adipisci: non igitur ab aeterno justificati sanctificati aut reconciliati, quamvis electi & praedestinati ab aeterno. Sed nemo clarius hoc docuit quam ipse Apostolus, qui eos ipsos, quos dixit electos ante jacta mundi fundamenta, tamen natura fuisse filios irae demonstrat, Ephes. ii. 3. & ac diu mansisse absque Christo, alienos a Republica Israelis, & extraneos a pactis promissionis, spem non habentes, Deo expertes in mundo: Tunc vero in Christo Jesu qui olim erant procul propinquos factos fuisse, cum per sanguinem Christi fide apprehensi Deo reconciliati essent, vers. 12, 13, &c. Si igitur Paulo fidem adhibemus, utcunque electio & praedestinatio hominum sit ab aeterno Dei amore aeterna, tamen justificatio & reconciliatio eorundem non manifestari aut revelari dicenda est quando credunt in Christum, sed tum primum fieri & constitui.
english: Nor does the clause “he had us accepted in his beloved Son” block this (Ephesians 1:6). The Greek verb ἐχαρίτωσεν seems to point to the present state of the elect already regenerated, more than to God’s eternal purpose. So Beza renders it, “he freely makes them gracious to himself”—that is, he has now freely justified believers and admitted them into the state of actual reconciliation. If someone reads that acceptance as God’s eternal love embracing the elect not yet born, then the acceptance names the purpose of communicating his goodness, not the act of communication itself—as was already answered from Aquinas above. Beza also notes rightly in his comments on verse 5 that the elect obtain wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption freely through faith in their own time. They were not, then, justified, sanctified, or reconciled from eternity, though they were elect and predestined from eternity (Ephesians 1:5). No one taught this more clearly than the Apostle himself. The very people he called elect before the world’s foundations were laid he also shows were by nature children of wrath (Ephesians 2:3), and long remained without Christ, aliens from Israel’s commonwealth, strangers to the covenants of promise, without hope, and without God in the world. Then, in Christ Jesus, those who were once far off were made near when, through Christ’s blood grasped by faith, they were reconciled to God (Ephesians 2:12–13 and following). If we trust Paul, then—however eternal human election and predestination are from God’s eternal love—their justification and reconciliation are not to be called a mere manifestation or unveiling when they believe in Christ. That is when they first come to be and are constituted.

source_text:
2. Tim. i. 9, 10. Dicit Apostolus, electis Datam fuisse gratiam in Christo Jesu ante tempora seculorum; patefactam autem fuisse eandem gratiam per adventum Servatoris nostri Jesu Christi: At Deus illis videtur plane reconciliatus ante tempora seculorum quibus dedit gratiam in Christo ante tempora seculorum.

Resp. Propter firmitatem & immobilitatem Divini propositi illa gratia dicitur ante tempora seculorum data electis, quae ante tempora seculorum fuit illis destinata: An hoc igitur loco aeterna datio est aeterna praeparatio gratiae electis suo tempore infallibiliter dandae. Sic Augustinus, Apostolus datam dixit gratiam, quando nec erant adhuc quibus daretur, quoniam in dispositione ac praedestinatione Dei jam factum erat quod suo tempore futurum erat, De doctr. Christ. lib. 3. cap. 34. Sic Junius in haec ipsa verba, Datam esse dicit ab aeterno gratiam, ad quam ab aeterno fuimus praedestinati. Nec aliter eam exposuit Calvinus; Donatio haec, inquit, gratiae cujus meminit Apostolus, nihil aliud est quam praedestinatio qua sumus adoptati in Dei filios. Paulo post, Dedit, quod nullo merito provocante nondum natis assignavit, ac in thesauris suis repositum habuit, donec re ipsa patefaceret nihil se frustra statuere. Recte ergo hinc deducamus gratiam justificationis, reconciliationis & salutis fuisse actu aeterno assignatam electis omnibus, & quasi repositam & reservatam illis in thesauro Divini amoris; sed fuisse actu in eos collatam ante fidem & conversionem eorundem non recte deducitur. Ipsa justificatio & reconciliatio electorum non dicitur tum patefacta & manifestata quando credunt in Christum, sed tum donata & constituta: Quod vero tum revelatum & manifestatum dicitur, est illud aeternum beneplacitum sive propositum Dei de servandis electis; quod innotescit nobis postquam Spiritu & fide donati Justificationem & reconciliationem cum Deo sumus consequuti.
english: 2 Timothy 1:9–10. The Apostle says grace was given to the elect in Christ Jesus before the ages of the world, and that the same grace was made manifest through the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ. So God seems plainly reconciled already, before the ages, to those to whom he gave grace in Christ before the ages.

Response. Because the divine purpose is firm and unmovable, that grace is said to have been given to the elect before the ages which was destined for them before the ages. In this place, then, eternal giving is eternal preparation of the grace that will be given to the elect without fail in their own time. So Augustine: the Apostle said grace was given when those who would receive it did not yet exist, because in God’s disposition and predestination what was to come in its time was already fixed (On Christian Doctrine, book 3, chapter 34). So Junius on these very words: grace was given from eternity, the grace to which we were predestined from eternity. Calvin expounds it no other way. “This donation of grace of which the Apostle speaks,” he says, “is nothing but the predestination by which we are adopted as God’s children.” A little later: “He gave”—what, with no merit prompting him, he assigned to those not yet born and kept stored in his treasuries until the thing itself would show that he decrees nothing in vain. From this we may rightly gather that the grace of justification, reconciliation, and salvation was by an eternal act assigned to all the elect, and as it were stored and reserved for them in the treasury of divine love. That it was by an act conferred on them before their faith and conversion does not follow. The elect’s justification and reconciliation themselves are not said to be opened and manifested when they believe in Christ; they are then given and constituted. What is said to be revealed and manifested then is God’s eternal good pleasure—his purpose to save the elect—which becomes known to us after, gifted with the Spirit and with faith, we have obtained justification and reconciliation with God.

source_text: Sunt quaedam alia loca quae afferuntur ut probent reconciliationem nostram cum Deo non tum fieri cum per fidem amplectimur Mediatorem, sed electos omnes fuisse Deo ab aeterno reconciliatos. Hujusmodi sunt, Rom. v. 10. Cum inimici eramus, reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem filii sui. Item, Ephes. ii. 4, 5. Propter multam charitatem qua dilexit nos, etiam cum mortui eramus in peccatis, una vivificavit nos cum Christo. Denique Coloss. i. 21, 22. Vos, Cum eratis alienati & inimici mente in operibus malis, nunc sane reconciliavit in corpore carnis suae per mortem, &c. Ex hisce locis apparet reconciliationem non consequi actum fidei, sed Deum esse reconciliatum suis etiam tum cum illi increduli & inimici existant Deo. Non enim argumentum est Dei placabilis & reconciliabilis, sed placati & actu reconciliati, quando homines dignatur talibus beneficiis.
english: Still other places are brought to prove that reconciliation with God does not begin when through faith we embrace the Mediator, but that every elect person was already reconciled to God from eternity. Romans 5:10 is of that kind: "when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son." So is Ephesians 2:4–5: "because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, he made us alive together with Christ." And so is Colossians 1:21–22: "you who were once alienated and enemies in mind in evil works he has now indeed reconciled in the body of his flesh through death," and so on.

From those places the adversaries infer that reconciliation does not wait on the act of faith. God, they say, is already reconciled to his own even while they still stand unbelieving and hostile to him. Benefits like these, they argue, are not the mark of a God merely placable and reconcilable, but of one already placated and actually reconciled.

source_text:
Resp. Si per reconciliationem nil aliud denotetur, quam inclinatio & propensio Divinae voluntatis ad remissionem indulgandam, & pacem ineundam cum omnibus qui fide amplexuri sunt redemtorem, fatemur Deum stare reconciliatum toti humano generi virtute mortis Christi, etiam cum nos illi manemus inimici. Sed in hoc (ut dictum est supra) gradus potius situs est ad actualem & personalem nostram reconciliationem, quam ipsa actualis singularium personarum reconciliatio. Porro, si per reconciliationem intelligamus aeternam Dei dilectionem, juxta quam decrevit certas quasdam personas in tempore vocare, justificare, reconciliare sibi & servare, non inficias eo Deum hoc sensu dici posse benevolum omnibus electis, etiam tum cum in impietate sua & infidelitate versantur. Sed haec benevolentia quae praecedit fidem cordibus electorum inspiratam, continet solummodo propositum ineundae pacis cum illis, non confert illis statum obtentae pacis & actualis reconciliationis. Hisce praemissis respondeo, in omnibus illis locis sermonem esse aut de gradu illo ad reconciliationem personalem, aut de electis credentibus & in statu actualis reconciliationis non nisi fide interveniente constitutis; Nostram igitur sententiam confirmant potius oppositam. Nam quod dicitur Rom. V. 10. Cum inimici eramus, reconciliati fuimus Deo per mortem Filii, &c. alium sensum non habet quam, Homines ex statu inimicitiarum transferri in statum reconciliationis actualis cum Deo per mortem Christi, simulac in Christum crediderint. Id inde liquet, quod Apostolus vers. 1. hujus capitis hanc pacem sive reconciliationem cum Deo ad eos solos restringit qui sunt per fidem justificati, versu etiam 11. loquitur de eadem actuali reconciliatione tanquam de novo constituta, Nunc, inquit, reconciliationem assecuti sumus, idest, Nunc postquam in Christum credidimus. Alterum locum quod attinet, Ephes. ii. 4, 5. verissimum est, Deum nos mortuos vivificasse cum Christo: sed sicut non vivificavit actualiter nisi fide prius inspirata, ita nec reconciliavit. Deo enim reconciliari est a reatu mortis liberari, collocari in statu vitae spiritualis, & donari haereditario jure ad vitam aeternam: quae electis minime competunt ex eo solo quod electi, sed tum demum cum efficaciter vocati & ad Deum conversi fuerint. Docuit hoc ipse Apostolus versu 8. Gratia estis salvati per fidem: Idque non ex vobis: Dei donum est.

Ultimus locus ex Coloss. i. 21, 22. desumptus diserte sententiam nostram confirmat; scilicet nec ipso actu aeterno Dei praedestinantis, nec ipso merito Christi pro electis suis morientis, homines evadere statim justificatos, & Deo reconciliatos. Quid enim aliud pra se ferunt haec verba, Quondam abalienatos nunc sane reconciliavit, quam nos tum demum per sanguinem Christi obtinere remissionem peccatorum & reconciliationem actualem cum Deo, cum per fidem Christo inserti, in actualem participationem & possessionem meritorum & justitiae ejus admittimur? Plura ad hujus theseos explicationem congerere non est necesse. Ex eis quae dicta sunt satis constare potest, eos universalem vim mortis Christi extra justos suos limites extendere, qui ipso facto Christi morientis omnes mortales promiscue in statum gratiae restitutos arbitrantur; nec minus illos, qui omnes praedestinatos propter meritum Christi, etiam ante fidem adhibitam Evangelio, ab aeterno justificatos & actu reconciliatos Deo defendunt.
english: Response. If by reconciliation nothing is meant but an inclination and readiness of the divine will to grant remission and to make peace with all who will embrace the Redeemer by faith, then we confess that God stands reconciled to the whole human race by the force of Christ’s death, even while we remain his enemies. But that (as said above) is a step toward our actual and personal reconciliation, not yet the actual reconciliation of particular persons. Further, if by reconciliation we mean God’s eternal love—by which he decreed to call, justify, reconcile to himself, and save certain people in time—I do not deny that God in that sense can be called benevolent to all the elect, even while they are still sunk in impiety and unbelief. But that benevolence, which precedes faith breathed into the elect’s hearts, holds only the purpose of making peace with them. It does not give them the state of peace already obtained, or of actual reconciliation.

With that said, I answer that in all those places the talk is either about that step toward personal reconciliation, or about believing elect people already set in the state of actual reconciliation only with faith intervening. So the places confirm our view rather than the contrary. Romans 5:10 (“when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of the Son,” and so on) means nothing else than that people are moved from enmity into actual reconciliation with God through Christ’s death as soon as they have believed in Christ. That is plain because in verse 1 of the same chapter the Apostle restricts this peace—or reconciliation—with God to those alone who are justified through faith (Romans 5:1); and in verse 11 he speaks of the same actual reconciliation as newly constituted: “Now,” he says, “we have obtained reconciliation”—that is, now after we have believed in Christ (Romans 5:11).

As for Ephesians 2:4–5, it is most true that God made us, who were dead, alive with Christ. But just as he did not make us alive in act until faith was first inspired, so neither did he reconcile us. To be reconciled to God is to be freed from death’s guilt, placed in spiritual life, and gifted with a hereditary right to eternal life. Those goods do not belong to the elect merely because they are elect. They belong at last when they have been effectually called and turned to God. The Apostle himself teaches this in verse 8: “By grace you have been saved through faith—and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8).

The last place, drawn from Colossians 1:21–22, expressly confirms our sentence: neither God’s eternal predestinating act itself, nor Christ’s merit itself in dying for his elect, makes people at once justified and reconciled to God. What else do the words “once alienated, he has now indeed reconciled” mean, except that we obtain remission of sins and actual reconciliation with God through Christ’s blood only when, inserted into Christ by faith, we are admitted into actual share and possession of his merits and righteousness? There is no need to pile up more for explaining this thesis. From what has been said it is plain enough that those stretch the universal force of Christ’s death beyond its just limits who, by the bare deed of Christ dying, judge every mortal indiscriminately restored into the state of grace—and no less those who defend that all the predestined, for Christ’s merit, were justified from eternity and actually reconciled to God even before faith was applied to the gospel.

source_text:
CAPUT VI. Thesis ultima proponitur & confirmatur.

Universalem mortis Christi virtutem & efficaciam tribus thesibus explicatam vobis exhibuimus. In prima demonstratum est, Hanc Christi mortem a Deo constitutam, atque humano generi propositam, tanquam universale remedium omnibus & singulis hominibus applicabile. In secunda exposuimus quo sensu Christus pro omnibus mortuus dicatur, sive quo sensu Christi mors universalis causa salutis in bonum totius humani generis stabilita agnoscatur: Nempe, non (ut quidam volunt) ratione nudae sufficientiae sive intrinseci valoris, quo respectu mors Christi, vel sanguis Filii Dei, est pretium hominibus angelisque omnibus ac singulis redimendis plusquam sufficiens, sed ratione foederis Evangelici hac Christi morte ac sanguine stabiliti & confirmati, juxta cujus foederis tenorem, omnibus & singulis hominibus accrevit jus, sub fidei conditione vendicandi sibi remissionem peccatorum & vitam aeternam. Hisce duabus thesibus subjunximus tertiam, qua ostensum est, Posita hac universali virtute mortis Christi, atque hoc universali foedere Evangelico ad quemlibet hominem spectante, tamen hanc vel illam singularem personam habere quidem solo beneficio hujus mortis Deum obligatum ad pacem cum illo ineundam, vitamque illi dandam, si crediderit; non autem habere actualem justificationem aut reconciliationem, sive actualem statum gratiae & salutis, antequam credat. Jam restat quarta & ultima thesis, quae inserviat potissimum eximendo cuidam scrupulo ex animis eorum qui hanc universalem, quam defendimus, mortis Christi efficaciam amplius extendunt quam rei veritas patietur.
english: Chapter 6. The last thesis is set out and confirmed.

We have already laid before you the universal force and efficacy of Christ’s death in three theses. In the first we showed that God appointed this death of Christ and set it before the human race as a universal remedy applicable to every human being. In the second we explained in what sense Christ is said to have died for all—or in what sense his death is owned as a universal cause of salvation established for the good of the whole human race. Not, as some want, merely by bare sufficiency or intrinsic worth, in which respect Christ’s death, or the blood of the Son of God, is a price more than enough to redeem every human and every angel. Rather, by the gospel covenant established and confirmed in this death and blood of Christ. By the terms of that covenant every human being gained a right, under the condition of faith, to claim remission of sins and eternal life.

To those two theses we added a third. Even with this universal force of Christ’s death in place, and with this universal gospel covenant looking to any person whatsoever, this or that particular person does have, by the sole benefit of that death, God bound to make peace with him and to give him life if he believes. He does not yet have actual justification or reconciliation—or the actual state of grace and salvation—before he believes. There remains a fourth and final thesis. Its chief work is to clear a scruple from the minds of those who stretch this universal efficacy of Christ’s death, which we defend, farther than the truth of the matter will bear.

source_text:
Sunt enim nonnulli, qui ex eo quod mors Christi, sensu praedicto, humano generi, sive omnibus & singulis hominibus, impensa affirmatur, statim inferunt, Divinae justitiae & bonitati illud jam incumbere, ut omnibus, pro quibus Christum sic in mortem dedit, administret media ad fidem ingenerandam necessaria. Quia autem luce meridiana clarius liquet, Ethnicis & Paganis, quibus nunquam affulsit lux Evangelii, non esse data media quae immediate sufficiant ad fidem in iis producendam, eo confugiunt, ut dicant etiam talibus dari semper media sufficientia, quibus mediate, & quasi per gradus ad fidem Christi duci potuissent, si istis bene usi fuissent. Si quis autem quaerat, quae sint illa gratiae media, quae omnibus praestare, omnesque ad fidem Christi sufficienter ducere potuissent, Naturam Gratiae nomine obvolutam nobis obtrudunt. Dicunt enim reliquias quasdam vitae spiritualis omnibus hominibus inesse, scilicet in intellectu aliquam Dei cognitionem, in affectu ad bonum cognitum aliquod desiderium, quibus donis naturalibus si homo recte utatur, Deum illum majori gratia cumulaturum, & fide salutifera donaturum. Videtur Aquinas in hanc sententiam propendere, Quaest. 14. De veritate, art. 11, Resp. ad 1, Ubi scribit hunc in modum, Si quis in sylvis enutritus ductum rationis naturalis sequeretur in appetitu boni, & fuga mali; certissime tenendum est quod ei Deus vel per internam inspirationem revelaret ea quae ad credendum sunt necessaria, vel aliquem fidei praedicatorem ad eum dirigeret. Eo igitur redit horum sententia, ut existiment Deum efficacia & merito mortis Christi, jam quasi statuta lege adstrictum esse, ut media sufficientia omnibus suppeditet quibus ad Christum ducantur si voluerint; ita ut ex parte Dei nihil desideretur, quo minus omnes ad fidem & fructuosam participationem mortis Christi perveniant. Ad hujus difficultatis enodationem hanc thesin explicandam & confirmandam suscepimus.

Thesis IV.
Posita Christi morte omnibus hominibus applicabili sub conditione fidei, stat cum bonitate & justitia Divina suppeditare vel negare, sive nationibus sive singularibus hominibus, media applicationis, idque pro beneplacito voluntatis suae, non pro disparitate voluntatum humanarum.
english: Some people argue at once from the claim that Christ’s death, in the sense already given, was spent for the human race—for every human being—that divine justice and goodness now require God to administer to all for whom he thus gave Christ to death the means needed to generate faith. Yet it is clearer than noon that ethnics and pagans, on whom the light of the gospel never shone, have not been given means that immediately suffice to produce faith in them. So the same people take refuge here: they say even such people are always given sufficient means by which, mediately and as if by degrees, they could have been led to faith in Christ if they had used those means well.

Ask what those means of grace are that could have stood ready for all and led all sufficiently to faith in Christ, and they thrust Nature upon us wrapped in the name of Grace. They say remnants of spiritual life remain in every human—some knowledge of God in the intellect, some desire for the known good in the affection—and that if a person uses those natural gifts rightly, God will heap greater grace on him and gift him with saving faith. Aquinas seems to lean that way in De veritate, question 14, article 11, reply to the first objection, where he writes: if someone reared in the woods followed the lead of natural reason in appetite for good and flight from evil, it must be held with full certainty that God would either reveal by inward inspiration what is necessary for belief, or send some preacher of the faith to him.

So their view comes to this: by the efficacy and merit of Christ’s death God is already bound as by statute to supply everyone with sufficient means to be led to Christ if they will, so that nothing is wanting on God’s side to keep anyone from faith and a fruitful share in Christ’s death. To untie that knot we have taken up this thesis to explain and confirm it.

Thesis IV. Once Christ’s death is posited as applicable to all humans under the condition of faith, it stands with divine goodness and justice to supply or deny the means of application—to nations or to particular persons—according to the good pleasure of his will, not according to the disparity of human wills.

source_text: Paucula praemittam, dein ad thesin confirmandam accedam. Primo igitur observandum est, in contraria sententia constitutos putare, Deum quasi fixo decreto ac statuta lege obligatum, ut bene utentibus talento naturae impertiat talentum gratiae. Secundo, praesumunt quemlibet hominem Paganum, etiam in umbra mortis sedentem, posse pro libertate voluntatis suae bene aut male uti hoc talento naturali. Tertio, ab hoc discrimine recte aut secus utentium donis naturalibus, causam reddere conantur, cur Deus quosdam dignetur Evangelio & cognitione Christi illustrare, alios non dignetur. Si quis recte donis illis utatur, hunc paulatim ducendum statuunt in salutiferam Christi cognitionem: Si vero improbe illis abutatur, tum dicunt illum merito privari cognitione Christi. Augustinus videtur in contraria sententia fuisse constitutus, libro de Nat. & Gratia, cap. 8. & 9. Ubi quibusdam infantibus media salutis applicari non potuisse concedit; ubi etiam agnoscit adultos in ea regione defunctos ubi non potuerunt Christi nomen audire, per naturam & liberum arbitrium justos fieri nullo modo potuisse. Nos etiam affirmamus, nullum decretum, nullam Dei legem aut promissionem exstare, juxta quam certo quis posset concludere, Hic homo recte aut minus male usus est lumine naturali, ergo Deus illuminabit eum gratia supernaturali. Dicit quidem Arminius, Deum hoc spopondisse isto Christi dicto, HABENTI DABITUR. Sed multo verius & doctius Reverendus Sarisburiensis, Fallaciam innuit, hic committit Arminius, qui habenti in statu naturae per saltum promittit donum in statu gratiae, & incredulorum diligentiae lucem fidei mercedem facit. Nam quod in re, & quo in genere usus, in eodem quoque incrementum promittitur. Alvarez homo Pontificius nobis hac in re suffragatur, Nulla lex fuit unquam statuta de dandis auxiliis gratiae, facientibus totum quod in se est ex facultate naturae; neque Christus Dominus morte sua meruit, aut mereri voluit talem legem. Apostolus Paulus dispensationem gratiae supernaturalis procedere docet, non secundum usum & opera voluntatis humanae, sed secundum propositum & consilium voluntatis Divinae: Operator omnia secundum propositum & consilium voluntatis suae, Ephes. i. 11.
english: A few preliminaries, then I turn to confirming the thesis. First, notice that those on the opposite side think God is bound by a fixed decree and statute to give the talent of grace to those who use the talent of nature well. Second, they presume that any pagan, even one sitting in the shadow of death, can by free choice use that natural talent well or badly. Third, from that difference between those who use natural gifts rightly and those who do not, they try to explain why God deigns to light some with the gospel and the knowledge of Christ and does not deign to light others. Use the gifts rightly, they say, and the person is gradually to be led into saving knowledge of Christ; abuse them wickedly, and he is justly stripped of that knowledge.

Augustine seems to stand on the opposite side in De Natura et Gratia, chapters 8 and 9. There he grants that for certain infants the means of salvation could not be applied; and he also owns that adults who died in a region where they could not hear Christ’s name could in no way become just by nature and free choice. We likewise affirm that no decree, law, or promise of God exists by which anyone could safely conclude: this person used natural light rightly, or less badly; therefore God will illuminate him with supernatural grace.

Arminius does say God pledged this by Christ’s word, “To the one who has, it will be given” (Matthew 13:12). But the Reverend of Salisbury speaks more truly and more learnedly: Arminius hints a fallacy here, and commits it—leaping from the one who has in the state of nature to a gift in the state of grace, and making the light of faith the wage of unbelievers’ diligence. For what is promised, and in what kind the use falls, is increase in that same kind. Alvarez, a Roman Catholic writer, votes with us here: no law was ever enacted that helps of grace must be given to those who do all that is in them from nature’s faculty; nor did the Lord Christ by his death merit, or will to merit, such a law. The Apostle Paul teaches that the dispensation of supernatural grace runs not according to the use and works of the human will, but according to the purpose and counsel of the divine will: “He works all things according to the purpose and counsel of his will” (Ephesians 1:11).

source_text: Secundo, licet in hominibus Ethnicis agnoscamus manere quasdam scintillas luminis naturalis, & imperfectum quoddam desiderium boni moralis, tamen, ut optime idem, quem antea laudavimus, Sarisburiensis, Quae deformata ista rudera habitatorem non habent nisi Diabolum, harum reliquiarum in media corruptione nisi corruptus usus esse non potest. Dent nobis adversarii vel unum hominem ab orbe condito, qui bono usu naturae pertraxit ad se donum gratiae. Impossibile est (moraliter loquendo) ut ethnicus in statu naturae corruptae non ponat obices quam plurimos gratiae divinae: tantum abest ut bene utendo naturalibus, possit ad se pertrahere gratuita & supernaturalia. Vere Aquinas Contr. Gent. lib. 3. pag. 160, Si per inordinationem praecedentem liberum arbitrium ad malum declinaverit, non erit omnino in potestate nullum impedimentum gratiae praestare. Qui igitur opinantur dari gratiam Evangelicam illis omnibus qui recte utuntur lumine naturae, & obicem gratiae haud opponunt, somniant tales homines in statu corruptae naturae, quales nec fuisse unquam, nec esse, nec fore credibile est. Nam quicquid objiciatur, nullus potest hunc obicem tollere nisi Deus; ut vere docet Bradwardinus de causa Dei, contr. Pelag. lib. 2. cap. 32.
english: Second, though we grant that in ethnic people some sparks of natural light remain, and a certain imperfect desire for moral good, still—as the same Salisbury we praised earlier puts it best—those deformed ruins have no inhabitant but the Devil, and of those remnants in the midst of corruption there can be only a corrupted use. Let the adversaries show us even one person since the world began who by good use of nature drew the gift of grace to himself. Speaking morally, it is impossible that an ethnic person in corrupted nature should not set very many obstacles in grace’s way. Far from it that by using natural things well he can haul gratuitous and supernatural gifts to himself.

Aquinas says truly in Contra Gentiles, book 3, page 160: if through a prior disorder free choice has declined to evil, it will not be altogether in its power to present no impediment to grace. So those who think evangelical grace is given to everyone who uses nature’s light rightly and does not oppose an obstacle to grace are dreaming up people in corrupted nature such as it is not credible ever existed, exist now, or ever will. Whatever is objected, no one can remove that obstacle but God—as Bradwardine truly teaches in De causa Dei against Pelagius, book 2, chapter 32.

source_text: Tertio & ultimo, asserimus, attestante sacra Scriptura & ipsa experientia, Evangelium aliaque salutis media non fuisse hominibus concessa aut negata, exinde quod quidam lumine naturali recte, aut saltem minus male usi fuerint, alii eodem lumine perverse & improbe abusi fuerint. Nam ex sacris Scripturis apparet lumen Evangelii affulsisse illis inopinantibus, qui lumine sive talento naturali pessime abutebantur. Tales fuerunt Romani, Corinthii, Ephesii, quibus per Apostolos fax Evangelii accensa est, quando in coeno superstitionum & libidinum volutabantur. Illud etiam non minus manifestum est, quamplurimis Evangelium nunquam fuisse revelatum qui minus improbe vixerunt. Quis nescit inter Philosophos Socratem, Platonem, Xenocratem, inter Romanos Fabricium, Scipionem, Catonem, lumine naturae prae caeteris hominibus bene usos fuisse: nemo tamen horum Evangelicae gratiae idcirco particeps evasit. Non ergo in meliore aut pejore usu luminis naturalis quaerenda est causa dati aut negati Evangelii & luminis supernaturalis, sed in Dei vocantis aut non vocantis beneplacito. Hisce praelibatis ad ipsam thesin veniamus; Quam primis confirmamus argumento ducto a morte Christi unde adversarii putant se posse contrarium inferre.
english: Third and last, we assert—with sacred Scripture and experience itself as witnesses—that the gospel and the other means of salvation were not granted or denied to people because some used natural light rightly, or at least less badly, while others abused the same light perversely and wickedly. Sacred Scripture shows that the light of the gospel shone on people who did not expect it, people who were abusing natural light or talent in the worst way. Such were the Romans, Corinthians, and Ephesians: through the apostles the torch of the gospel was lit for them while they were still wallowing in the filth of superstitions and lusts. No less plain is this: to very many who lived less wickedly the gospel was never revealed.

Who does not know that among the philosophers Socrates, Plato, and Xenocrates, and among the Romans Fabricius, Scipio, and Cato, used nature’s light well beyond other people? Yet none of them became a partaker of evangelical grace on that account. So the cause of the gospel and of supernatural light, given or denied, is not to be sought in better or worse use of natural light, but in the good pleasure of God who calls or does not call. With those points tasted first, we come to the thesis itself. We confirm it first by an argument drawn from the death of Christ—the very place from which the adversaries think they can infer the contrary.

source_text: Si Christi morte stabilitum sit pactum secundum quod cuivis credenti promittitur remissio peccatorum, nullum autem pactum stabilitum sit, secundum quod cuivis homini ethnico naturalibus donis recte, aut minus male utenti promittatur Evangelium, tum temerarium est, posita Christi morte, concludere Deum ex fidelitate, vel ex bonitate, vel ex justitia, vel quoquo pacto teneri propter meliorem usum naturae revelare hominibus mysterium gratiae Evangelicae. Sed certissimum est, tale pactum nusquam exstare: Ergo revelatio vel denegatio Evangelii ex beneplacito Dei dependet, abscondentis illud vel revelantis prout sibi placuerit, non ex diversis hominum actibus. Majorem inde confirmamus, quod Deus nemini tenetur, nemini quicquam debet, nisi ex promissione gratuita & voluntaria: Quis enim prior dedit illi, & retribuetur ei? Rom. xi. 35. In quam sententiam Augustinus, debitorem Dominus ipse se facit, non accipiendo, sed promittendo. In Psal. 83. Nihil spirituale promittit corruptae naturae operibus, quantumvis splendidis. Nullam sibi dixit legem, qua arceatur ne donet bona spiritualia hominibus, quantumvis improbis, & omni flagitiorum genere coopertis. Non ergo debemus a disparitate hominum vel operationum humanarum rationem reddere, cur Evangelium & cognitio Christi quibusdam impertiatur, quibusdam non, sed acquiescendum est in beneplacito voluntatis Divinae: juxta illud Apostoli, 2 Tim. i. 9. Vocavit nos vocatione sua, non secundum opera nostra, sed secundum propositum suum & gratiam quae data est nobis in Christo Jesu ante tempora secularia. Sed adhuc obtendi potest. Utcunque Deus neque ex debito, neque ex promisso aliquo morte Christi firmato teneatur revelare Christum bene utentibus lumine naturae, tamen cum ex gratia non promissa multa soleat dare hominibus, quid impedit quin dicamus illum servare hunc modum communem in distribuenda gratia Evangelica, ut concedat eam iis qui rectius utuntur lumine naturali, non concedat iis qui abutendo prae caeteris lumine naturae, indigniores se reddiderunt lumine gratiae? Impedit quo minus hoc admittamus perpetua Scripturae testificatio in contrarium, quae non ad hominem melius operantem, sed ad Deum magis amantem & miserentem unius quam alterius, refert salutiferae gratiae communicationem, Rom. ix. Impedit etiam ipsa experientia. Saepe enim fit, ut homo ab ineunte pueritia modestior, temperantior, & ex magna parte libidinum victor, eo loco vivat & moriatur ubi gratia Christiana ei praedicari nullo modo possit: Alter libidini deditus, facinoribus coopertus, ita a Deo gubernetur ut audiat, credat & salvetur. Dicimus itaque omnes mortales ex malo usu naturae sese indignos reddere Evangelio: Deum in communicando aut negando Evangelio non solere pensare gradus dignitatis & indignitatis humanae, atque hinc petere regulam communem gratiae indulgendae aut non indulgendae; sed aliquando negare eam illis qui minus male usi sunt reliquiis naturae, & interim concedere eam illis qui multo pejus iisdem abutuntur; aliquando e contra: unde apparet rationem discriminis cur Deus hunc dignetur gratia, illum non dignetur, ad beneplacitum ipsius Dei referri oportere, non ad dispares hominum operationes.
english: If by Christ’s death a covenant has been established under which remission of sins is promised to any believer, but no covenant has been established under which the gospel is promised to any ethnic person who uses natural gifts rightly, or less badly, then it is rash—Christ’s death being granted—to conclude that God is bound by faithfulness, goodness, justice, or any bond whatever, on account of better use of nature, to reveal to people the mystery of evangelical grace. Yet it is most certain that no such covenant exists anywhere. Therefore the revelation or denial of the gospel depends on God’s good pleasure, who hides it or reveals it as he pleases, not on the varied acts of human beings.

We confirm the major premise from this: God is bound to no one and owes nothing to anyone except by a free and voluntary promise—“For who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him?” (Romans 11:35). Into that sense Augustine speaks: the Lord makes himself a debtor not by receiving, but by promising (on Psalm 83). He promises nothing spiritual to the works of corrupted nature, however splendid. He has set himself no law that would bar him from giving spiritual goods to people, however wicked and covered with every kind of crime. So we must not explain from the disparity of persons or of human works why the gospel and the knowledge of Christ are given to some and not to others. We must rest in the good pleasure of the divine will, according to the Apostle: “He called us with his calling, not according to our works, but according to his purpose and the grace that was given to us in Christ Jesus before the ages began” (2 Timothy 1:9).

Still someone may press: even if God is bound neither by debt nor by any promise sealed by Christ’s death to reveal Christ to those who use nature’s light well, still—since from unpromised grace he often gives many things to people—what keeps us from saying he keeps this common pattern in distributing evangelical grace: grant it to those who use natural light more rightly, and withhold it from those who, by abusing nature’s light worse than others, have made themselves more unworthy of the light of grace? Scripture’s steady witness against that blocks us. It refers the gift of saving grace not to the person who works better, but to God loving and pitying one more than another (Romans 9). Experience blocks it too.
