Often a person more modest and temperate from early childhood, and for the most part master of lusts, lives and dies where Christian grace cannot be preached to him at all; while another given to lust and covered with crimes is so governed by God that he hears, believes, and is saved.

So we say every mortal by bad use of nature makes himself unworthy of the gospel; and that God, in giving or denying the gospel, does not weigh degrees of human dignity and unworthiness and from them draw a common rule for indulging grace or withholding it. Sometimes he denies it to those who have used nature’s remnants less badly, and meanwhile grants it to those who abuse the same remnants far worse; sometimes the reverse. So the reason why God deigns to give grace to this one and not to that one must be referred to God’s own good pleasure, not to unequal human works.

source_text: Secundo, probamus, non esse contrarium bonitati Divinae, etiam posita Christi morte, media tamen applicationis quibuscunque hominibus pro suo beneplacito haud impertire: Quia ipsa mors Christi est Beneficium ab ipso Deo gratis impensum humano generi: At aequum & congruum est, ut penes benefactorem sit libera sui beneficii applicatio; qui ex datione unius beneficii nunquam tenetur ad dationem alterius, nisi talis promissio intervenerit: quam promissionem, de concedendis mediis quibus mors Christi applicetur, neque omnes homines promiscue, nec quisquam singularis homo singulariter sibi factam potest recte asserere. Porro, bonitati Divinae disconvenit, non quodvis beneficium cuivis non elargiri, sed nocumentum cuiquam inferre, aut debitum aliquod bonum injuste cuiquam denegare aut subtrahere. Illuminatio autem per gratiam Evangelicam, supposita Christi morte, non est tamen debita naturae jam peccato corruptae. Sic Bannezius, In 1a. qu. 23. art. 3. pag. 279. Non est eadem ratio de illuminatione naturali & supernaturali, quia naturalis debita est ipsi naturae: illuminatio autem gratiae non est debita naturae, praesertim jam peccato corruptae, sed ex gratia confertur. Si ex gratia confertur, tum non omnibus debetur; Nam inter duodecim sententias quae ad fidem Catholicam pertinent, hanc secundam posuit Augustinus, Epist. 107. Gratiam Dei non dari omnibus hominibus. Si ex gratia confertur, tum non datur aut negatur pro bono aut malo usu luminis naturalis: nam ut recte Prosper, Resp. 8. ad Capit. Gallor. Impietas est affirmare ipsam gratiam qua salvamur aut bonis meritis rependi, aut malis arceri. Et, De vocat. Gent. Nulla sunt tam detestanda facinora quae possunt gratiae arcere donum. Qui igitur volentes humanis conjecturis justitiam & bonitatem Dei defendere, contendunt illum suppeditare gratuita salutis media illis omnibus qui recte aut minus male utuntur donis naturalibus, negare autem aliis qui iisdem donis fuerunt abusi (ut cum Augustino loquar) ignorantes altitudinem gratiae, fabulas improbabiles texuerunt. Velimus igitur nolimus, si causa quaeratur cur hisce singularibus hominibus concedantur illa media quibus Christum sibi applicant ad salutem, aliis non concedantur, disparitas hominum aut humanarum operationum praetermittenda est, & ad liberrimum Dei beneplacitum adscendendum; Cum causa eadem simul implicet omnes, Nec discernantur merito, qui munere distant, Ut eleganter Prosper, Carmine De Ingratis, cap. 25.
english: Second, we prove that it is not contrary to divine goodness—even once Christ’s death is granted—still to withhold the means of application from any people he pleases. Christ’s death itself is a benefit God freely spent on the human race. It is fair and fitting that free application of that benefit remain with the benefactor. From giving one gift he is never bound to give another unless a promise intervenes; and no one can rightly claim such a promise about the means by which Christ’s death is applied—neither the whole race in a lump, nor any single person for himself alone.

What jars with divine goodness is not that God does not lavish every benefit on every person, but that he would injure anyone, or unjustly deny or withdraw a good that is owed. Illumination by evangelical grace, even with Christ’s death supposed, is still not owed to nature already corrupted by sin. So Bannezius (on the First Part, question 23, article 3, page 279): natural and supernatural illumination do not stand on the same footing, for natural light is owed to nature itself, while the light of grace is not owed to nature—least of all to nature already spoiled by sin—but is conferred by grace. If it is conferred by grace, it is not owed to all. Among twelve sentences that belong to the Catholic faith, Augustine set this second one in Epistle 107: that the grace of God is not given to all people. If it is conferred by grace, it is not given or denied according to good or bad use of natural light. Prosper is right (Response 8 to the Chapters of the Gauls): it is impiety to say that the grace by which we are saved is either repaid to good merits or fenced off by evils. And in On the Calling of the Gentiles: there are no crimes so detestable that they can fence off the gift of grace.

Those who try to defend God’s justice and goodness by human guesswork, and contend that he supplies free means of salvation to everyone who uses natural gifts rightly or less badly, but denies them to those who have abused the same gifts, are—speaking with Augustine—ignorant of the height of grace, and have woven improbable fables. Like it or not, if we ask why those means by which people apply Christ to themselves for salvation are granted to these particular persons and not to others, we must set aside the disparity of persons or of human works and rise to God’s freest good pleasure: “When the same cause binds all at once, / nor are they discerned by merit who differ by gift,” as Prosper puts it elegantly in the Poem On the Ungrateful, chapter 25.

source_text: A facto ad jus sic argumentamur. Deus nihil facere praetermittit, quod non facere vel a bonitate, vel a justitia, vel a prudentia Divina est alienum. Nefas est hac de re dubitare, cum impossibile sit eum qui est ipsa Bonitas, Justitia & Sapientia, in agendo vel non agendo a regula bonitatis, justitiae aut sapientiae unquam discedere. Attexo igitur Minorem, & affirmo, Posita Christi morte, Deum tamen negasse olim, & nunc negare multis nationibus, multis singularibus hominibus media illa, sine quibus mors Christi nemini applicatur. Hoc luculenter patebit, sive consideremus media salutis immediata, quibus scilicet homo collocatur in statu vitae spiritualis & salutis, atque in actuali participatione mortis & meritorum Christi, qualia sunt Paenitentia, Fides, Regeneratio, Sanctificatio; sive perpendamus media externa, quibus tanquam instrumentis Deus utitur ad illa priora producenda, qualia sunt Missio Doctorum & pastorum, Praedicatio Evangelii, caeteraque omnia opitulamenta absque quibus illa interiora & immediata salutis media ordinarie effici non possunt. Quod attinet ad priora, ipsa fides & salutifera agnitio Christi est speciale donum datum his, negatum illis, pro beneplacito Divinae voluntatis: Vobis datum est nosse mysteria regni caelorum; illis non est datum, Matth. xiii. 11. Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi fuerit ei datum a Patre meo, Joh. vi. 65. Gratia salvati estis per fidem: & hoc non ex vobis: Dei donum est, Ephes. ii. 8. Fides non est omnium, 2 Thess. iii. 2. Par ratio est paenitentiae, regenerationis, sanctificationis, quae omnia speciali misericordia procurante dantur quibusdam, eadem misericordia opes suas minime explicante aliis denegantur. Converte nos, Domine, ad te, & convertemur, Thren. v. 21. Misereatur cujus vult, quem vult indurat, Rom. ix. 18. Non ex sanguinibus, neque ex voluntate viri, sed ex Deo nati sunt, Joh. i. 13. Benedictus Deus qui secundum suam misericordiam regeneravit nos, 1 Pet. i. 3. Mitto caetera. Ex hisce constat, Deum media illa, in quibus conjunctio cum Christo & salus immediate constituta est, dare aut negare hominibus pro beneplacito voluntatis suae, non pro discrimine voluntatis humanae. Hoc omnes Patres orthodoxi contra Pelagianos fortiter defendunt. Ambrosius in Luc. vii. 9. Deus quem dignatur vocat, & quem vult religiosum facit. Augustinus, Epist. 107. Scimus gratiam non omnibus hominibus dari, sed nec secundum merita voluntatis eorum quibus datur. In eadem epistola porro docet, Eos quibus haec gratia non datur, nullo plerunque merito, nulla voluntate distare, sed similem cum eis quibus datur habere causam, &c. Fulgentius, lib. De Incarn. & grat. cap. 19. Sicut in nativitate carnali omnem nascentis hominis voluntatem praecedit operis Divini formatio, sic in spirituali nativitate, qua veterem hominem deponere incipimus, nemo potest habere bonam voluntatem motu proprio. Et cap. 21, Si Deus per suam gratiam homini non dederit, nunquam potest homo in Deum velle credere, quia hanc ipsam voluntatem gratia non invenit, sed operatur in homine. Clarum est igitur, Deum non dare haec interna media promiscue omnibus hominibus, quibus Christi mortem sibi possunt applicare. Neque hic obtendere possunt adversarii, hanc fidei dationem, & non-dationem Divinam ex resistentia, aut non-resistentia humanarum voluntatum originem ducere, cum Scripturae expresse hoc revocent ad beneplacitum Dei misereri volentis aut nolentis, ac Patres expressis verbis excludant disparitatem humanarum voluntatum ante receptam gratiam.
english: From fact to right we argue this way. God leaves undone nothing that it would be alien to divine goodness, justice, or prudence not to do. It is wrong to doubt that, for he who is Goodness, Justice, and Wisdom themselves cannot, in acting or not acting, ever leave the rule of goodness, justice, or wisdom. So I attach the minor and affirm: even with Christ’s death granted, God has denied in the past, and still denies, to many nations and many particular people those means without which Christ’s death is applied to no one.

That will be plain if we look either at the immediate means of salvation—repentance, faith, regeneration, sanctification—by which a person is set in spiritual life and salvation and in actual share of Christ’s death and merits, or at the external means God uses as instruments to produce those first ones: the sending of teachers and pastors, the preaching of the gospel, and every other help without which those inward, immediate means cannot ordinarily be wrought.

As for the first set, faith itself and saving knowledge of Christ is a special gift given to some and denied to others, according to the good pleasure of the divine will: “To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven; to them it has not been given” (Matthew 13:11). “No one can come to me unless it has been given him by my Father” (John 6:65). “By grace you have been saved through faith—and this not of yourselves; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8). “Faith is not of all” (2 Thessalonians 3:2). The same holds for repentance, regeneration, and sanctification: a special mercy that procures them gives them to some, and the same mercy, not unfolding its riches, denies them to others. “Turn us, O Lord, to yourself, and we shall be turned” (Lamentations 5:21). “He has mercy on whom he wills; whom he wills he hardens” (Romans 9:18). “Not of bloods, nor of the will of man, but of God they were born” (John 1:13). “Blessed be God who according to his mercy has regenerated us” (1 Peter 1:3). I pass over the rest. From these it is clear that God gives or denies those means in which union with Christ and salvation are immediately set according to the good pleasure of his will, not according to a difference in the human will.

All the orthodox Fathers press this hard against the Pelagians. Ambrose on Luke 7:9: God calls whom he deigns, and makes devout whom he wills. Augustine, Epistle 107: We know grace is not given to all people, nor according to the merits of the will of those who receive it. In the same letter he adds that those denied this grace often differ by no merit and no will, but share a like condition with those who receive it. Fulgentius, On the Incarnation and Grace, chapter 19: As in fleshly birth the formation of the divine work precedes every will of the one being born, so in spiritual birth, by which we begin to put off the old self, no one can have a good will by his own motion. And chapter 21: If God has not given to a person through his grace, that person can never will to believe in God, because grace does not find this will already there—it works it in the person. So God does not hand out these inward means promiscuously to everyone who might apply Christ’s death to himself. Nor may our opponents claim that God’s giving or withholding of faith springs from human wills resisting or not resisting, since Scripture expressly refers this to God’s good pleasure to pity or not to pity, and the Fathers in plain words shut out any disparity of human wills before grace is received.

source_text: Hactenus de mediis immediatis disputatum est: Ad media horum mediorum descendamus. Christi mors ac meritum habuit in acceptatione Dei ab origine mundi suam efficaciam: Deus tamen sub Vetere Testamento externa applicationis media non omnibus hominibus universim concessit, sed, ut loquitur Psalmista, Verbum suum denunciat Jacobo: non fecit taliter omni nationi, Psal. cxlvii. 19, 20. Et in eandem sententiam Paulus, Act. xiv. 16. Deus praeteritis aetatibus sivit omnes gentes ambulare in viis suis. Prosper hoc idem annotavit, Non est, inquit, remotum ab inspectione communi, quot secula, quam innumera hominum millia erroribus suis impietatibusque dimissa, sine ulla veri Dei cognitione defecerint, De lib. arbitr. pag. 225. Et De vocat. Gent. 2, 17, Novi Testamenti tempora respiciens, dicit, Sunt etiam nunc in extremis mundi partibus aliquae nationes, quibus gratia Salvatoris nondum illuxit. Ex quibus sequitur, etiam posita Christi morte, Deum nihilominus haud teneri ratione bonitatis aut justitiae suae media omnibus & singulis providere & offerre, quibus possunt Christum sibi applicare. In Deo enim a facto ad jus optime sequitur argumentum tam affirmando quam negando; Deus hoc facit, ergo juste facit; Deus hoc non facit, ergo nullo jure tenetur ut faciat.
english: So far we have argued about the immediate means. Now we come down to the means of those means. Christ’s death and merit have had their force in God’s acceptance from the world’s beginning. Yet under the Old Testament God did not grant the external means of application to every human being alike. As the Psalmist says, “He declares his word to Jacob; he has not done thus to every nation” (Psalm 147:19–20). Paul speaks the same way: “In past ages God allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways” (Acts 14:16).

Prosper marked the same point: it is not far from ordinary observation, he says, through how many ages countless thousands of people, left to their errors and impieties, have perished without any knowledge of the true God (On Free Choice, page 225). Looking to New Testament times (On the Calling of the Gentiles 2.17), he adds: even now in the farthest parts of the world there are nations on whom the Savior’s grace has not yet shone. From this it follows that even with Christ’s death granted, God is still not bound by his goodness or justice to provide and offer to every person the means by which they can apply Christ to themselves. In God the move from fact to right works both ways: God does this, therefore he does it justly; God does not do this, therefore no right binds him to do it.

source_text: Sed huic argumento occurrunt nonnulli respondendo, Quod Evangelium ubique non praedicetur, causa non tam haec est, quod a Deo non mittantur qui praedicent, quam quod qui mittuntur ire recusent. Sic Corvinus, contra Tilenum, pag. 105. Verum si Deus ratione bonitatis suae & justitiae, quasi ex congruitate quadam, Christi morte supposita, teneretur media applicationis sufficientia omnibus communicare, non sineret quenquam ob incuriam alterius debito beneficio fraudari, praesertim tali, absque quo nulla salus est sperabilis. Imo contradictionem implicat, Deum ex lege ordinaria providere & administrare omnibus haec media ad Christi applicationem spectantia, & quibusdam eadem non administrare, obstante scilicet praedicatorum incuria: Cum ipsa cura praedicatorum non esset annumeranda hisce mediis, sine quibus cognitio & applicatio Christi praedicati haberi nequit. Porro, Si Dei bonitas aut justitia hoc requireret, ut haec media Christi applicandi omnibus administrarentur, proculdubio in aliquibus saltem praedicatoribus hunc animum & hanc curam praedicandi & proferendi Evangelii ad singulas nationes accendisset. Ipse enim est qui operarios pro beneplacito suo novit in messem protrudere. Denique quae incuria praedicatorum in causa fuit, quod ducentis ab hinc annis Evangelium Americanis a nemine fuit praedicatum, quando de hisce nationibus nemo per somnium cogitaverat? Redeundum itaque est ad causam altiorem, nempe liberum Dei beneplacitum in hisce mediis gratificandis, aut negandis, qui per specialem quandam providentiam ea procurat administranda populis, vel non administranda per ministros suos, ut videre licet Actor. xvi. 6 &c. Vetiti sunt loqui verbum Dei in Asia, & tendebant ire in Bithyniam, & non permisit Spiritus, &c. Secundo respondent, eos qui longo tempore gratia Evangelica caruerunt, eam a majoribus suis repudiavisse: & sic posteros merito privari praeconio Evangelii, quod majores illorum contempserunt: Non itaque ad absolutam Dei voluntatem referendum esse, quod quidam salutari luce Evangelii non illustrentur. Sed neque haec bene cohaerent cum istorum placitis. Nam si Deus, ad mortem Christi habito respectu, omnibus hominibus tenetur media salutis sufficienter administrare, parum aequum videtur ut, propter praedicationem verbi temporibus Noachi a majoribus contemptam, Evangelium post multa annorum millia eorundem posteris denegatur. Si enim, non obstante Adami peccato, Christi morte impetratum sit (ex istorum sententia) ut media salutis sufficientia omnibus administrentur, a ratione & aequitate alienum est, hanc legem quasi ordinariam infringere, praetextu peccatorum ab aliis quibuscunque majoribus nostris commissorum. Sicut igitur propter ipsum Adami peccatum Deus juste possit posteris ejus quodvis beneficium spirituale denegare, ita fatemur, ex peccatis aliorum majorum posse quoque Deum occasionem sumere negandi nobis quodvis beneficium gratuitum. Verum si Christi morte, Dei bonitate concurrente, lex stabilita sit de administrandis gratiae mediis; jam sicut propter Adami peccatum, qui gessit in se personam omnium suorum posterorum, Deus non vult hoc suum quasi statutum abrogare, ita propter peccata aliorum, qui minime sustinent hanc communem humani generis personam, multo minus consentaneum est ut posteri hoc beneficio priventur. Frustra igitur ad peccata majorum confugiunt, ut ejus rei negatae rationem reddant, quam virtute mortis Christi ac bonitatis Divinae omnibus & singulis, ex decreto Divino praeparatam atque statuta lege quasi debitam, praefitentur.
english: Some meet this argument by saying the gospel is not preached everywhere less because God fails to send preachers than because those who are sent refuse to go. So Corvinus against Tilenus, page 105. But if God, by his goodness and justice, as if by a kind of congruence, and with Christ’s death supposed, were bound to communicate sufficient means of application to everyone, he would not let anyone be cheated of an owed benefit by another’s carelessness—least of all a benefit without which no salvation can be hoped for. It is even a contradiction to say that by ordinary law God provides and administers to all these means that look to applying Christ, and yet withholds them from some because of the preachers’ neglect—when the very care of the preachers would have to be counted among those means, without which knowledge and application of the Christ who is preached cannot be had.

Further, if God’s goodness or justice required that these means of applying Christ be administered to all, he would without doubt have kindled in at least some preachers the will and care to preach and carry the gospel to every nation. He himself knows how to thrust laborers into the harvest according to his good pleasure. Finally, what preacher-neglect explains that two hundred years ago the gospel was preached by no one among the Americans, when no one had even dreamed those nations existed? We must therefore rise to a higher cause: God’s free good pleasure in granting or denying these means. By a special providence he sees to it that they are administered to peoples, or not administered, through his ministers—as Acts 16:6 and following shows: “They were forbidden to speak the word of God in Asia, and they were intending to go into Bithynia, and the Spirit did not permit them,” and so on.

Second, they answer that those long without evangelical grace had already repudiated it in their ancestors, and so the descendants are rightly stripped of the gospel proclamation their ancestors despised; therefore the fact that some are not lit by the gospel’s saving light should not be referred to God’s absolute will. But this does not hang with their own views. If God, with an eye to Christ’s death, is bound to administer sufficient means of salvation to all people, it is hardly fair that, because ancestors despised the preached word in Noah’s day, the gospel should be denied to their posterity after many thousands of years. If—Adam’s sin notwithstanding—Christ’s death has (on their showing) secured that sufficient means of salvation be administered to all, it is alien to reason and equity to break that quasi-ordinary law on the pretext of sins committed by any other ancestors of ours.

Just as God could justly deny any spiritual benefit to Adam’s posterity because of Adam’s own sin, so we grant that from other ancestors’ sins God may also take occasion to deny us any free benefit. But if by Christ’s death, with God’s goodness concurring, a law has been set about administering the means of grace, then just as God will not abrogate that quasi-statute because of Adam’s sin—who bore in himself the person of all his posterity—so it is far less fitting that posterity be robbed of this benefit because of the sins of others who do not sustain that common person of the human race. They flee in vain to ancestral sins to explain the denial of a thing which, by the virtue of Christ’s death and of divine goodness, they themselves claim was prepared for all and each by divine decree and as if owed by fixed law.

source_text: Tertio respondent, Evangelicam gratiam quibusdam denegari, quia continuis contra legem praevaricationibus indignos sese praestiterunt quibus gratia Divina offeratur. Sed haec responsio sententiae nostrae veritatem magis illustrabit. Nam illud imprimis sumo (quod nemo sanus negabit) quemlibet hominem in statu corruptae naturae Evangelica gratia indignum (si ejus peccata attendantur) sese praestitisse: tum & illud addo, Dignitatem & indignitatem hominum, sive majorem & minorem indignitatem, non esse illam regulam secundum quam Deus procedit in dispensando vel denegando Evangelio sive singularibus personis sive nationibus. Quibus positis, sequetur indignitatem semper reperiri in iis quibus Evangelium negatum, sed in iis etiam quibus conceditur. Habebit ergo haec indignitas naturam circumstantiae, quae semper concomitatur personas quibus datur & quibus non datur Evangelium; sed non habebit rationem causae discriminantis, cur hisce detur, illis non detur Evangelium. Hac igitur in re ad solum placitum Divinae voluntatis est deveniendum, qui facientibus & non-facientibus quod in se est, quando sibi placet auxilia confert, ut loquitur Alvarez, De Auxil. disp. 58. Sed quia haec responsio, quae indignitate hominum gratiam Evangelicam arceri docet, videtur tacite innuere, quosdam dignitate eorundem eandem procurari potuisse, audiamus quid orthodoxi Patres contra Pelagianos in hoc ipso negotio docuerint. Augustinus Epist. 107. pag. 500. ostendit salvificam Christi gratiam non concedi aut negari hominibus secundum hanc regulam majoris aut minoris indignitatis. Brevitatis causa verba non appono. Prosper saepissime hoc inculcat: De vocat. Gent. l. 1. c. 15. Liberatur pars hominum, parte pereunte: & si hoc voluntatum meritis voluerimus adscribere, ut malos neglexisse gratia, bonos autem elegisse videatur, resistet nobis innumerabilium causa populorum, quibus per tot secula nulla caelestis doctrinae annunciatio coruscavit. Nec meliores fuisse illorum posteros possumus dicere, quibus lux orta est, &c. Idem Prosper in Carmine De Ingratis, cap. 12, ostendit hanc fuisse Pelagianorum ipsissimam sententiam, nempe, Quod Deus pro bonitate sua omnes ad gratiam vocare velit, sed quod voluntas nonnullorum, Lumine primo Per vitia oppressa, sit facta indigna secundo, At ille e contra, cap. 14. exempla proferri posse contendit Quae doceant virtute Dei conversa malorum Corda, quibus rei nihil unquam insiderat, & quae Nullum justitiae signum sensumve gerebant. Summa hujus argumenti huc redit, Gratiam Evangelicam non dari hominibus quia digni eadem judicantur, cum nemo dignus tanto munere reperitur; neque negari hominibus quia indigniores caeteris exstiterunt, cum pessimis hoc lumen concessum fuerit, & aliis interim minus depravatis denegatum. Acquiescendum igitur in arcano voluntatis Divinae beneplacito, qui, ut magis splendeat sua misericordia, non regulariter lumen Evangelii concedit bene aut minus male utentibus lumine naturae; sed e contra infideles & negligentes vocat ad seipsum, atque peccatores indignos & ingratos. Atque hinc patet, semper liberum Deo manere, & a bonitate ejus nullo modo alienum esse, dare vel non dare quibusvis hominibus Evangelium aliaque media ad applicationem meritorum Christi necessaria, pro beneplacito voluntatis suae, nulla habita ratione dignitatis aut indignitatis, vel majoris & minoris indignitatis humanae.
english: Third, they answer that evangelical grace is denied to some because by continual law-breaking they have made themselves unworthy of those to whom divine grace should be offered. This reply will only make our position clearer. First I take what no sober mind will deny: every person in corrupted nature has made himself unworthy of evangelical grace, if you attend to his sins. Then I add that human dignity and unworthiness—or greater and lesser unworthiness—is not the rule by which God proceeds in dispensing or denying the gospel to particular persons or to nations. That being so, unworthiness is always found in those denied the gospel, and also in those who receive it. So this unworthiness has the nature of a circumstance that always accompanies both those who get the gospel and those who do not; it does not have the force of a discriminating cause why it is given to these and not to those. In this matter we must come down to the sole pleasure of the divine will, who, when it pleases him, confers helps both on those who do and on those who do not do what is in them—as Alvarez says in On Helps, disputation 58.

But because this reply, which teaches that human unworthiness fences off evangelical grace, seems quietly to hint that some could have procured the same by their dignity, hear what the orthodox Fathers taught the Pelagians on this very point. Augustine, Epistle 107, page 500, shows that Christ’s saving grace is not granted or denied by the rule of greater or lesser unworthiness. For brevity I omit the words. Prosper presses this again and again (On the Calling of the Gentiles, book 1, chapter 15): a part of humankind is set free while a part perishes; and if we ascribe that to the merits of wills, so that grace seems to have neglected the bad and chosen the good, the case of innumerable peoples will rise against us, to whom through so many ages no announcement of heavenly teaching has flashed. Nor can we say that those later ones on whom the light has risen were better, and so on. In the Poem On the Ungrateful, chapter 12, the same Prosper shows that the Pelagians’ own opinion was this: God by his goodness wills to call all to grace, but the will of some, oppressed by vices under the first light, has been made unworthy of the second. Against them, in chapter 14, he contends that examples can be brought of wicked hearts converted by God’s power, hearts in which nothing of the matter had ever settled, and which bore no sign or sense of justice.

The sum of the argument comes to this: evangelical grace is not given because people are judged worthy of it—no one worthy of so great a gift is found—nor is it denied because some have stood more unworthy than the rest, since this light has been granted to the worst and meanwhile denied to others less depraved. We must therefore rest in the secret good pleasure of the divine will, who, that his mercy may shine the more, does not regularly grant the gospel’s light to those who use nature’s light well or less badly, but on the contrary calls the faithless and negligent to himself, and unworthy, ungrateful sinners. From this it is plain that it always remains free for God, and in no way alien to his goodness, to give or not to give to any people whatever the gospel and the other means needed for applying Christ’s merits, according to the good pleasure of his will, with no account taken of dignity or unworthiness, or of greater and lesser human unworthiness.

source_text: Hoc idem probari potest ex incommodis manifestis quibus urgetur sententia contraria. Nam si hoc morte Christi sit universaliter impetratum, ut Deus ex ipso decreto, sive lege quadam congruitatis teneatur, quantum in se est, omnibus & singulis hominibus gratiam Evangelicae praedicationis atque internae sanctificationis concedere, tum sequetur, rationem primariam cur hic de facto fiat particeps utriusque gratiae, ille non fiat, in eo sitam, quod hic obice opposito hanc gratiam repulerit, aut ne offeretur omnino impedierit, ille nec repulerit nec impedierit. Hanc consequentiam non refugiunt adversarii. Nam vocationis Evangelicae & gratiae salutiferae negatae aut concessae discrimen non in meram Dei voluntatem reducunt, sed in conditiones sive dispositiones diversas ex parte hominum consideratas. Sic Corvinus, Contra Tilen. pag. 489. Deus licet ubique verbum crucis non praedicet, omnibus tamen iis illud praedicare paratus est, qui ministerio legis sese debite subjiciunt, hoc est, qui sequuntur lucem legis naturalis etiam in Ethnicorum cordibus vigentis. De donis naturalibus differens, pag. 118. dicit, Deum haec dona gentilibus reliquisse, ut siquidem secundum Dei intentionem istis donis uterentur, ad Deum pro mensura suae cognitionis glorificandum, ad Christum ipsiusque cognitionem ducerentur: contra vero, in sua ignorantia relinquerentur, si veritatem quam habebant in injustitia detinerent. Hic aperte suspendit vocationem Evangelicam ex usu aut abusu donorum naturalium.
english: The same point can be proved from the plain inconveniences that press the contrary view. If by Christ's death it has been universally obtained that God is bound—by the decree itself, or by some law of congruity—to grant, as far as in him lies, to every human being the grace of gospel preaching and of inward sanctification, then the chief reason why one person in fact shares both graces and another does not will lie here: that one has thrust up an obstacle and pushed the grace away, or has blocked it from being offered at all, while the other has neither pushed it away nor blocked it. Our opponents do not shrink from that consequence. They do not reduce the difference between evangelical calling and saving grace denied or granted to God's bare will, but to different conditions or dispositions on the human side. So Corvinus against Tilenus, page 489: though God does not preach the word of the cross everywhere, he is still ready to preach it to all who duly submit themselves to the ministry of the law—that is, who follow the light of the natural law alive even in Gentile hearts. Writing on natural gifts, page 118, he says God left those gifts to the nations so that if they used them according to God's intention, they would be led to glorify God in the measure of their knowledge, and on to Christ and the knowledge of him; but if they held down in injustice the truth they had, they would be left in their ignorance. Here he openly hangs the gospel call on the use or abuse of natural gifts.

source_text: Idem Corvinus internam gratiam vivificantem ita ex ordinaria lege omnibus expositam tuetur, ut ipsum discrimen cur hic de facto particeps talis gratiae evadat, ille non evadat, ad discrimen humanarum voluntatum reducat, non ad beneplacitum Divinum. Imo Certum esse, ait, nullius conversionem praecise a Deo intendi. Verum utcunque haec adblandiantur rationi humanae, tamen contrariantur Scripturae Divinae, & incommodis manifestis obrui possunt. Nam si admittamus vel exteriorem vocationem Evangelicam, vel interiorem & efficacem infusionem gratiae regenerantis, dari & negari pro diversis hominum dispositionibus aut operationibus; Primo sequeretur, liberum arbitrium in statu corrupto, Evangelica luce nondum collustratum, posse adeo bene uti donis suis naturalibus, ut Deus inde secundum legem ordinariam, a bonitate sua sibi dictam, teneatur homini animali spiritualem gratiam impertire. At hoc est contra Apostolum dicentem, Si ex operibus, gratia non est gratia, Rom. xi. 6. Non enim miseratione tribuentis, sed aequitate retribuentis eam acciperemus, ut loquitur Fulgentius De Incarn. & grat. Christi, cap. 18.
english: The same Corvinus so defends inward life-giving grace as laid open to all by an ordinary law that he reduces the very difference why one person in fact shares that grace and another does not to a difference of human wills, not to the divine good pleasure. Indeed he says it is certain that no one's conversion is precisely intended by God. But however much this flatters human reason, it still runs against divine Scripture and can be crushed by plain inconveniences. If we grant that either the outward gospel call, or the inward and effectual infusion of regenerating grace, is given and denied according to different human dispositions or operations, then first it would follow that free choice in the corrupted state, not yet lit by gospel light, can so well use its natural gifts that God is bound—by the ordinary law his own goodness dictates to him—to give spiritual grace to the natural man. That is against the Apostle: if it is from works, grace is no longer grace (Romans 11:6). We would receive it not by the pity of the giver, but by the equity of a repayor, as Fulgentius says in On the Incarnation and Grace of Christ, chapter 18.

source_text: Secundo (quod omnes orthodoxi aversantur) sequeretur etiam praedestinationis & praeteritionis rationem ex hominum diversis qualitatibus, aut actibus esse assignandam. Ratio siquidem praedestinationis, quae est gratiae praeparatio, non potest diversa esse a ratione gratiae, quae est ipsa collatio. Qui igitur gratiae datae aut non datae rationem ab humanis dispositionibus aut operationibus petendam docet, idem praedestinationis & praeteritionis rationem inde petat est necesse. Tertio, sequeretur Deum legi a se positae contravenire, quando ponentibus obicem gratiae hanc gratiam quasi ingerit; quod Paulo factum ipse Apostolus humillime confitetur: quem in flagranti peccato deprehensum, & contra Christum ruentem, ad cognitionem & gratiam Christi Deus misericorditer vocavit. De quo praeclare Fulgentius, De Incarn. & Grat. cap. 18. In quo Dei misericordia nos praeveniat, vel praeveniens quales inveniat, non in quolibet alio, sed in se ipso nobis gentium Magister ostendit, dicens, Qui prius fui blasphemus, &c. Innuit scilicet Pater, omnes mortales esse refractarios, donec gratia praeveniens eos subjugaverit.
english: Second—and every orthodox writer shrinks from this—it would also follow that the reason of predestination and of preterition must be assigned from people's different qualities or acts. For the reason of predestination, which is the preparation of grace, cannot differ from the reason of grace, which is the gift itself. So anyone who teaches that the reason grace is given or withheld must be sought in human dispositions or operations must of necessity seek the reason of predestination and preterition there too. Third, it would follow that God breaks the law he himself set when he as good as forces this grace on those who have put an obstacle in its way—which the Apostle himself most humbly confesses happened to Paul: caught in open sin and rushing against Christ, God mercifully called him to the knowledge and grace of Christ. Fulgentius puts it finely in On the Incarnation and Grace, chapter 18: how God's mercy goes before us, and what sort it finds when it does, the Teacher of the nations shows not in someone else but in himself, saying, I who was formerly a blasphemer, and so on (1 Timothy 1:13). The Father hints that every mortal is refractory until preventing grace has brought him under.

source_text: Quarto, admitte hanc gratiae donationem aut negationem, prout humanae voluntates obicem posuerint aut non posuerint, everteris fere omnia in Conciliis contra Pelagianos definita; quale est illud inprimis in Diospolitano Concilio sancitum contra Pelagium, Fateatur gratiam non dari ex merito, ut vera sit gratia, id est gratis data, per ejus misericordiam qui dixit, MISEREBOR CUIUS MISERTUS FUERO. Dari enim aut non dari gratiam prout quis recte naturalibus donis usus fuerit aut non fuerit, vel (ut alii loquuntur) prout quis fecerit aut non fecerit quod in se est, apud Patres idem est quod dari ex meritis, & negari ex demeritis. Porro, nec stabit illud Patrum Africanorum in Epistola sua synodica. Ipsa gratia nullatenus agnoscitur, nisi detur: quae quamdiu non est in homine, tamdiu necesse est ut ei sermone repugnet aut opere. Quomodo intelligi potest, Ethnicis in statu corruptae naturae constitutis, ea quasi lege gratiam Evangelicam donandam, si gratiae obicem non posuerint, cum tamdiu necesse sit (necessitate nimirum pravae & habitualis dispositionis) ut gratiae resistant, quamdiu eadem careant? Denique, corruent illa Arausicani Concilii decreta, canone 4. Si quis, ut a peccato purgemur, voluntatem nostram Deum expectare contendit, non autem, ut etiam purgari velimus, per sancti Spiritus operationem & infusionem in nobis fieri confitetur, resistit Apostolo. Et Can. 6. Si quis humilitati & obedientiae humanae subjungit gratiae adjutorium, &c. resistit Apostolo. Mitto caetera.
english: Fourth, grant that grace is given or denied according as human wills have or have not set an obstacle, and you overturn nearly everything the Councils defined against the Pelagians. First among them is what the Council of Diospolis sanctioned against Pelagius: let him confess that grace is not given from merit, so that it may be true grace—that is, freely given—through the mercy of him who said, I will have mercy on whom I have mercy (Exodus 33:19; Romans 9:15). For to give or withhold grace according as someone has used natural gifts rightly or not, or (as others put it) according as someone has or has not done what lies in him, is for the Fathers the same as giving from merits and denying from demerits. Nor will that word of the African Fathers in their synodical letter stand: grace itself is not recognized at all unless it is given; and as long as it is not in a person, he must of necessity resist it in word or deed. How can it make sense that Gentiles in corrupted nature are to receive evangelical grace by that quasi-law if they have not set an obstacle to grace, when by the necessity of a depraved and habitual disposition they must resist grace the whole time they lack it? Finally those decrees of the Council of Orange fall—canon 4: if anyone contends that God waits for our will so that we may be purged from sin, but will not confess that even our willing to be purged is wrought in us by the Holy Spirit's operation and infusion, he resists the Apostle; and canon 6: if anyone subjoins the help of grace to human humility and obedience, and so on, he resists the Apostle. I leave the rest.

source_text: Exponant nobis quomodo Deus non dicatur expectare voluntatem humanam, & obedientiae naturalis legis in cordibus hominum scriptae subjungere gratiae supernaturalis adjutorium, si posita Christi morte secundum hunc agendi modum Deus gratiam indat omnibus, si donis naturalibus recte utantur, non indat, si non utantur. Cum ergo haec omnia sint a veritate alienissima, restat ut dicamus Deum, non obstante merito mortis Christi, gratiam applicandi hoc meritum dare, vel negare posse, & solere singularibus hominibus, pro beneplacito & libertate voluntatis suae, non pro meritis aut operationibus diversis voluntatum humanarum.
english: Let them explain how God is not said to wait for the human will, and to hang the help of supernatural grace on obedience to the natural law written in human hearts, if—Christ's death once granted—God on this way of acting gives grace to all who use natural gifts rightly, and withholds it from those who do not. Since all of that is utterly foreign to the truth, it remains to say that God, the merit of Christ's death notwithstanding, can give or deny the grace of applying that merit, and ordinarily does so to particular persons by the good pleasure and freedom of his will—not by merits, or by the different operations of human wills.
